Lord Lytton (Viceroy 1876–80) implemented a Free Trade-orthodox policy: grain exports to Britain continued (record wheat exports of 6.4 million quarters in 1877–78); famine relief through the Anti-Charitable Contributions Act suppressed private relief efforts; the test-work principle (relief only to those performing hard labour at survival-floor wages) excluded the elderly and dependents. The Madras Government's relief commissioner Richard Temple set the Madras-Lyttonian ration at 16 ounces of grain per day (~1,600 kcal) for a labouring man. The famine triggered the Indian Famine Commission (1878–80) under Sir Richard Strachey, whose Report (1880) produced the Indian Famine Codes — provincial relief manuals that, however imperfectly, institutionalised the principle of state responsibility for famine relief. Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts (2000) frames the 1876–78 famine as a colonial-policy choice rather than a natural disaster; the framing is the standard scholarly position.

sources.label: Mike Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts: El Niño Famines and the Making of the Third World (2001)
Indian Famine Commission Report (1880; Richard Strachey)
William Digby, The Famine Campaign in Southern India 1876–78 (1878)

events.title: Indian Famine of 1899–1900
events.tooltip: Indian Famine 1899–1900 — ~1 million dead under Lord Curzon
events.summary: Drought across Central Provinces, Berar, Bombay, Hyderabad. Curzon applied the Famine Codes — mortality lower than 1876–78 but still ~1 million.
events.detail: The 1899–1900 famine followed the 1899 monsoon failure across an arc from the Punjab through Rajputana, the Central Provinces, Berar, and Bombay (the most affected). The areas covered overlapped substantially with the 1896–97 famine, leaving cultivator and pastoralist populations doubly hit. Mortality estimates: 1 million (cautious) to 4.5 million (Mike Davis, including the 1896–97 episode). Lord Curzon (Viceroy 1899–1905) ordered relief operations under the post-1880 Famine Codes — at peak ~6.5 million on relief works in summer 1900 — but the relief ration remained at the Lyttonian standard and exclusionary. Plague was the second-order killer: the bubonic plague pandemic that had reached Bombay 1896 spread through the famine-weakened population; the plague-and-famine combined mortality in Berar alone reached an estimated half-million. The famine prompted the second Famine Commission (1901, Sir Anthony MacDonnell) — the codes were tightened, but the underlying question of grain exports during famine remained unaddressed. The 1899–1900 famine was the last of the catastrophic late-Victorian famines; the next episode, Bengal 1943, would have a different proximate cause.

sources.label: Indian Famine Commission Report (1901; Anthony MacDonnell)
Romesh Chunder Dutt, Open Letters to Lord Curzon (1900)
Mike Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts (2001)

events.title: Bengal Famine 1943
events.tooltip: Bengal Famine 1943 — ~3 million dead; wartime rice diversion under Linlithgow
events.summary: Wartime rice diversion, denial policy, cyclone-damaged crop, Churchill's refusal of Australian wheat shipments. ~3 million dead in eastern Bengal.
events.detail: The Bengal famine of 1943 — third of the post-1857 catastrophic famines — killed an estimated 2.1–3 million in rural eastern Bengal. The proximate causes were three: (i) the October 1942 Midnapore cyclone destroyed the winter rice crop; (ii) the Burma fall (March 1942) cut off rice imports from Burma which had supplied 15% of Bengal's normal consumption; (iii) the Denial Policy — the British wartime removal of boats and stockpiled rice from coastal Bengal to prevent their use by an anticipated Japanese invasion — eliminated transport and reserves. The famine deepened through summer 1943; mortality peaked September–October 1943 in Midnapore, Tipperah, Noakhali, Bakharganj. Churchill's War Cabinet refused multiple shipping requests for Australian and North American wheat (correspondence: 'starvation of anyhow underfed Bengalis is less serious than that of sturdy Greeks'); famine mortality continued into 1944. Wavell (Viceroy from October 1943) unilaterally diverted Army troop-rations to relief and broke the back of the mortality. Amartya Sen's Poverty and Famines (1981) — drawing principally on the 1943 Bengal famine — argued famines under colonialism were policy-of-distribution failures, not absolute-shortage failures; the entitlements framework that resulted reshaped famine economics. The Famine Inquiry Commission Report (1945; Sir John Woodhead) acknowledged administrative failure but stopped short of attributing the famine to British policy.

sources.label: Madhusree Mukerjee, Churchill's Secret War: The British Empire and the Ravaging of India during World War II (2010)
Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation (1981)
Famine Inquiry Commission Report on Bengal (1945; Sir John Woodhead)

events.title: Tughluq Doab Famine
events.tooltip: Doab famine under Muhammad bin Tughluq, c. 1335–1342
events.summary: Seven-year famine across the Ganges-Yamuna doab under Muhammad bin Tughluq — drought compounded by punitive revenue and the Daulatabad capital transfer.
events.detail: The Doab famine of c. 1335–42 was the most prolonged Delhi Sultanate famine documented. Three causes converged: (i) consecutive monsoon failures across the Ganges-Yamuna doab through the mid-1330s; (ii) Muhammad bin Tughluq's punitive revenue increases in the doab to fund his Khurasan and Qarachil campaigns — chroniclers (Ziauddin Barani, Ibn Battuta) describe peasants abandoning villages and fleeing into forests to escape collection; (iii) the 1327 capital transfer from Delhi to Daulatabad and its 1335 partial reversal had drained Delhi of population and economic activity. Tughluq established a famine relief program (the takkavi loans, the Diwan-i-Kohi agricultural department), but the relief came too late and was poorly administered. Mortality figures are not contemporaneously recorded — Ibn Battuta wrote of villages 'so depopulated that the very memory of cultivation was lost'. Population estimates suggest the Delhi region alone lost 30–40% of its inhabitants over the famine years. The famine is the canonical example in early Indo-Persian historiography of revenue policy and famine mortality interacting destructively — the same diagnostic frame Edmund Burke would deploy for the 1770 Bengal famine four centuries later.

sources.label: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi (c. 1357)
Ibn Battuta, Rihla (1355)
Irfan Habib, Economic History of Medieval India 1200–1500 (2011)

events.title: Deccan–Gujarat Famine under Shah Jahan
events.tooltip: Deccan and Gujarat famine, 1630–1632 — ~7.4 million dead in Gujarat alone
events.summary: Two-year drought across Gujarat, Khandesh, and the Ahmednagar Deccan — ~7.4 million dead in Gujarat alone per contemporary Mughal and Dutch accounts.
events.detail: The 1630–32 famine across western India was among the deadliest documented pre-colonial Indian famines. Two consecutive monsoon failures (1630, 1631) hit Gujarat, Khandesh, and the Ahmednagar Deccan; the Mughal Deccan campaign (Shah Jahan's army was in active operation against Ahmednagar through 1630–31) exacerbated grain shortage by army requisitioning. The Mughal court chronicler Abdul Hamid Lahori (Padshahnama) and the Dutch VOC factor at Surat Pieter van den Broecke recorded mortality at scale: van den Broecke's Hof estimate put Gujarat deaths at ~3 million; Lahori at ~7.4 million; modern demographers (Habib, Moosvi) treat the Mughal figure as an upper bound on the order of 5 million. English East India Company traveller Peter Mundy's diary of his 1630 Gujarat journey describes carcasses on the highway every few miles, mass-grave plague, and cannibalism. Shah Jahan's relief operations — sadqa distribution at Ahmedabad, tax remission, 5,000 rupee per day langar at Burhanpur — were substantial by Mughal standards but inadequate to the scale. The famine is the case Mughal-era historians cite as evidence that famine mortality on this scale was structural to the subcontinent's monsoon-dependent agriculture, not a colonial novelty.

sources.label: Abdul Hamid Lahori, Padshahnama (c. 1648)
Peter Mundy, The Travels of Peter Mundy in Europe and Asia 1608–1667 (Hakluyt Society 1907)
Shireen Moosvi, Economy of the Mughal Empire c. 1595 (1987)

events.title: Chalisa Famine
events.tooltip: Chalisa Famine, 1783–84 — ~11 million dead across northern India
events.summary: Drought across Delhi, Awadh, Rohilkhand, eastern Punjab — ~11 million dead. Named for VS 1840 ('chalisa' = forty); coincided with late-Mughal collapse.
events.detail: The Chalisa famine — named for the Vikram Samvat year 1840 (1783–84 CE), 'chalisa' meaning 'forty' — was the deadliest northern-Indian famine of the eighteenth century. Drought across Delhi, the Doab, Awadh, Rohilkhand, eastern Punjab, and parts of Rajputana followed two consecutive monsoon failures. Mortality estimates: ~11 million across the affected regions (William Crooke's 1894 estimate, broadly accepted). The famine struck during the period of Mughal collapse and post-Panipat 1761 political reordering: Shah Alam II at Delhi was politically powerless; the Marathas under Mahadji Scindia held the central Doab; Awadh under Asaf-ud-Daulah ran an autonomous administration; the EIC was consolidating Bengal but had not yet assumed responsibility for upper India. There was no central authority capable of organised relief. Asaf-ud-Daulah's Bara Imambara at Lucknow — the colossal arched hall built 1784 — was constructed as a famine-relief project employing thousands of cultivator-refugees on a make-work basis through the famine years; its scale is the single physical monument to the Chalisa. The famine ran into the Doji bara famine of 1791–92 less than a decade later — back-to-back catastrophic mortality events that hollowed out late-Mughal demography.

sources.label: William Crooke, The Tribes and Castes of the North-Western Provinces and Oudh (1896)
C.A. Bayly, Rulers, Townsmen and Bazaars 1770–1870 (1983)

events.title: Doji Bara ('Skull') Famine
events.tooltip: Doji Bara Famine, 1791–92 — ~11 million dead across south and central India
events.summary: Drought across Madras, Hyderabad, Maratha Deccan, Gujarat — ~11 million dead. Named 'skull famine' because the dead were too many to bury for years.
events.detail: The Doji bara famine of 1791–92 — 'doji bara' is the Marathi term for the Vikram Samvat year of mortality, with 'skull famine' the colloquial English rendering — was the deadliest single-year famine on the eighteenth-century subcontinent. The 1789–90 El Niño produced consecutive monsoon failures across south India, the Hyderabad Nizam's territories, the Maratha Deccan, Gujarat, and parts of Madras; secondary mortality from cholera and dysentery ran through 1792–93. Mortality estimates: ~11 million across the affected regions (Cornelius Walford's 1879 estimate). The famine struck during the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92) — Cornwallis's combined EIC, Maratha, Nizam coalition campaigns against Tipu Sultan disrupted Deccan grain markets and removed cultivators to military service. The 'skull' name referred to the bones that lay unburied across affected regions for years; the EIC's official report on the famine described carriage roads through Hyderabad and Mysore where 'human bones were so numerous that the wheels and feet ground them to powder for weeks'. Tipu Sultan's Mysore administration ran a relief grain-loan programme through 1791–92; the Hyderabad Nizam's relief was minimal. Together with the 1783–84 Chalisa, the Doji bara represents one of the worst back-to-back demographic catastrophes in subcontinental history — preceding the 1857 rebellion's political dislocations by a generation.
figures: Nizam Ali Khan Asaf Jah II

sources.label: Cornelius Walford, The Famines of the World: Past and Present (1879)
Bombay Government, Selections from the Records: Famine Report (1865 ed.)
Mike Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts (2001), background chapter on pre-colonial famines

events.title: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire
events.tooltip: Chandragupta I crowned at Pataliputra, c. 320 CE; founds the Gupta Empire
events.summary: Chandragupta I, marrying the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi, consolidated Magadha and founded the Guptas — the second subcontinental imperial state.
events.detail: Chandragupta I (no relation to the Mauryan Chandragupta of six centuries earlier) consolidated power in Magadha around 320 CE and was crowned Maharajadhiraja ('great king of kings') at Pataliputra. His marriage to Kumaradevi of the Lichchhavi clan — celebrated on the empire's gold coinage — gave him a political-territorial alliance that anchored the new dynasty. The Guptas inherited an India fragmented since the Mauryan collapse five centuries earlier into Saka, Kushan, Satavahana, and Kshatrapa polities; Chandragupta I and his successors progressively reabsorbed the heartland into a single imperial framework. The Gupta period (320–550 CE) is conventionally read as Indian classical antiquity's high point: Sanskrit drama (Kalidasa), Sanskrit lyric (Bhartrihari), mathematics (Aryabhata's invention of the place-value zero), astronomy (Varahamihira), the Vishnu temple architectural canon, the iconographic types that became standard for Hindu sculpture, the Kamasutra and the Manusmriti's final redaction.

sources.label: Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Samudragupta (4th c. CE; D.R. Bhandarkar, Inscriptions of the Early Gupta Kings, 1981)
Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India (2002), ch. 9
Hermann Kulke & Dietmar Rothermund, A History of India (4th ed., 2004), ch. 4

events.title: Samudragupta's conquests and the Allahabad prashasti
events.tooltip: Samudragupta's conquests, c. 335–375 CE; Allahabad pillar prashasti
events.summary: Samudragupta's conquests reached from the Hindu Kush to Sri Lanka — recorded in the Allahabad Pillar prashasti by his court poet Harisena.
events.detail: Samudragupta (r. c. 335–375 CE) extended Gupta authority across most of north India and tributary into the Deccan and the south. The Allahabad Pillar prashasti — composed by his court poet Harisena and inscribed on the same pillar that two centuries earlier had carried Ashoka's edicts — is the most ambitious imperial-inscription corpus from ancient India after the Ashokan edicts. It records Samudragupta uprooting nine north Indian kings, defeating eleven southern and Deccan rulers and reinstalling them as tributaries (graha-mokṣa, 'capture and release'), and receiving tribute from frontier states (Saka satrapies, Kushan successors) and overseas kingdoms including Sri Lanka. He is also credited with performing the Vedic horse-sacrifice (ashvamedha), revived from Mauryan-era disuse, and minting the gold coinage that includes a famous lyrist-king type showing him playing the veena. The empire he built is the territorial frame his son Chandragupta II would administer at peak.

caused_by.gloss: Chandragupta I's Magadha-Lichchhavi consolidation gave Samudragupta the institutional and military base for the conquests; the prashasti is explicit that Samudragupta inherits and extends the imperial project his father founded.

sources.label: Harisena, Allahabad Pillar Prashasti (4th c. CE; D.R. Bhandarkar, Inscriptions of the Early Gupta Kings, 1981)
Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India (2002), ch. 9

events.title: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya and the Iron Pillar
events.tooltip: Chandragupta II rules at Gupta peak, c. 380–415 CE; Iron Pillar erected
events.summary: Chandragupta II's reign was the Gupta cultural and territorial peak — Saka satrapies annexed, Faxian visits, the Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscribed.
events.detail: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (r. c. 380–415 CE) ruled the Gupta empire at its peak. He completed Samudragupta's project by annexing the Western Kshatrapa Saka satrapies (c. 388–409 CE), bringing the Gujarat-Malwa coast and the Indian Ocean trade ports under direct Gupta control. The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian (Fa-Hsien) travelled through the empire 405–411 CE en route to Sri Lanka and recorded an admiring account: cities prosperous, courts orderly, Buddhist monasteries flourishing, tax burden moderate. Chandragupta II's court at Ujjain (his second capital, retained as a winter seat) is traditionally credited with the navaratna ('nine jewels') of Sanskrit literature, including Kalidasa (poet-dramatist of Abhijnanasakuntalam), Varahamihira (astronomer), and Dhanvantari (medicine) — though most of these attributions are later legend. The Mehrauli Iron Pillar at Delhi, originally erected at Udayagiri and bearing a Sanskrit eulogy of a 'Chandra' identified with Chandragupta II, has stood without significant rusting for 1,600 years — an unsolved metallurgical puzzle.

location.name: Ujjain (winter capital; Iron Pillar at Mehrauli, Delhi)

caused_by.gloss: Samudragupta's tributary system was the territorial frame Chandragupta II inherited; the Saka annexation was the single major outstanding imperial extension Samudragupta had not completed.

sources.label: Faxian, A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms (5th c. CE; James Legge trans., 1886)
Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription (D.R. Bhandarkar, Inscriptions of the Early Gupta Kings, 1981)
S.R. Goyal, A History of the Imperial Guptas (1967)

events.title: Skandagupta defeats the Huna invasion
events.tooltip: Skandagupta defeats the Hephthalite Hunas at the northwest, c. 460 CE
events.summary: Skandagupta's repulse of the Hephthalite Huns delayed Gupta collapse — but Hun pressure and the cost of defence broke the empire within decades.
events.detail: The Hephthalite Huns (Huna in Sanskrit) — a Central Asian steppe confederation that had also broken into the Eastern Roman and Sasanian frontiers — pushed across the Hindu Kush passes from the 450s CE. Skandagupta (r. c. 455–467 CE), the last great Gupta emperor, repulsed the first major Huna invasion in c. 460 — recorded in the Bhitari and Junagadh inscriptions which credit him with the victory. The defence preserved the Gupta heartland through the 460s but exhausted the imperial treasury (the Junagadh inscription records the rebuilding of the Sudarshana lake breached by the Huna campaign). After Skandagupta's death the Hunas returned in greater force under Toramana and his son Mihirakula (early 6th c.), occupying Punjab and Malwa; the Gupta administrative apparatus collapsed by c. 550 CE. Yashodharman of Malwa is credited with finally defeating Mihirakula c. 528 CE — but the Gupta unified state did not recover. The post-Gupta political fragmentation of north India lasted over six and a half centuries until the Delhi Sultanate.

location.name: Junagadh (Sudarshana lake site; major Skandagupta inscription)

caused_by.gloss: The peak under Chandragupta II positioned the Guptas to mount the defence Skandagupta executed; the cost of repulse and the cumulative weakness from the Saka campaigns combined into the post-Skandagupta collapse.

sources.label: Skandagupta's Bhitari and Junagadh inscriptions (5th c. CE; D.R. Bhandarkar, Inscriptions of the Early Gupta Kings, 1981)
S.R. Goyal, A History of the Imperial Guptas (1967)

events.title: Indian National Congress founded
events.tooltip: Indian National Congress founded, 1885
events.summary: 72 delegates met at Bombay to launch the Indian National Congress, an early forum for educated Indian opinion within the imperial framework.
events.detail: The first session was convened by Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant, with W.C. Bonnerjee as president. Membership was overwhelmingly upper-caste, English-educated, and professional. The early Congress was avowedly loyalist — its demands were for greater Indian representation in the civil service and legislative councils, not independence. The radicalisation came later, accelerated by Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905) and the failure of moderate constitutionalism. By the 1920s the body that began as a debating society had become the political vehicle of a mass movement.

sources.label: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989)

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.tooltip: Curzon partitions Bengal, 1905
events.summary: Curzon's split of Bengal into Hindu-majority west and Muslim-majority east galvanised the first mass agitation in colonial India.
events.detail: Lord Curzon argued the partition was an administrative measure for a province too large to govern. Indian opinion read it as a deliberate communal wedge. The Swadeshi movement that followed — boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian-made cloth, mass meetings in Calcutta — was the first agitation that successfully linked elite politics to street mobilisation. The partition was annulled in 1911 under King George V's Delhi Durbar, but the political memory remained. Bengal would be partitioned again in 1947, on lines roughly tracing Curzon's.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983)

events.title: Lajpat Rai writes The Story of My Deportation
events.tooltip: Lajpat Rai deported to Mandalay; writes account, 1907–1908
events.summary: Detained without trial under Regulation III, Lajpat Rai spent six months in Mandalay then published the first prison-writing of the Indian freedom movement.
events.detail: Lala Lajpat Rai was arrested in Lahore on 9 May 1907 under Regulation III of 1818 — the colonial law permitting indefinite detention without trial — for his agitation against the Punjab Colonization Bill and his role in the Swadeshi mobilisation. He was deported to Mandalay, Burma, and held in solitary confinement for six months before release on 11 November 1907 after a campaign by Indian nationalist opinion and Liberal MPs in the British Parliament. On return he wrote The Story of My Deportation, published Lahore 1908 — a 200-page first-person account of the arrest, the sea voyage, the Mandalay confinement, and the political reading he had carried with him. It is the earliest published prison-writing of the Indian freedom movement; the genre that would carry through Aurobindo, Gandhi at Yerwada, Bhagat Singh's notebooks, and Nehru's Discovery of India begins here.

caused_by.gloss: The Swadeshi mobilisation triggered by Curzon's Bengal partition spread to Punjab via Lajpat Rai's anti-Colonization-Bill agitation; the deportation was the colonial state's preferred response.

sources.label: Lala Lajpat Rai, The Story of My Deportation (Lahore: Punjabee Press, 1908)
V.C. Joshi (ed.), Lala Lajpat Rai: Writings and Speeches (2 vols., 1966)
Vijay Chandra Joshi, Lajpat Rai: Life and Work (1973)

events.title: Champaran Satyagraha
events.tooltip: Gandhi's first Indian satyagraha — Champaran indigo planters, 1917
events.summary: Champaran tenant Raj Kumar Shukla brought Gandhi to Bihar to investigate the indigo planter system; the resulting satyagraha was Gandhi's first inside India.
events.detail: The Champaran indigo system — 'tinkathia' — required ryots to plant 3 of every 20 katthas of their holding with indigo for European planters at fixed below-market prices, with debt bondage common. Raj Kumar Shukla, a Champaran tenant who had attended the 1916 Lucknow Congress session, persuaded Gandhi to visit. Gandhi reached Champaran on 10 April 1917, was served with an order to leave the district, refused, and was arrested. The case was withdrawn under public pressure; Gandhi conducted a six-month inquiry collecting testimony from approximately 8,000 ryots. The Champaran Agrarian Committee Report (October 1917) recommended abolition of tinkathia and partial restitution of overcharged rents. The Champaran Agrarian Act (1918) implemented the reforms. Champaran is the satyagraha that established Gandhi as a national figure inside India — the prior reputation was South African; this was the first Indian application of the same method.

sources.label: Rajendra Prasad, Champaran (1928, autobiographical account in Gujarati; Eng. trans. 1949)
Jacques Pouchepadass, Champaran and Gandhi: Planters, Peasants and Gandhian Politics (1999)

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
events.tooltip: Jallianwala Bagh massacre, Amritsar, 1919
events.summary: British troops under Brigadier-General Dyer fired without warning into a crowd of 15–20,000 gathered at an enclosed garden in Amritsar on Baisakhi.
events.detail: The Defence of India Act gave Punjab's Lt. Governor O'Dwyer wide powers, including bans on public assembly. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer reached Amritsar on 11 April 1919. Two days later, on the festival of Baisakhi, a crowd had gathered in Jallianwala Bagh — an enclosed garden with a single narrow exit. Dyer marched in 50 riflemen, blocked the exit, and ordered fire without warning. Shooting continued for about ten minutes until ammunition was exhausted. Official British figures recorded 379 dead; the Congress inquiry put the toll above 1,000. The Hunter Commission later condemned Dyer's conduct, but Parliament voted him a public pension. The massacre converted constitutional moderates into nationalists nearly overnight.

sources.label: Kim A. Wagner, Jallianwala Bagh: An Empire of Fear and the Making of the Amritsar Massacre (2019)

events.title: Non-Cooperation Movement
events.tooltip: Non-Cooperation Movement, 1920–22
events.summary: Gandhi's first nationwide campaign — a boycott of British titles, courts, schools, and goods, joined to the Khilafat movement.
events.detail: Launched at the Calcutta Special Session of Congress in September 1920 and ratified at Nagpur in December, the Non-Cooperation Movement called for the surrender of British honours, withdrawal from government schools and courts, and a boycott of foreign cloth. By late 1921 it had reached scales no earlier campaign had: tens of thousands of students out of school, a near-total boycott of legislative elections, the Khilafat alliance giving it Hindu–Muslim breadth. Then, in February 1922, news arrived from Chauri Chaura. Gandhi suspended the movement within five days, against the wishes of nearly every senior Congress leader. He was arrested in March and sentenced to six years.

caused_by.gloss: The massacre and the Hunter Commission whitewash converted Gandhi from a constitutional cooperator into the architect of mass non-cooperation. He returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal in protest.

sources.label: Judith M. Brown, Gandhi's Rise to Power: Indian Politics 1915–1922 (1972)

events.title: Chauri Chaura incident
events.tooltip: Chauri Chaura incident, 1922
events.summary: A procession in eastern UP killed 22 police and burned their station. Gandhi suspended the entire Non-Cooperation Movement within five days.
events.detail: On 4 February 1922, in a small market town in eastern United Provinces, a Khilafat–Non-Cooperation procession passed the Chauri Chaura police station. Police taunted the marchers, then opened fire when they refused to disperse, killing three. The crowd surged back, set fire to the station, and killed 22 policemen — most cut down as they fled the burning building. Gandhi received the news at Bardoli, where he was about to launch a no-tax campaign. Within five days he had unilaterally suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement, citing the violation of non-violence. Most Congress leaders disagreed publicly. Subhas Bose later called the suspension a 'national calamity.' Gandhi spent the next six years out of mass politics.

sources.label: Shahid Amin, Event, Metaphor, Memory: Chauri Chaura 1922–1992 (1995)

events.title: Gandhi writes The Story of My Experiments with Truth
events.tooltip: Gandhi writes Atmakatha at Sabarmati and Yerwada, 1925–1929
events.summary: Begun at Sabarmati after Chauri Chaura, Gandhi's Gujarati autobiography frames every choice — diet, household, satyagraha — as a moral experiment.
events.detail: Gandhi began the Atmakatha (autobiography) in Gujarati on 29 November 1925, serialised week by week in his journal Navjivan, with Mahadev Desai's English translation appearing simultaneously in Young India. Published in book form as Satyana Prayogo athva Atmakatha — Volume I in 1927, Volume II in 1929. Covers childhood at Porbandar, the years in England studying law, two decades in South Africa, return to India in 1915, and the satyagraha campaigns up to 1921 — deliberately stopping before the Chauri Chaura suspension. The 'experiments' framing is the book's signature move: every decision (vegetarianism, brahmacharya, the spinning wheel, household money) is offered as a test in moral physics. Reads less as memoir than as Augustinian self-examination transposed to a colonial-era reformer. Among the most translated Indian books of the 20th century.

caused_by.gloss: The post-Chauri-Chaura pause in mass action freed Gandhi for the long autobiographical work that he had previously deferred; the book starts in 1925 because the movement isn't running.

links.label: Wikipedia: The Story of My Experiments with Truth

sources.label: M.K. Gandhi, An Autobiography or The Story of My Experiments with Truth (trans. Mahadev Desai; Navajivan, 1927–1929)
Ramachandra Guha, Gandhi Before India (2013) and Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World (2018)
Tridip Suhrud, 'Gandhi's Key Writings: In Search of Unity', in The Cambridge Companion to Gandhi (2011)

events.title: Selected Letters of Sarojini Naidu
events.tooltip: Sarojini Naidu's letters, Congress presidency to UP governorship, 1925–1947
events.summary: Letters from Sarojini Naidu's Congress presidency (1925) through her UP governorship (1947) — the woman in the inner circle of Indian leadership.
events.detail: Sarojini Naidu's collected correspondence — published in volumes from 1925 onward, expanded posthumously by her daughter Padmaja Naidu — is the most complete record of a woman in the inner circle of Indian political leadership across two decades. Letters to Gandhi (whom she nicknamed 'Mickey Mouse'), Nehru, Tagore, Edmund Gosse (her early literary mentor at Cambridge), Edwin Lutyens, Sir Akbar Hydari, and her own family at Hyderabad. Covers her Congress presidency (Kanpur 1925, the first Indian woman to hold the post), her command of the salt campaigns at Dharasana when Gandhi was arrested, the 1931 Round Table negotiations in London, the Quit India arrest and Aga Khan Palace detention, and her post-Independence governorship of the United Provinces (1947–49). Distinct from her better-known poetry — the letters reveal the political negotiator, the satyagraha logistician, the salon hostess of nationalist Hyderabad.

location.name: Hyderabad (home base; campaigns spanned the subcontinent)

sources.label: Makarand Paranjape (ed.), Sarojini Naidu: Selected Letters, 1890s to 1940s (Kali for Women, 1996)
Padmini Sengupta, Sarojini Naidu: A Biography (1966)
Tara Ali Baig, Sarojini Naidu: Portrait of a Patriot (1974)

events.title: Simon Commission protest, Lahore
events.tooltip: Simon Commission protest at Lahore, 1928
events.summary: An all-white commission on Indian constitutional reform was met with 'Simon Go Back' protests; Lala Lajpat Rai died of injuries from the Lahore demonstration.
events.detail: The Simon Commission, appointed in November 1927, contained no Indian members. Congress and the Muslim League both boycotted it. When the Commission reached Lahore on 30 October 1928, Lala Lajpat Rai led a demonstration that was charged by police; Rai was severely beaten and died on 17 November of injuries his physicians attributed to the assault. His death radicalised the next generation, including Bhagat Singh, who avenged him by shooting the British police officer J.P. Saunders in December 1928. The Commission's report, when finally published in 1930, was overtaken by events.

sources.label: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989), ch. 21

events.title: Lahore Session — Purna Swaraj declaration
events.tooltip: Lahore Session: Purna Swaraj, 1929
events.summary: The Lahore Congress declared 'complete independence' (Purna Swaraj) as its goal and authorised civil disobedience.
events.detail: Until 1929 Congress's official aim was Dominion status within the British Empire. The Lahore Session, with Jawaharlal Nehru as president, broke with that. The Purna Swaraj resolution committed Congress to complete independence and authorised the working committee to launch civil disobedience. At the stroke of midnight on 31 December 1929, on the banks of the Ravi, the tricolour was unfurled. 26 January 1930 was declared the first Independence Day; the date was kept as Republic Day after 1950. The session also gave Gandhi the authority that he would exercise three months later at Dandi.

caused_by.gloss: The Simon boycott and Lajpat Rai's death persuaded Congress that the constitutional path was closed; Nehru and Bose pushed the dominion-status majority into the Purna Swaraj position.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983), ch. 6

events.title: Salt March (Dandi March)
events.tooltip: Salt March to Dandi, 1930
events.summary: Gandhi's 24-day march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to break the British salt monopoly — the opening act of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
events.detail: On 12 March 1930 Gandhi and 78 hand-picked satyagrahis left Sabarmati Ashram for the coastal village of Dandi, 240 miles south. The march was deliberately slow — about 12 miles a day — to maximise press coverage and to recruit walkers from villages along the route. By the time they reached Dandi on 5 April, Gandhi led several thousand. On the morning of 6 April he stooped and picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking a tax law punishable by jail. The act triggered nationwide salt-making, mass arrests of perhaps 60,000 people, and the wider Civil Disobedience Movement. The discipline and theatre of the march — meticulous, slow, photographed daily — were Gandhi's answer to the chaos of Chauri Chaura eight years earlier.

caused_by.gloss: The Purna Swaraj resolution authorised civil disobedience and handed Gandhi the timing of its launch. He spent the next ten weeks selecting the salt tax as the symbolic target.

sources.label: Thomas Weber, On the Salt March: The Historiography of Gandhi's March to Dandi (1997)

events.title: Civil Disobedience Movement
events.tooltip: Civil Disobedience Movement, 1930–34
events.summary: Mass picketing of liquor and foreign-cloth shops, no-tax campaigns, and salt rush. Paused by the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, exhausted by 1934.
events.detail: The Salt March opened a wave of disobedience that took different shapes in different regions: mass picketing of liquor shops in Bombay and Madras, no-tax campaigns in Gujarat (Bardoli, Kheda) and the United Provinces, the Pathan Khudai Khidmatgars in the North-West Frontier, the salt rush on the Bengal and Madras coasts. The Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 paused the movement; the Second Round Table Conference in London failed; the movement was revived in January 1932 and then ground down by mass arrests. Its political achievement was forcing Britain to legislate provincial autonomy in the Government of India Act 1935 — which fell well short of dominion status, but committed Whitehall to constitutional incrementalism it could not retreat from.

caused_by.gloss: The Salt March was both the opening act of the movement and its template — one symbolic, photographed act of law-breaking, replicated by millions.

sources.label: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989), ch. 23–24

events.title: Round Table Conferences
events.tooltip: Three Round Table Conferences in London, 1930–1932; Gandhi attends the second
events.summary: Three London conferences on Indian constitutional reform — Congress boycotted the first; Gandhi attended the second alone; the third seeded the 1935 Act.
events.detail: The British government convened three Round Table Conferences at St James's Palace, London, between November 1930 and December 1932 — the principal pre-1935 negotiation forum on Indian constitutional reform. The first (12 November 1930 – 19 January 1931) was boycotted by the Congress, then in jail under the Civil Disobedience Movement; it produced the federal-structure-with-princely-states framework but no Congress assent. The second (7 September – 1 December 1931) was attended by Gandhi alone for the Congress, after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) had suspended civil disobedience. Gandhi's insistence that Congress alone represented all Indians collided with separate-electorates demands from B.R. Ambedkar (for the Depressed Classes), the Muslim League, the Sikhs, and other interests; the conference deadlocked. The third (17 November – 24 December 1932) was attended by neither Congress nor most major Indian parties; it produced the constitutional framework that became the Government of India Act 1935 — the legal template the independent Indian Republic largely inherited in 1950.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983), ch. 6
Judith M. Brown, Gandhi: Prisoner of Hope (1989), ch. 7

events.title: Execution of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev
events.tooltip: Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev hanged at Lahore Central Jail, 23 March 1931
events.summary: Bhagat Singh, Shivaram Rajguru, Sukhdev Thapar hanged at Lahore Central Jail under the Lahore Conspiracy Case verdict — eleven hours before announced time.
events.detail: Bhagat Singh (23), Shivaram Rajguru (22), and Sukhdev Thapar (23), Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) revolutionaries, were hanged at Lahore Central Jail on 23 March 1931 — eleven hours before the announced 6:00 AM execution time, to forestall public protests outside the jail. They had been convicted in the Lahore Conspiracy Case for the December 1928 killing of John Saunders, a Lahore police assistant superintendent (mistaken for the senior officer responsible for the lathi-charge that killed Lala Lajpat Rai weeks earlier), and for the April 1929 Bhagat-Singh-and-Batukeshwar-Dutt bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi (a deliberately non-lethal protest, leaflets reading 'it takes a loud noise to make the deaf hear'). The trial — held in absentia for portions when the defendants refused to participate — became a major political event; Gandhi failed to secure clemency in his Round Table negotiation with Lord Irwin. The bodies were cremated secretly at Hussainiwala on the Sutlej; Bhagat Singh has the distinction of being among the most-cited Indian revolutionaries across ideologically opposed political traditions in the post-1947 period.

caused_by.gloss: The Simon protest produced the lathi-charge that killed Lajpat Rai; the HSRA's revenge-killing of Saunders in December 1928 was the proximate act for which Bhagat Singh and Rajguru were tried, alongside the Assembly bombing.

sources.label: A.G. Noorani, The Trial of Bhagat Singh: Politics of Justice (1996; rev. 2005)
Chaman Lal (ed.), Bhagat Singh: The Jail Notebook and Other Writings (2007)

events.title: Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar
events.tooltip: Gandhi-Ambedkar Poona Pact, 24 September 1932; ends Gandhi's Yerwada fast
events.summary: Gandhi's six-day Yerwada fast against the Communal Award ended with the Poona Pact — reserved seats in joint electorate replacing separate electorates.
events.detail: The British Communal Award (16 August 1932), announced by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald after the Round Table Conferences' deadlock, granted separate electorates to the Depressed Classes (Dalits) — separate from the Hindu electorate, with reserved constituencies in which only Dalits could vote. B.R. Ambedkar had argued for this as essential to political representation independent of the caste-Hindu elite. Gandhi, opposed on the principle that separate electorates would permanently divide the Hindu community, began a fast unto death at Yerwada Jail (Pune) on 20 September 1932. After six days of negotiation between Ambedkar and Hindu reformist intermediaries (Madan Mohan Malaviya, M.C. Rajah), the Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932: separate electorates were dropped in favour of joint electorates with substantially expanded reserved seats (148 for Depressed Classes in the provincial legislatures, against the Communal Award's 71). Ambedkar's later writings (notably What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables, 1945) read the Pact as a coerced settlement under fast pressure; the seat-reservation framework persists in the Indian constitution.

caused_by.gloss: The Round Table deadlock over separate electorates pushed MacDonald to impose the Communal Award unilaterally; Gandhi's fast and the resulting Poona Pact are the immediate political response to the Award.

sources.label: B.R. Ambedkar, What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (Thacker, 1945)
Eleanor Zelliot, From Untouchable to Dalit (1992), ch. 5
Christophe Jaffrelot, Dr Ambedkar and Untouchability (2005), ch. 3

events.title: Ambedkar publishes Annihilation of Caste
events.tooltip: Ambedkar self-publishes Annihilation of Caste, Bombay, 1936
events.summary: Withdrawn from a Lahore reform conference for being too radical, Ambedkar self-published the address as a 96-page polemic and answered Gandhi's review.
events.detail: Ambedkar drafted Annihilation of Caste in 1935–36 as the presidential address for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal's annual conference at Lahore, scheduled May 1936. The Mandal — a Hindu reform body — read the text and withdrew the invitation when Ambedkar refused to alter the passages arguing that caste could not be reformed within Hinduism and that Hindus seeking equality should leave the religion. Ambedkar self-published the undelivered address as a 96-page book in May 1936 from Bombay. Gandhi published a hostile review in Harijan; Ambedkar replied with the polemical preface to the second edition (1937), which is now read as integral to the work. Among the most directly argued first-person texts in the Indian canon — not memoir as such but argued autobiography of an intellectual position, with the author's own life-story embedded as evidence in the polemic. The book reframed the caste question for the 20th century.

date.display: May 1936 (1st ed.); 1937 (2nd ed. with preface to Gandhi)

sources.label: B.R. Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste (1936; annotated critical ed. S. Anand with introduction by Arundhati Roy, Navayana, 2014)
Christophe Jaffrelot, Dr Ambedkar and Untouchability: Analysing and Fighting Caste (2005)
Gail Omvedt, Ambedkar: Towards an Enlightened India (2004)

events.title: Subhas Chandra Bose writes The Indian Struggle
events.tooltip: Bose writes Indian Struggle in Vienna exile, 1934; pub. London 1935
events.summary: Deported from India after the 1932 arrests, Bose wrote a 400-page history of 1920–1934 in Vienna. Banned in India by the Raj on publication.
events.detail: Subhas Chandra Bose was deported to Europe in February 1933 after his second imprisonment under the Defence of India Rules. Through 1934, working from Vienna with secretarial help from Emilie Schenkl, he wrote The Indian Struggle 1920–1934 — a 400-page history of the Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, and Round Table phases from a Bengal-Forward-Bloc vantage that was systematically critical of Gandhi's tactical choices. Published by Wishart in London, January 1935; banned in British India on publication. The completing volume covering 1935–1942 was written between his 1941 escape from Calcutta house arrest and his death in 1945; published posthumously 1948. Together the two volumes are the fullest first-person record of the Congress left's reading of the freedom struggle, distinct from both the Gandhian and the Nehruvian accounts.

date.display: Written Vienna 1934; pub. London Jan 1935 (vol. 2 posthumous 1948)

location.name: Calcutta (Bose's political base; written in Vienna exile)

sources.label: Subhas Chandra Bose, The Indian Struggle 1920–1942 (combined ed., Asia Publishing House, 1964)
Sugata Bose, His Majesty's Opponent: Subhas Chandra Bose and India's Struggle Against Empire (2011), ch. 6
Leonard A. Gordon, Brothers Against the Raj: A Biography of Indian Nationalists Sarat and Subhas Chandra Bose (1990)

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.tooltip: Quit India launched at Bombay, 1942
events.summary: Gandhi's 'Do or die' demand for immediate British withdrawal. With its leadership arrested, the movement spiralled into the largest uprising of the struggle.
events.detail: On 8 August 1942, the All-India Congress Committee meeting at Bombay's Gowalia Tank Maidan passed the Quit India resolution. Gandhi gave the speech containing the line 'Do or die' and was arrested before dawn on 9 August along with the entire Congress working committee. With its leadership in jail, the movement spiralled out of central control. Crowds attacked railway stations, post offices, and police outposts across Bihar, the United Provinces, and Bengal. British retaliation included machine-gun fire from low-flying aircraft. By the year's end, over 60,000 had been arrested and roughly 1,000 killed. Quit India is often called the last mass movement of the freedom struggle — by the time the Congress leaders were released in 1945, the political question was no longer whether Britain would leave, only when and on what terms.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983), ch. 7
Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989), ch. 32

events.title: Nehru writes The Discovery of India
events.tooltip: Nehru drafts Discovery of India, Ahmednagar Fort, 1944–45
events.summary: Imprisoned after Quit India, Nehru wrote The Discovery of India between April 1944 and September 1945 — the third book of his prison trilogy, published 1946.
events.detail: Arrested on 9 August 1942 and held without trial, Nehru spent 1,041 days in Ahmednagar Fort with eleven other Congress leaders. Between April 1944 and September 1945 he drafted the 600-page Discovery of India in longhand, working through readings supplied by Maulana Azad and Pattabhi Sitaramayya among others. The book argues for an Indian civilisational continuity — Vedic, Buddhist, Mughal, modern — that could underwrite a secular republic, against both colonial 'no India before us' historiography and Hindu-nationalist communal essentialism. It was published in 1946 by Signet Press, Calcutta, completing his prison trilogy after Glimpses of World History (1934) and Toward Freedom (1936). The framing — composite, civilisational, secular — would become the founding ideology of the Indian state Nehru led from 1947.

caused_by.gloss: The Quit India arrests put Nehru and the entire Congress working committee in Ahmednagar Fort for nearly three years; Discovery of India is the most ambitious of the books that came out of that confinement.

sources.label: Jawaharlal Nehru, The Discovery of India (Signet Press, 1946)
Sarvepalli Gopal, Jawaharlal Nehru: A Biography, Vol. 1 (1975), ch. 18
Benjamin Zachariah, Nehru (Routledge, 2004), ch. 4

events.title: INA at Imphal–Kohima
events.tooltip: Battle of Imphal–Kohima, March–July 1944; Bose's INA + Japanese 15th Army
events.summary: Subhas Bose's Azad Hind Fauj fought with the Japanese 15th Army at Imphal–Kohima, March–July 1944 — the high water of the Burma campaign before defeat.
events.detail: Subhas Chandra Bose, having escaped Calcutta house arrest in January 1941 and reached Berlin then (via U-boat) Tokyo in 1943, took command of the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj — INA) on 4 July 1943 and proclaimed the Provisional Government of Azad Hind at Singapore on 21 October 1943. The INA, fighting alongside the Imperial Japanese Army's 15th Army under Lt-Gen Renya Mutaguchi, launched the U-Go operation in March 1944 — crossing the Chindwin and pushing into Manipur and the Naga Hills. The Battles of Imphal (8 March – 3 July 1944) and Kohima (4 April – 22 June 1944) were the campaign's twin peaks: Kohima's Tennis Court battle is among the most-cited British-Indian military engagements of WWII. The British 14th Army under General William Slim broke the Japanese-INA advance through superior logistics and air supply; an estimated 53,000 Japanese-INA casualties (mostly to disease and starvation in monsoon retreat) versus 16,500 Allied. The defeat ended Japanese hopes in the Burma theatre and the INA's military project; the 1945–46 INA trials at the Red Fort in Delhi (Shah Nawaz Khan, P.K. Sahgal, G.S. Dhillon) became a major nationalist political event in the run-up to independence.

caused_by.gloss: Bose's exile-political project documented in The Indian Struggle and continued at Berlin/Tokyo culminated in the INA campaign — Imphal–Kohima is the military extension of the political work the 1935 book frames.

sources.label: Sugata Bose, His Majesty's Opponent: Subhas Chandra Bose and India's Struggle Against Empire (2011)
Robert Lyman, Slim, Master of War (2004)
Joyce Lebra, The Indian National Army and Japan (1971; rev. 2008)

events.title: Direct Action Day, Calcutta
events.tooltip: Direct Action Day, Calcutta, 1946
events.summary: The Muslim League's call for 'direct action' triggered four days of communal killings in Calcutta. Roughly 4,000 dead. The case for a united India was broken.
events.detail: After the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan to keep India united, the Muslim League called for Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946. In Calcutta, the only major city with a League-led provincial government, the demonstration tipped into four days of communal violence — initiated by League cadres, met and exceeded by Hindu and Sikh crowds. Estimates put the dead between 4,000 and 10,000, with some 100,000 wounded or homeless. The 'Great Calcutta Killings' destroyed whatever residual belief existed in the political class that an undivided India could be governed; from there, partition was a question of when and how, not whether. The violence spread to Bihar (October), Noakhali (October–November), and the Punjab (March 1947) before culminating in the partition migrations.

sources.label: Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan (2007)

events.title: Independence and Partition
events.tooltip: Independence and Partition, 1947
events.summary: India and Pakistan became independent on 14–15 August 1947. The migrations and killings that followed were the largest population transfer in human history.
events.detail: India became independent at midnight on 14–15 August 1947; Pakistan a day earlier. The line dividing them — drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India — was published only on 17 August. The intervening uncertainty cost lives. An estimated 14 million people crossed in the largest migration in human history; between 200,000 and two million were killed in the violence that accompanied it, mostly in Punjab and Bengal. The structures of the new states were inherited largely intact — civil service, army, currency, parliamentary form — but the cost of the transfer of power was paid in the millions of lives uprooted along an arbitrary line. Nehru's 'tryst with destiny' speech to the Constituent Assembly, delivered hours before midnight, did not mention partition.

caused_by.gloss: Quit India settled the question of whether Britain would leave; what remained was when and on what terms.
The Calcutta killings destroyed the political consensus around a united India and made partition the path of least resistance for a departing power.

sources.label: Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition (2007)
Ramachandra Guha, India After Gandhi (2007), ch. 1–2

events.title: Maulana Azad dictates India Wins Freedom
events.tooltip: Azad's partition memoir, dictated Delhi 1957–58, suppressed pages opened 1988
events.summary: Azad dictated his partition memoir to Humayun Kabir 1957–58; the 30-page section critical of Nehru and Patel was sealed for 30 years.
events.detail: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad — Congress President 1939–46, India's first Education Minister, the senior Muslim Congress leader through partition — dictated his memoir India Wins Freedom to his secretary Humayun Kabir between 1957 and his death in February 1958. Published February 1959. Covers the 1937–47 decade in detail: the Cripps Mission (1942), Quit India and Azad's Ahmednagar Fort imprisonment with Nehru, the Cabinet Mission (1946), Mountbatten's June 1947 plan, Azad's opposition to partition. The book's most controversial section — 30 pages dealing critically with Nehru and Patel's roles in accepting partition — was withheld at Azad's instruction until 1988, thirty years after his death. When opened in 1988, the suppressed pages caused political controversy in India for their direct criticism of the Nehru-Patel partition decisions. The fullest first-person record of partition negotiations from a Congress Muslim's perspective, and a deliberate act of posthumous score-settling.

caused_by.gloss: Azad's memoir is the longest-form first-person reckoning with the partition decision; the suppressed pages indict the Nehru-Patel acquiescence in the Mountbatten plan.

sources.label: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, India Wins Freedom (Orient Longmans, 1959; complete edition with the suppressed pages, 1988)
Rajmohan Gandhi, Eight Lives: A Study of the Hindu-Muslim Encounter (1986), ch. on Azad
Ian Henderson Douglas, Abul Kalam Azad: An Intellectual and Religious Biography (1988)

events.title: Ryotwari Settlement of Madras
events.tooltip: Ryotwari Settlement of Madras Presidency under Thomas Munro, 1820
events.summary: Munro fixed Madras revenue directly with the cultivator (ryot) — no zamindari intermediary; periodic resettlement; rates at half to two-thirds of net produce.
events.detail: Sir Thomas Munro, Governor of Madras 1820–27, built on his Baramahal experiments of the 1790s and the Ceded Districts settlement of 1801–07 to systematise the Ryotwari principle across the Madras Presidency from 1820. Three distinguishing features: (i) The settlement was made directly with each ryot (peasant cultivator), recognising him as the proprietor of his holding — no zamindari intermediary. (ii) Revenue was assessed per field on a thirty-year cycle (later twenty), based on a survey of soil quality and net produce; the assessment was nominally one-half of net produce but ran to two-thirds in many districts. (iii) Defaulting cultivators forfeited the land to the state rather than to a zamindar. The system covered Madras Presidency (later, after 1835, Bombay Presidency under R.K. Pringle and Goldsmid) — about a third of British India. Distinct from Bengal Permanent Settlement: revenue was not fixed in perpetuity; the cultivator bore the assessment risk directly; small-holding rural society was preserved. Distinct from Mahalwari: the unit of assessment was the individual field, not the village. Munro's commitment to peasant proprietorship was ideological (the Scottish Enlightenment-influenced Madras school) as well as practical; the Ryotwari areas had higher per-acre revenue extraction than Permanent Settlement Bengal but more responsive crisis-relief at the cultivator level.

sources.label: Burton Stein, Thomas Munro: The Origins of the Colonial State and his Vision of Empire (1989)
Nilmani Mukherjee, The Ryotwari System in Madras 1792–1827 (1962)

events.title: Mahalwari Settlement of the North-Western Provinces
events.tooltip: Mahalwari Settlement under Holt Mackenzie's Regulation VII, 1822
events.summary: Holt Mackenzie's Regulation VII fixed revenue at the village (mahal) under joint co-sharer responsibility — third colonial land system, Doab to Punjab.
events.detail: Regulation VII of 1822, drafted by Holt Mackenzie as Secretary to the Board of Revenue, established the Mahalwari settlement principle for the North-Western Provinces (the Doab and adjacent Awadh-frontier districts ceded to the EIC by Awadh in 1801–02 and the Maratha cessions of 1803). The settlement was made with the entire village (mahal) as the co-responsible unit — the village proprietary body (the bhaichara or the recognised lambardars) signed a joint settlement, with internal allocation and recovery left to village internal arrangement. The principle drew on the Mughal-era jamabandi village settlements that had survived in the Doab. Mahalwari was extended by the 1833 Regulation IX (with a thirty-year resettlement cycle) and applied to the Punjab after 1849, parts of the Central Provinces, and Awadh after 1859. The system's distinguishing claim was that it preserved customary village structures — the village panchayat-and-co-sharer body — that Permanent Settlement had bypassed and Ryotwari had atomised. In practice the settlement assessments were demanding (60% of rental in early settlements, eased to 50% by 1855), village joint responsibility produced cascading defaults during downturns, and the customary structures eroded. The Mahalwari areas became the agrarian heart of the 1857 rebellion and, later, of the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation peasant mobilisations of 1920–22.

sources.label: Eric Stokes, The Peasant and the Raj (1978)
Asiya Siddiqi, Agrarian Change in a Northern Indian State 1819–1833 (1973)

events.title: Achaemenid Persia annexes the Indus valley
events.tooltip: Darius I annexes the Indus valley as the satrapy of Hindush, c. 518 BCE
events.summary: Darius I extended Achaemenid Persia to the Indus, establishing the satrapy of Hindush — first documented imperial absorption of subcontinental territory.
events.detail: Darius I of Persia, building on Cyrus the Great's earlier eastern campaigns, annexed the Indus valley around 518 BCE and organised it as the satrapy of Hindush (Old Persian Hi(n)duš), recorded in his Behistun inscription (c. 519 BCE) and the Naqsh-i-Rustam tomb inscription. The Achaemenid province paid the highest tribute of any satrapy in Herodotus's account — 360 Euboic talents of gold dust annually. Indian troops served in Xerxes's army at the Battle of Plataea (479 BCE) and contributed cavalry to the failed Greek campaigns. The two centuries of Achaemenid presence on the northwest frontier introduced Aramaic administrative scripts (the Kharosthi script of later Mauryan northwest edicts derives from Aramaic), Persian coinage practices, and architectural motifs visible in Mauryan capitals at Pataliputra (the famous bell-shaped capitals at Sarnath echo Persepolis). Alexander's 326 BCE invasion would target the post-Achaemenid northwest two centuries later.

sources.label: Herodotus, Histories III.94 (5th c. BCE; Robin Waterfield trans., 1998)
Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (2002), ch. on the eastern satrapies

events.title: Buddha's parinirvana at Kushinagar
events.tooltip: Siddhartha Gautama Buddha's parinirvana at Kushinagar, c. 483 BCE
events.summary: Siddhartha Gautama Buddha died at Kushinagar after a 45-year teaching mission — the founding event of the Buddhist sangha and tradition.
events.detail: Siddhartha Gautama Buddha (traditional dates 563–483 BCE; modern critical scholarship places death c. 410–400 BCE) attained parinirvana at Kushinagar in the Malla republic of north India after a 45-year teaching mission across Magadha, Kosala, and the surrounding Mahajanapada states. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta records his last meal (sukara-maddava — disputed translation as pork or mushroom), final sermon, and instructions to the sangha to take refuge in the Dhamma rather than a successor. His remains were divided among eight Mahajanapada states for stupa enshrinement; Ashoka two centuries later collected and redistributed the relics across his empire. The parinirvana inaugurated the Buddhist tradition that would, under Mauryan and Kushan patronage, become the dominant transregional Indian religious export — to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China, Tibet, and Southeast Asia.

date.display: c. 483 BCE (traditional; modern critical c. 410–400 BCE)

sources.label: Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16; Maurice Walshe trans., The Long Discourses of the Buddha, 1995)
Richard Gombrich, Theravada Buddhism: A Social History from Ancient Benares to Modern Colombo (2nd ed., 2006)
Heinz Bechert (ed.), The Dating of the Historical Buddha (3 vols., 1991–1997)

events.title: Alexander defeats Porus at the Hydaspes
events.tooltip: Alexander defeats Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, May 326 BCE
events.summary: Alexander defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) — his easternmost major battle; the army mutinied at the Beas weeks later, ending the campaign.
events.detail: Alexander III of Macedon crossed the Indus in spring 326 BCE after the Persian Achaemenid satrapy collapse, marching east through Taxila (whose ruler Ambhi submitted) toward the Punjab. King Porus (Sanskrit Puru / Paurava) of the Jhelum-Chenab doab refused tribute. The Battle of the Hydaspes — fought on the river's east bank in May 326 BCE during a monsoon thunderstorm — was Alexander's most difficult battle: Porus's war elephants disrupted the Macedonian phalanx; Alexander's son-in-law Hephaestion's cavalry crossing was hard-won. Porus was captured and famously asked to be treated 'as a king'; Alexander reinstated him as a vassal. The Macedonian army mutinied at the Beas (Hyphasis) river two months later, refusing to march further east toward Magadha; Alexander turned south down the Indus. He died at Babylon in 323 BCE; his Indian conquests were retained by Seleucus, then ceded to Chandragupta Maurya in 305 BCE.

caused_by.gloss: Alexander's campaign followed the Achaemenid imperial corridor — the same northwest passes, the same satrapal administrative geography Persia had built two centuries earlier.

sources.label: Arrian, Anabasis Alexandri V (2nd c. CE; Aubrey de Sélincourt trans., 1958)
A.B. Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988), ch. 5

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
events.tooltip: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nandas at Pataliputra, c. 322 BCE
events.summary: Chandragupta, advised by Chanakya (Kautilya), overthrew the last Nanda king and founded the Maurya Empire — the first subcontinental imperial state.
events.detail: Chandragupta Maurya, supported by his Brahmin minister Chanakya (also Kautilya, traditional author of the Arthashastra), overthrew Dhana Nanda of the Nanda dynasty at Pataliputra around 322 BCE. The empire he founded — the Mauryan — was the first to unify most of the subcontinent under a single political authority, eventually stretching from Afghanistan to Karnataka. After defeating Seleucus I Nicator's eastern campaign (305 BCE), Chandragupta secured the Hindu Kush satrapies in exchange for 500 war elephants and a marriage alliance. Megasthenes, Seleucus's ambassador, resided at Pataliputra and wrote the Indica (now lost, surviving in fragments), the earliest Greek ethnographic account of India. Jain tradition records that Chandragupta abdicated late in life, joined the Digambara monastic order under Bhadrabahu, and died by ritual fasting (sallekhana) at Shravanabelagola c. 297 BCE.

caused_by.gloss: The Macedonian campaign destabilised the northwest and demonstrated Nanda vulnerability; Chandragupta's overthrow exploited the post-Alexander power vacuum and absorbed the Macedonian territorial inheritance after the 305 BCE Seleucid settlement.

sources.label: Megasthenes, Indica (c. 300 BCE; surviving fragments in J.W. McCrindle, Ancient India as Described by Megasthenes and Arrian, 1877)
Romila Thapar, The Mauryas Revisited (1987)
Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; rev. 2012)

events.title: Ashoka's Kalinga War and dhamma turn
events.tooltip: Ashoka conquers Kalinga; recoils into dhamma policy, c. 261 BCE
events.summary: Ashoka conquered Kalinga at terrible cost — 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported by his own count in Rock Edict XIII — and turned to dhamma rule.
events.detail: Ashoka acceded to the Mauryan throne around 268 BCE after a contested succession. His invasion of Kalinga (modern coastal Odisha) c. 261 BCE — the only major military campaign of his reign — produced casualties he himself documented in Rock Edict XIII at Shahbazgarhi and elsewhere: 100,000 killed in battle, 150,000 deported, many times that number dead from secondary causes. The text records his pasch ('thereafter') turn to a policy of dhamma — a syncretic ethics drawn from Buddhist, Jain, and Brahmanical sources, emphasising non-violence, religious tolerance, the welfare of subjects, and refusal of further military conquest. Ashoka dispatched dhamma-mahamatras (officers) across his empire and sent missionaries to Sri Lanka (his son Mahinda) and Greek-ruled successor states (Antiochus II, Ptolemy II Philadelphus) — among the first documented international ethical-religious diplomacy. The Kalinga turn is the most significant attested instance of an emperor publicly renouncing military conquest in the ancient world.

caused_by.gloss: Three generations of Mauryan expansion (Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka) brought Kalinga within striking distance; the Kalinga War was the imperial logic's terminal extension before Ashoka reversed it.

sources.label: Ashoka, Major Rock Edict XIII (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Kalsi, Girnar versions; D.C. Sircar, Inscriptions of Asoka, 1957)
Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; rev. 2012)
Patrick Olivelle (ed.), Aśoka in History and Historical Memory (2009)

events.title: Ashoka's edicts proclaimed across the empire
events.tooltip: Ashoka issues Rock and Pillar Edicts, c. 257–232 BCE
events.summary: Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts — the earliest surviving Indian inscriptions — proclaimed dhamma policy in Prakrit, Greek, and Aramaic across the empire.
events.detail: Ashoka's edicts, issued progressively between c. 257 BCE and his death c. 232 BCE, are the earliest surviving Indian inscriptions and the most extensive imperial-proclamation corpus from the ancient world. They survive in three categories: Major Rock Edicts (14 series, c. 257–256 BCE) at fourteen sites from Shahbazgarhi (modern KPK, Pakistan) to Yerragudi (Andhra); Pillar Edicts (7 series, c. 243 BCE) on freestanding sandstone pillars topped by lion or bull capitals (Sarnath, Lauriya-Nandangarh, Allahabad); and the Minor Rock Edicts. The texts are in Prakrit (Brahmi script in most of India, Kharosthi in the northwest); the Kandahar bilingual is in Greek and Aramaic. Substantively the edicts proclaim dhamma policy: respect for parents and elders, kindness to slaves and servants, restraint in spending and acquiring, religious tolerance ('all sects are to be respected'), abolition of royal hunts, planting of medicinal herbs and shade trees along highways. Among the founding documents of the Indian state's self-conception.

location.name: Sarnath (Pillar Edict site; representative of empire-wide proclamation)

caused_by.gloss: The edicts are the public-policy form of the Kalinga turn — Rock Edict XIII itself records Ashoka's recoil from the war as the founding statement of dhamma rule.

sources.label: D.C. Sircar, Inscriptions of Asoka (3rd ed., 1975)
Harry Falk, Aśokan Sites and Artefacts: A Source-Book with Bibliography (2006)

events.title: Pushyamitra Sunga overthrows the Mauryas
events.tooltip: Pushyamitra Sunga kills Brihadratha at Pataliputra; Sunga dynasty c. 185 BCE
events.summary: Pushyamitra Sunga, Mauryan senapati, assassinated emperor Brihadratha during a military review and founded the Sunga dynasty — end of the Maurya.
events.detail: The Mauryan empire fragmented across the half-century after Ashoka's death (c. 232 BCE) under his successors Dasharatha, Samprati, and others. The senapati (commander-in-chief) Pushyamitra Sunga assassinated the last Mauryan emperor Brihadratha during a military review at Pataliputra around 185 BCE, founding the Sunga dynasty. Bana's 7th-century Harshacharita and Buddhist sources accuse Pushyamitra of persecuting Buddhists; modern scholarship treats the persecution claim as overstated, though the Sungas certainly patronised Brahmanical revival (the second horse-sacrifice Pushyamitra performed is documented in Ayodhya inscriptions). The Sunga dynasty (185–73 BCE) ruled a contracted territory — Magadha and the central Gangetic valley — facing Indo-Greek pressure from the northwest (Demetrius II, Menander I) and Satavahana competition from the Deccan. The Mauryan imperial framework was not reconstituted; subcontinental political fragmentation lasted until the Guptas five centuries later.

caused_by.gloss: Ashoka's renunciation of further conquest and his expensive dhamma-bureaucracy contributed to the post-Ashokan fiscal-military weakening that made the Sunga coup possible — Pushyamitra's seizure of power was the army's reassertion against the dhamma state.

sources.label: Bana, Harshacharita (7th c. CE; E.B. Cowell & F.W. Thomas trans., 1897)
Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; rev. 2012)

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.tooltip: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, 1526
events.summary: Babur's 12,000 horsemen routed the 100,000-strong Lodi army by combining wagon-fortified gunpowder artillery with mounted archery and cavalry envelopment.
events.detail: Ibrahim Lodi marched north from Delhi to crush the Timurid raider his nobles had invited in. He met the Mughals at Panipat on the morning of 21 April 1526 with a numerical advantage of about eight to one. Babur had spent days fortifying his front with 700 carts roped together and trenches on the flanks. When the Lodi advance stalled against the wagon-laager, his Turkish gunner Ustad Ali Quli's matchlocks opened fire, and the wings rolled inward in the classic tulghuma envelopment. Ibrahim Lodi died on the field. Babur entered Delhi three days later. The Mughal claim to Hindustan starts here.

sources.label: Babur, Baburnama (trans. W. Thackston, 1996)
Stephen F. Dale, The Garden of the Eight Paradises (2004)

caused_by.gloss: Lahore in 1524 was the staging point; Daulat Khan Lodi's subsequent betrayal made the march on Delhi inevitable.
Ibrahim Lodi's centralising estrangement of the Afghan nobility was the political precondition for Daulat Khan's invitation; Babur arrived as the nobility's preferred counterweight.

events.title: Battle of Khanwa
events.tooltip: Babur defeats Rana Sanga at Khanwa, 1527
events.summary: Babur's gunpowder line broke a Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar at Khanwa, locking in Mughal control of the north Indian plain.
events.detail: Defeating the Lodi army at Panipat had won Babur Delhi but not the north. Rana Sanga of Mewar had assembled the largest Rajput coalition in living memory — perhaps 100,000 horse with the rajas of Marwar, Amber, and Gwalior — to expel the Mughals. The two sides met at Khanwa, 60 km west of Agra, on 16 March 1527. Babur's matchlock-and-wagon front held; his cavalry wings turned the flanks; Rana Sanga was wounded and carried from the field. The Rajput defeat was decisive enough that Babur could declare a ghaza, take the title Ghazi, and leave the Doab for his next campaign. Mewar would not threaten the Mughal centre again until the 1570s.

sources.label: Babur, Baburnama (trans. W. Thackston, 1996)
Satish Chandra, Medieval India — Part Two (1999)

caused_by.gloss: Panipat made Babur a Delhi-bound power; Khanwa was the Rajput attempt to expel him before he consolidated.

events.title: Battle of Ghaghra
events.tooltip: Babur defeats Afghan-Bengal alliance at Ghaghra, 1529
events.summary: Babur's third great battle broke an alliance of Afghan nobles and Bengal at the Ghaghra–Ganges confluence, securing his eastern frontier.
events.detail: The defeated Lodi nobility had retreated east into Bihar and the eastern Doab; by 1528 they were rebuilding under Mahmud Lodi with material backing from Nusrat Shah of Bengal. Babur marched downriver and met them where the Ghaghra meets the Ganges in May 1529. The fighting was as much riverine as land — Babur committed his small flotilla to break the Bengali boats — and the Afghan line broke after his nephew Askari turned the right flank. The terms imposed on Bengal recognised Mughal supremacy; the Afghan coalition that would later carry Sher Shah was scattered, not destroyed. Babur returned to Agra and died eighteen months later.

sources.label: Babur, Baburnama (trans. W. Thackston, 1996)

caused_by.gloss: Khanwa removed the Rajput threat; Babur could now turn east against the Afghan rump.

events.title: Death of Babur, accession of Humayun
events.tooltip: Babur dies at Agra, Humayun crowned, 1530
events.summary: Babur died at Agra on 26 December 1530; his eldest son Humayun took the throne three days later, inheriting a victory record but no administration.
events.detail: Babur had ruled Hindustan for less than five years. His Baburnama is the candid record of a man who saw himself as a restless Timurid prince, not the founder of an empire. He fell ill in late 1530, reputedly after vowing to take on his son Humayun's fever in his own body. Humayun acceded on 29 December but inherited a kingdom held together only by his father's reputation: a treasury already strained, half-brothers with their own armies, and a Doab still raw from three years of war. Within nine years he would be exiled to Persia. The interregnum that followed belonged to the Sur dynasty.

date.display: Babur died 26 December 1530; Humayun crowned 29 December

sources.label: Stephen F. Dale, The Garden of the Eight Paradises (2004)

events.title: Babur composes the Baburnama
events.tooltip: Babur writes the Baburnama across his life, completed Agra c. 1530
events.summary: The only surviving Timurid royal autobiography. Written in Chagatai Turkish across thirty-five years, ending unfinished at Babur's death in Agra.
events.detail: Babur began writing the Vaqai (later known as the Baburnama) in his late teens and continued sporadically through his Hindu Kush exile, the Kabul years, and the Hindustan campaign — a thirty-five-year arc. Composed in Chagatai Turkish, the work has two long surviving stretches (1494–1508, 1519–1529) with a gap of unknown cause in the middle. The candour is what distinguishes it: Babur describes his own defeats, depressions, drinking bouts, and political miscalculations in the same plain register as his victories. Translated into Persian under Akbar by Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan in 1589, becoming the foundational text of Mughal court historiography. Modern scholarly translations include those of Annette Beveridge (1922) and Wheeler Thackston (1996). Among the few honest royal autobiographies in any pre-modern tradition.

caused_by.gloss: The 1501 loss of Samarkand is the formative defeat the Baburnama returns to repeatedly — the wound that shaped a lifetime of self-examination in writing.

sources.label: Wheeler M. Thackston (trans.), The Baburnama: Memoirs of Babur, Prince and Emperor (1996)
Stephen F. Dale, The Garden of the Eight Paradises: Bābur and the Culture of Empire (2004)
Annette Beveridge (trans.), The Bābur-nāma in English (1922)

events.title: Second Battle of Panipat
events.tooltip: Bairam Khan defeats Hemu at Panipat, 1556
events.summary: Bairam Khan's Mughal army defeated Hemu, the Hindu general who styled himself Vikramaditya, securing the boy-emperor Akbar's throne.
events.detail: Humayun had reclaimed Delhi in 1555 only to die six months later, falling down the stairs of his library. His thirteen-year-old son Akbar was crowned in February 1556 in a garden at Kalanaur. Within months the late Sur regime's general Hemu — a salt-trader's son who had risen to wazir — captured Agra and Delhi and proclaimed himself Hemchandra Vikramaditya. The Mughal regent Bairam Khan marched north and met him on the same ground Babur had fought thirty years earlier. An arrow struck Hemu in the eye; his elephant turned; his army broke. Akbar, brought to the field, beheaded the wounded Hemu — an act later sources soften but contemporaries record. The Mughal restoration was complete.

sources.label: Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama (trans. H. Beveridge, 1907)
Satish Chandra, Medieval India — Part Two (1999)

caused_by.gloss: Sher Shah's reformed Sur empire fragmented after his death; its general Hemu's bid for power was the regime's last act.

events.title: Akbar crowned at Kalanaur
events.tooltip: Akbar crowned at Kalanaur, aged 13, 1556
events.summary: Akbar succeeded Humayun in a hastily-built brick enclosure in Punjab, with Bairam Khan as regent for the next four years.
events.detail: Humayun's death on 24 January 1556 — falling down the steps of his library at Purana Qila with his arms full of books — left a thirteen-year-old prince at Kalanaur in Punjab as the next Mughal emperor. Bairam Khan staged the coronation on a brick platform on 14 February so the throne would not pass to a Sur claimant in the interim. The boy-emperor would not rule in his own name until 1560, when he removed Bairam Khan from the regency. Akbar's reign of forty-nine years would refit the empire administratively, militarily, and ideologically; almost everything later generations call 'Mughal' was assembled in those decades.

sources.label: Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama (trans. H. Beveridge, 1907)

events.title: Foundation of Fatehpur Sikri
events.tooltip: Akbar founds Fatehpur Sikri, 1571
events.summary: Akbar built a new capital on a sandstone ridge near the Sufi shaikh Salim Chishti's hermitage; it was occupied for fourteen years before water failed it.
events.detail: The childless Akbar visited the hermit Salim Chishti at Sikri in 1568; his first surviving son was born within the year and named Salim. The ridge above the village became the site of an entirely new capital — Diwan-i-Khas, Buland Darwaza, the Jama Masjid, the Panch Mahal, the tomb of Chishti himself — built in red sandstone in a hybrid Indo-Timurid idiom. The court moved there in 1571. The Ibadat Khana debates of religious scholars from every tradition were staged in those halls in the late 1570s. By 1585 the city was abandoned, conventionally for want of water, more plausibly because Akbar had moved his court to the Punjab to handle Uzbek and Afghan campaigns. The buildings survive almost intact.

sources.label: Catherine Asher, Architecture of Mughal India (1992)

events.title: Battle of Haldighati
events.tooltip: Akbar's army vs Maharana Pratap, Haldighati, 1576
events.summary: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's army to a tactical draw and never accepted Mughal vassalage — the Sisodias of Mewar were the only major Rajput house that didn't.
events.detail: Akbar had brought most Rajput houses into the imperial service through marriage alliances and mansabs by the 1570s. The Sisodias of Mewar refused. On 18 June 1576 Akbar's army under Man Singh of Amber and Asaf Khan met Maharana Pratap's smaller force in the narrow defile of Haldighati between Khamnor and Gogunda. The fighting was inconclusive; Pratap escaped on his horse Chetak after the animal carried him across a ravine and died of its wounds. The Mughals occupied the abandoned Mewar capital of Chittor but never broke the resistance. Pratap regained much of the territory before his death in 1597. Mewar accepted Mughal suzerainty only in 1615, under his grandson Karan Singh.

sources.label: Satish Chandra, Medieval India — Part Two (1999)

events.title: Mansabdari system codified
events.tooltip: Akbar formalises mansab ranks, 1577
events.summary: Akbar formalised a single hierarchy of military-administrative ranks (mansabs), each obliging cavalry strength and rated for cash pay.
events.detail: The mansabdari system gave the empire a single ledger for army and bureaucracy at once. A mansab was a numerical rank — zat for personal status, sawar for the cavalry the holder owed — running from 10 to 7,000 (and higher for princes). Pay was in cash from the central treasury or in the form of an assignment (jagir) on a specified land revenue.
