Niazi's surrender of 93,000 Pakistani troops at Dhaka — the largest military surrender since WWII. The Republic of Bangladesh was proclaimed; Mujib released from West Pakistani imprisonment in January 1972 returned as its founding prime minister. The 1972 Simla Agreement formalised the post-war settlement.

caused_by.gloss: The 1947 partition's two-wing Pakistan was structurally unstable; the East-Pakistan-becomes-Bangladesh outcome of 1971 is the long unwinding of the Two-Nation Theory's geographic incoherence.

sources.label: Srinath Raghavan, 1971: A Global History of the Creation of Bangladesh (2013)
Sarmila Bose, Dead Reckoning: Memories of the 1971 Bangladesh War (2011)
Gary J. Bass, The Blood Telegram: Nixon, Kissinger, and a Forgotten Genocide (2013)

events.title: Pokhran-I — Smiling Buddha nuclear test
events.tooltip: India's first nuclear test, Pokhran (Rajasthan), 18 May 1974
events.summary: India detonated its first nuclear device at Pokhran on 18 May 1974 — code-named Smiling Buddha; declared 'peaceful nuclear explosion' to limit sanctions.
events.detail: India's nuclear weapons programme — initiated under Homi Bhabha in the 1950s, accelerated after the 1962 Sino-Indian war and China's 1964 nuclear test, and approved by Indira Gandhi in 1972 — culminated in the underground detonation of a plutonium device at Pokhran in the Thar desert, Rajasthan, at 8:05 AM IST on 18 May 1974. Yield estimated at 8–12 kilotons (Indian official) or 4–6 kt (Western seismic estimates). The test was framed as a 'Peaceful Nuclear Explosion' (PNE) to limit international sanctions — Indira Gandhi's choice of the Buddha-day code-name 'Smiling Buddha' and the PNE framing were deliberate diplomatic ambiguity. Canada (which had supplied the CIRUS reactor whose plutonium was used) and the United States imposed nuclear-cooperation sanctions; the international Nuclear Suppliers Group was formed in 1975 specifically in response to Pokhran-I. India remained outside the NPT framework. The next test series — Pokhran-II in May 1998 under Vajpayee — would be unambiguous weapons tests, ending the PNE ambiguity.

sources.label: Raj Chengappa, Weapons of Peace: The Secret Story of India's Quest to be a Nuclear Power (2000)
George Perkovich, India's Nuclear Bomb: The Impact on Global Proliferation (1999)

events.title: The Emergency
events.tooltip: Emergency declared 25 June 1975; lifted, elections called January 1977
events.summary: Indira proclaimed Emergency after the Allahabad verdict, JP's mutiny call, and a paralysing rail strike — and lifted it 21 months later for elections she lost.
events.detail: By early 1975 the Indira Gandhi government faced a convergence of crises that no Indian PM had managed before. The 1973–74 oil shock had pushed inflation past 30%; the May 1974 All-India Railway Strike under George Fernandes (1.7 million workers, 20 days) had paralysed the economy and ended only after mass arrests; the Navnirman agitation in Gujarat (1974) had brought down the state government; the Bihar Movement under Jayaprakash Narayan had escalated from anti-corruption protest to a 25 June 1975 Ramlila Maidan rally where JP called on the army, police, and bureaucracy to refuse 'illegal and immoral orders' from the central government — read by the PMO as a call to mutiny. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court (Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha) had set aside Indira's 1971 Rae Bareli election on minor electoral-malpractice grounds, disqualifying her from Parliament for six years. On the night of 25–26 June 1975, citing 'internal disturbance' under Article 352, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed Emergency on Indira's advice. Civil liberties were suspended; ~110,000 detained without trial under MISA (JP, Morarji Desai, Vajpayee, Advani, Fernandes, RSS leaders); the press was censored; the 42nd Amendment radically expanded central power. Sanjay Gandhi's extra-constitutional power produced the slum demolitions and the coercive sterilisation drive (~6.2 million procedures in 1976, with documented coercion). And then — in a decision without parallel in 20th-century authoritarian history — Indira lifted the Emergency on 21 March 1977 and called free elections, which she lost decisively to the Janata coalition. She could have continued indefinitely; she chose not to. The Shah Commission (1978) documented the abuses; Indira returned to power in 1980. The Emergency remains the constitutional caesura of the Republic — and the standard against which all subsequent democratic backsliding is measured.

sources.label: Gyan Prakash, Emergency Chronicles: Indira Gandhi and Democracy's Turning Point (2018)
Shah Commission of Inquiry — Interim and Final Reports (1978)
Bipan Chandra, In the Name of Democracy: JP Movement and the Emergency (2003)

events.title: Mandal Commission implementation
events.tooltip: V.P. Singh implements Mandal — 27% OBC reservations, 7 August 1990
events.summary: V.P. Singh's announcement of 27% central-government OBC reservations triggered upper-caste anti-Mandal agitation and Rajiv Goswami's self-immolation.
events.detail: The Second Backward Classes Commission, constituted 1979 under former Bihar CM B.P. Mandal, had submitted its report in December 1980 recommending 27% reservation in central government jobs and public-sector education for Other Backward Classes (OBCs, identified across 3,743 castes constituting an estimated 52% of the population). The Indira and Rajiv Gandhi governments shelved it for a decade. Prime Minister V.P. Singh of the National Front coalition announced implementation on 7 August 1990 — partly to outflank his Janata Dal rival Devi Lal, partly as a long-held conviction. Upper-caste, mostly Brahmin and Bania, college-student protests erupted across north India within days. On 19 September 1990 Delhi University student Rajiv Goswami set himself on fire outside Deshbandhu College; he survived (died 2004 of related complications) but his act triggered an estimated 200+ self-immolation attempts, of which around 60 were fatal. The anti-Mandal agitation crippled north Indian universities through the autumn of 1990. The Supreme Court's 1992 Indra Sawhney verdict upheld the 27% OBC quota subject to a 'creamy layer' exclusion and a total-reservations cap of 50%. Politically, Mandal restructured Indian electoral mobilisation around caste — the rise of Mulayam Singh Yadav, Lalu Prasad Yadav, Mayawati, and the post-Mandal OBC and Dalit parties traces to this moment. The BJP's parallel Mandir mobilisation (Advani's Rath Yatra, September 1990; arrest at Samastipur 23 October 1990; collapse of V.P. Singh's government 7 November 1990) was the explicit Hindu-consolidation counter to caste-fragmentation.

sources.label: Christophe Jaffrelot, India's Silent Revolution: The Rise of the Lower Castes in North India (2003)
Report of the Backward Classes Commission (Mandal Report, Government of India, 1980)
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, AIR 1993 SC 477 (1992)

events.title: Advani's Ram Rath Yatra
events.tooltip: L.K. Advani's Somnath–Ayodhya Rath Yatra, 25 September – 23 October 1990
events.summary: Advani's motorised rath from Somnath toward Ayodhya — arrested at Samastipur by Lalu, collapsing V.P. Singh's government two weeks later.
events.detail: BJP president L.K. Advani conceived the Ram Rath Yatra as the mass-mobilisation arm of the VHP-led Ram Janmabhoomi movement, deliberately timed to counter V.P. Singh's 7 August 1990 Mandal Commission announcement (the Mandir-versus-Mandal axis the BJP would ride for the next decade). The yatra began at the Somnath temple in Gujarat on 25 September 1990 in a Toyota DCM truck retrofitted as a chariot, with planned terminus at Ayodhya on 30 October 1990 in time for the kar seva. Pramod Mahajan organised the logistics. The yatra passed through Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh, drawing crowds estimated at hundreds of thousands at major halts and triggering communal riots in its wake (Hyderabad, Khambhat, Aurangabad, and elsewhere — 564 dead nationally between September and November 1990 per Home Ministry figures). On 23 October 1990 the Bihar government under Chief Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav arrested Advani at Samastipur under the National Security Act. The BJP withdrew its outside support to V.P. Singh's National Front coalition; the Singh government lost a confidence vote on 7 November 1990 and resigned. The arrested kar seva nonetheless reached Ayodhya — a 30 October 1990 confrontation at the Babri Masjid saw UP police firing on kar sevaks (16 official deaths; the figure is contested upwards). The Mulayam Singh Yadav UP government's order to fire and the BJP's subsequent national mobilisation were the direct organisational rehearsal for the 6 December 1992 demolition.

date.display: 25 September – 23 October 1990 (V.P. Singh government fell 7 November)

location.name: Samastipur, Bihar (arrest site); Somnath (start) – Ayodhya (intended end)

caused_by.gloss: Advani's yatra was conceived as the Hindu-consolidation answer to V.P. Singh's 7 August 1990 OBC-quota announcement — the Mandir mobilisation deliberately positioned to override the Mandal-driven caste fragmentation of the Hindu vote.

sources.label: Christophe Jaffrelot, The Hindu Nationalist Movement and Indian Politics (1996)
L.K. Advani, My Country My Life (2008), chs. on the Yatra
Manoj Mitta and H.S. Phoolka, When a Tree Shook Delhi (2007) and contemporary Frontline coverage

events.title: Babri Masjid demolition
events.tooltip: Kar sevaks demolish the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya, 6 December 1992
events.summary: An estimated 150,000 kar sevaks demolished the 16th-century Babri Masjid at Ayodhya in five hours — communal riots killed ~2,000 across India that followed.
events.detail: The Ram Janmabhoomi movement, organised by the VHP–BJP–RSS Sangh Parivar from the early 1980s, claimed the Babri Masjid (built 1528, attributed to Mir Baqi under Babur) stood on the birthplace of the deity Ram. L.K. Advani's Somnath-to-Ayodhya Rath Yatra in September–October 1990 had been arrested at Samastipur, Bihar, by Lalu Prasad Yadav. On 6 December 1992 a kar seva organised at Ayodhya, attended by an estimated 150,000 supporters, breached police cordons and demolished the mosque in approximately five hours under the eyes of the Kalyan Singh BJP state government (which had assured the Supreme Court no demolition would occur). The Liberhan Commission of Inquiry (constituted ten days after the demolition; reported 2009) named 68 individuals as responsible. Communal riots across India in December 1992 – January 1993 killed approximately 2,000; the March 1993 Bombay serial blasts (257 killed) were the underworld response. The Allahabad High Court's 2010 verdict trifurcated the site; the Supreme Court's 2019 verdict (M Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das) reversed that and awarded the entire 2.77-acre site to the Ram Janmabhoomi trust — while expressly observing that the Archaeological Survey of India had found no evidence of a demolished Hindu temple directly underlying the mosque, and that the 1992 demolition itself was an 'egregious violation of the rule of law'. A separate 5-acre plot in Ayodhya was directed to be allocated to the Sunni Waqf Board.

caused_by.gloss: The Advani Rath Yatra was the explicit organisational rehearsal — the Sangh Parivar's coordinated mass-mobilisation logistics test, the BJP's withdrawal of support to V.P. Singh's government over Mandal, and the 30 October 1990 Ayodhya kar seva that the December 1992 demolition completed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Demolition of the Babri Masjid

sources.label: Christophe Jaffrelot, The Hindu Nationalist Movement and Indian Politics (1996)
Liberhan Commission Report (constituted 1992; presented 2009)
P.V. Narasimha Rao, Ayodhya: 6 December 1992 (posthumous, 2006)

events.title: Saha ionisation equation
events.tooltip: Saha ionisation equation, October 1920 — founds modern stellar spectroscopy
events.summary: Saha published the thermal-ionisation equation in Philosophical Magazine — links stellar spectra to atmospheric temperature; founds modern astrophysics.
events.detail: Meghnad Saha, working at University College London on the 1919 Premchand Roychand scholarship, published 'Ionisation in the Solar Chromosphere' in the Philosophical Magazine (vol. 40, October 1920). The Saha equation gives the ratio of singly-ionised atoms to neutral atoms in a thermal gas as a function of temperature, pressure, and ionisation potential — the missing link between observed stellar spectral lines and the physical conditions of stellar atmospheres. Eddington called the result 'amongst the dozen most important advances in theoretical astrophysics' of the early 20th century. H.N. Russell at Princeton extended it to the spectral classification of stars (1924); Cecilia Payne's 1925 PhD thesis used the Saha equation to demonstrate that stars are composed principally of hydrogen — the result that overturned the Earth-composition assumption of pre-1925 stellar astronomy. The Saha equation remains the textbook foundation of stellar atmospheric spectroscopy. Saha returned to India 1921, joined Allahabad University, founded the Indian National Academy of Sciences 1934 at Allahabad, and the Institute of Nuclear Physics at Calcutta 1950. Astrophysics-as-a-discipline traces back to this equation.

sources.label: M.N. Saha, 'Ionisation in the Solar Chromosphere', Philosophical Magazine 40 (1920), 472–488
S. Chatterjee, Meghnad Saha: A Personal and Scientific Biography (1994)

events.title: Discovery of the Raman effect
events.tooltip: Raman effect discovered, Calcutta, 28 February 1928 — Nobel Prize 1930
events.summary: Raman and K.S. Krishnan demonstrated inelastic light scattering at IACS Calcutta — Nobel Prize 1930, first Asian science Nobel.
events.detail: Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, working with K.S. Krishnan at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS) at Bowbazar, Calcutta, published 'A New Type of Secondary Radiation' in Nature (16 March 1928, dated work 28 February 1928). The effect: when monochromatic light is scattered by a molecule, a small fraction of the scattered light is shifted in frequency by the energy of the molecule's vibrational transitions — the inelastic Raman scattering. The seven-year programme leading to the discovery began with Raman's 1921 onboard observation of the deep blue colour of the Mediterranean — Lord Rayleigh had attributed it to sky-reflection; Raman traced it to molecular scattering by water itself. The 1928 measurement used a 1925 mercury arc lamp, a quartz spectrograph, and 60 different liquids. The Nobel Prize in Physics 1930 made him the first Asian science Nobel laureate; the Stockholm speech was given in English with explicit reference to the colonial-civilian-science environment in which the work was done. Raman spectroscopy became — and remains — one of the principal techniques of molecular structure determination across chemistry, biology, materials science, and pharmaceutical analysis. The 28 February anniversary is India's National Science Day.

location.name: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Calcutta

sources.label: C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan, 'A New Type of Secondary Radiation', Nature 121 (1928), 501–502
G. Venkataraman, Journey into Light: Life and Science of C.V. Raman (1988)

events.title: Madurai Sultanate founded
events.tooltip: Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan declares Madurai Sultanate, 1335
events.summary: Tughlaq governor Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan revolted from Madurai in 1335 — the southernmost Indian Muslim sultanate, ended by Vijayanagara in 1378.
events.detail: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's southern provincial system collapsed almost as fast as it was built. Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, the Tughlaq-appointed governor of Ma'bar (the Tamil country), declared independence in 1335 from Madurai, founding the Madurai Sultanate (also called the Ma'bar Sultanate). Ibn Battuta visited the court in 1342 and recorded the violence and instability of the regime — eight sultans in forty-three years, multiple murders. The Sultanate's capital was Madurai (with its Meenakshi Amman temple defaced or repurposed during this period); its territory ranged from the Coromandel coast to the Western Ghats. Vijayanagara's Kumara Kampana defeated the last Madurai sultan in 1378, ending the sultanate. The brief Madurai Sultanate is the southernmost reach of any Delhi-derived Muslim political power; nothing comparable would emerge so far south again until Hyder Ali's Mysore in the 18th century.

sources.label: Mehrdad Shokoohy, Muslim Architecture of South India: The Sultanate of Ma'bar (2003)
K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (1955)

events.title: Vijayanagara founded by Harihara and Bukka
events.tooltip: Harihara and Bukka Sangama found Vijayanagara at Hampi, 1336
events.summary: Harihara and Bukka Sangama, brothers and former Hoysala officers, founded the Vijayanagara empire on the south bank of the Tungabhadra at Hampi.
events.detail: Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, two of five Sangama brothers in service first to the Kakatiyas of Warangal and then (after 1323) the Hoysalas, founded Vijayanagara on 18 April 1336 on the south bank of the Tungabhadra river at Hampi. The conventional foundation story credits the Advaita scholar Vidyaranya of Sringeri Math with religious legitimation — though modern scholarship reads Vidyaranya's role as later attribution. The empire was built explicitly as a Hindu counter to Bahmani and the Madurai Sultanate; its 310-year run (1336–1646) was the longest unified Hindu-ruled imperial regime in South India since the Cholas. The capital at Hampi grew to perhaps 500,000 by Krishna Deva Raya's reign — among the largest cities in the world in the 16th century. Persian and European travellers (Abdur Razzak, Domingo Paes, Fernão Nunes) recorded a court of legendary wealth and cosmopolitan trade contacts.

caused_by.gloss: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Daulatabad project pulled north-Indian administrative weight south but failed; the Sangama brothers' founding of Vijayanagara is the southern political response to that Tughlaq overreach.

sources.label: Burton Stein, Vijayanagara (Cambridge New History of India I.2, 1989)
Phillip B. Wagoner, Tidings of the King: A Translation and Ethnohistorical Analysis of the Rāyavācakamu (1993)

events.title: Bijapur Sultanate founded
events.tooltip: Yusuf Adil Shah declares Bijapur independence from Bahmani, 1490
events.summary: Yusuf Adil Shah, the Bahmani governor of Bijapur, declared independence in 1490 — first of the five Deccan Sultanates that emerged from Bahmani fragmentation.
events.detail: Yusuf Adil Shah, a Persian-born former slave-noble of the Bahmani court (claiming descent from the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen), declared Bijapur an independent sultanate in 1490 as Bahmani central authority collapsed. The Adil Shahi dynasty he founded ruled for 196 years until Aurangzeb's annexation in 1686. Bijapur is the longest-lived of the Bahmani-successor sultanates, and the most architecturally and culturally distinctive — Persian artistic traditions fused with Marathi-Kannada vernaculars, Shi'a court ritual (unusual among Indian Muslim regimes), and the Gol Gumbaz of Mohammed Adil Shah (1656) is the second-largest dome in the world. Ibrahim Adil Shah II's Kitab-i Nauras (1599) is among the foundational texts of Hindustani classical music synthesis.

caused_by.gloss: Bahmani's gradual fragmentation through the late 15th century produced the five Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur 1490, Ahmadnagar 1490, Berar 1490, Bidar 1492, Golconda 1518); Bijapur was the wealthiest and longest-lived.

sources.label: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300–1761 (2005), ch. 4

events.title: Krishna Deva Raya's reign — Vijayanagara peak
events.tooltip: Krishna Deva Raya rules Vijayanagara, 1509–1529
events.summary: Krishna Deva Raya's reign was Vijayanagara's peak — defeated Bijapur and the Gajapatis, hosted Portuguese, sponsored Telugu-Sanskrit cultural flowering.
events.detail: Krishna Deva Raya of the Tuluva dynasty acceded in 1509 and ruled until 1529 — twenty years that mark Vijayanagara's territorial and cultural peak. He defeated the Adil Shahis (1510), the Gajapatis of Odisha (1518, taking Kondavidu and Vijayawada), and the Bahmani-Bidar combine repeatedly. Hampi at his court hosted Portuguese envoys (Domingo Paes, Fernão Nunes), Persian merchants, and a literary academy whose ashtadiggajas ('eight elephants') — Allasani Peddana, Nandi Thimmana, and others — produced the Telugu literary canon's foundational texts. Krishna Deva Raya himself wrote Amuktamalyada (in Telugu) and other works. He died unexpectedly in 1529; the Vijayanagara state survived another 36 years to Talikota.

caused_by.gloss: Vijayanagara's first 173 years were consolidation; Krishna Deva Raya's reign turned the consolidated empire into the dominant subcontinental Hindu-ruled regime of its time.

sources.label: Burton Stein, Vijayanagara (1989)
Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire: Vijayanagar (1900) — includes Paes & Nunes translations

events.title: Golconda Sultanate founded
events.tooltip: Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk declares Golconda independence from Bahmani, 1518
events.summary: Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk, Bahmani governor of Telingana, declared the Qutb Shahi sultanate at Golconda — diamond-rich and Persianate, ended by Aurangzeb in 1687.
events.detail: Sultan-Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk, a Persian-born former Bahmani slave-noble appointed governor of Telingana in 1496, declared independence after the Bahmani regent Mahmud Gawan's execution and the dynasty's collapse. The Qutb Shahi sultanate ruled from Golconda Fort (and from 1591 the new city of Hyderabad, founded by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah). Golconda's wealth came from the diamond mines of Kollur (the source of the Koh-i-Noor and other historic stones) and from Coromandel-coast textile trade through Masulipatnam. The dynasty's distinctive Indo-Persian Shi'a synthesis is preserved in the Charminar (1591), the Qutb Shahi tombs, and the Dakhni Urdu literary tradition. Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in October 1687 after an eight-month siege; the Qutb Shahi treasury, including diamonds, became part of the Mughal exchequer.

caused_by.gloss: The same Bahmani fragmentation that produced Bijapur in 1490 produced Golconda in 1518; the Qutb Shahi state ran the eastern half of the Deccan as Adil Shahi ran the west.

sources.label: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan (2005), ch. 5

events.title: Battle of Talikota — Vijayanagara falls
events.tooltip: Deccan Sultanate alliance defeats Vijayanagara at Talikota, 26 January 1565
events.summary: An alliance of Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, and Bidar defeated the Vijayanagara army at Talikota — Hampi was sacked over five months and never reoccupied.
events.detail: The four major Deccan Sultanates — Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar — set aside their mutual hostilities and combined forces against Vijayanagara under regent Aliya Rama Raya in late 1564. The battle was fought on the south bank of the Krishna near Talikota on 26 January 1565. Rama Raya was captured and beheaded mid-battle; the Vijayanagara cavalry collapsed; the Sultanate alliance pursued the routed army back to Hampi and sacked the capital over five months — a destruction so thorough that Hampi was never reoccupied as a major city. The Vijayanagara state survived in reduced form under the Aravidu dynasty from Penukonda and then Chandragiri until 1646, but the empire as a subcontinental power ended at Talikota. Its collapse opened the Deccan to Mughal expansion under Akbar and Aurangzeb.

caused_by.gloss: The Vijayanagara peak under Krishna Deva Raya generated the imperial pretensions that the Deccan Sultanates set aside their feuds to break — Talikota is the moment the alliance becomes possible.

sources.label: Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire: Vijayanagar (1900)
Richard M. Eaton & Phillip B. Wagoner, Power, Memory, Architecture: Contested Sites on India's Deccan Plateau, 1300–1600 (2014)

events.title: Battle of Colachel — Travancore defeats the Dutch
events.tooltip: Marthanda Varma's Travancore defeats Dutch VOC at Colachel, 10 August 1741
events.summary: Marthanda Varma's Travancore defeated the Dutch East India Company at Colachel — a rare major land defeat of a European power by an Asian state before WWII.
events.detail: Marthanda Varma's consolidation of southern Kerala from 1729 brought him into conflict with the Dutch East India Company (VOC), which controlled the Malabar pepper trade through fortified posts at Kochi and Quilon. After Travancore captured several VOC posts, the Dutch landed an expeditionary force under Captain Eustachius De Lannoy at Colachel (modern Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu) in 1741. Travancore's forces — armed with locally-made flintlocks and trained in modern infantry tactics by deserters from European armies — defeated the Dutch on 10 August 1741. De Lannoy and twenty-three other captured Dutch officers entered Travancore service; De Lannoy became the army's commander and modernised it along European lines for the next thirty-six years. The Dutch never recovered their Malabar position; the British (EIC) eventually replaced them in southern Kerala. Among the very few major land defeats of a European colonial power by an Asian state before the 20th century.

sources.label: K.M. Panikkar, Malabar and the Dutch (1931)
A. Sreedhara Menon, A Survey of Kerala History (1967; rev. 2007)

events.title: Trippadidanam — Marthanda Varma dedicates Travancore
events.tooltip: Marthanda Varma dedicates Travancore to Padmanabhaswamy, 3 January 1750
events.summary: Marthanda Varma dedicated Travancore to Sri Padmanabhaswamy — rulers became dasa of the deity, a sovereignty frame that survived British paramountcy.
events.detail: On 3 January 1750 (5 Makaram 925 in the Malayalam calendar) Marthanda Varma performed the trippadidanam — the formal dedication of the Travancore kingdom to the deity Sri Padmanabhaswamy at the temple in Thiruvananthapuram. The ruler became Padmanabha Dasa ('servant of Padmanabha'), holding the kingdom as the deity's regent rather than as sovereign. Successive Travancore rulers signed letters as Padmanabha Dasa; the legal-religious framing was used in 19th-century litigation against the British and survives in the Padmanabhaswamy temple's modern court cases. The 2011 Supreme Court-supervised opening of the temple's vaults discovered an estimated US$22 billion in gold, gems, and ceremonial objects accumulated over centuries — among the largest known temple treasures anywhere.

caused_by.gloss: The Dutch defeat secured Travancore's independence from European pressure in southern Kerala; the trippadidanam codified the religious-political frame of the consolidated kingdom Marthanda Varma had built.

sources.label: A. Sreedhara Menon, A Survey of Kerala History (rev. 2007)

events.title: Battle of Pollilur — Hyder Ali defeats the EIC
events.tooltip: Hyder Ali destroys EIC force under Baillie at Pollilur, 10 September 1780
events.summary: Hyder Ali's Mysore army destroyed an EIC detachment under Colonel William Baillie at Pollilur — among the EIC's worst defeats anywhere before the 19th century.
events.detail: The Second Anglo-Mysore War opened with Hyder Ali's invasion of the Carnatic in July 1780. On 10 September 1780 his force — including French-trained artillery — surrounded and destroyed an EIC detachment of 3,820 men under Colonel William Baillie at Pollilur, near Conjeeveram. The EIC casualties were catastrophic: about 360 killed in action, 200 wounded, the remainder captured. Baillie himself was wounded and died in Mysore captivity in 1782. The defeat was an immediate political shock — depicted in the famous Pollilur murals at Tipu Sultan's Daria Daulat Bagh palace at Srirangapatna (the only Indian battle painting cycle of the period). The EIC eventually recovered through Eyre Coote's victories and the 1784 Treaty of Mangalore, but Pollilur defined Mysore's reputation as the most formidable Indian opponent the EIC faced before Ranjit Singh.

sources.label: Mark Wilks, Historical Sketches of the South of India in an Attempt to Trace the History of Mysoor (3 vols., 1810–17)
Anne Buddle, Tigers Round the Throne: The Court of Tipu Sultan, 1750–1799 (1990)

events.title: Treaty of Mangalore — end of the Second Anglo-Mysore War
events.tooltip: Tipu Sultan and EIC sign Treaty of Mangalore, 11 March 1784
events.summary: Treaty restoring pre-war boundaries between Tipu Sultan and the EIC — the only treaty the EIC ever signed with an Indian state on roughly equal terms.
events.detail: The Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–1784) ended with the Treaty of Mangalore on 11 March 1784, signed by Tipu Sultan (newly succeeded after Hyder Ali's death in December 1782) and the EIC. The treaty restored the pre-war territorial status quo, exchanged prisoners, and established a Mysore-EIC commercial framework. It is the only Anglo-Indian treaty the EIC negotiated on substantially equal terms — Mysore had not been militarily defeated, the EIC was financially exhausted, and Warren Hastings ratified the treaty against the Madras Council's objections. The Court of Directors in London disowned it within two years, treating Mangalore as a humiliation that needed reversing. The Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–1792) was the EIC's effort to undo the treaty — and Wellesley's 1799 final assault on Srirangapatna ended Mysore as an independent power.

caused_by.gloss: Pollilur and the subsequent inconclusive campaigns brought both sides to a stalemate; the treaty was the formal recognition that neither could win the war militarily.

sources.label: Irfan Habib (ed.), State and Diplomacy under Tipu Sultan (2001)

events.title: Treaty of Seringapatam — end of Third Anglo-Mysore War
events.tooltip: Tipu Sultan cedes half his territory at Treaty of Seringapatam, 18 March 1792
events.summary: Tipu Sultan surrendered half his territory and 33 million rupees in war indemnity, plus two of his sons as hostages, to the EIC, Marathas, and Nizam.
events.detail: The Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–1792) was Cornwallis's deliberate dismantling of Mysore as a regional power. After eighteen months of campaigning culminating in the siege of Srirangapatna, Tipu Sultan signed the Treaty of Seringapatam on 18 March 1792. Mysore ceded approximately half its territory — Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul, Baramahal — divided between the EIC, the Marathas, and the Nizam of Hyderabad. War indemnity was set at 33 million rupees (roughly £3.3 million sterling). Tipu's two younger sons, Abdul Khaliq (eight) and Muizuddin (ten), were held as hostages at Madras for two years pending payment. The territorial losses crippled Mysore's revenue base; the seven-year buildup to the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) was Tipu attempting to recover the position the treaty took from him.

caused_by.gloss: The Court of Directors had disowned Mangalore as a humiliation; Cornwallis's 1790 invasion was the deliberate reversal of the 1784 stalemate, ending in the territorial dismemberment Mangalore had explicitly avoided.

sources.label: Irfan Habib (ed.), State and Diplomacy under Tipu Sultan (2001)

events.title: Wodeyar restoration at Mysore
events.tooltip: EIC restores Wodeyar dynasty at Mysore under five-year-old Krishnaraja III, 1799
events.summary: After Tipu's death the EIC restored the Wodeyar dynasty under five-year-old Krishnaraja III — Mysore became a princely state under British paramountcy.
events.detail: After the 4 May 1799 storming of Srirangapatna and Tipu Sultan's death, Wellesley faced the question of what to do with the conquered Mysore territory. Direct EIC annexation would have over-extended administrative resources; cession to the Nizam or Marathas would have empowered competitors. The compromise was the Wodeyar restoration — installing the five-year-old Krishnaraja III, whose family had been the pre-Hyder-Ali Mysore rulers since 1399, as nominal sovereign under EIC paramountcy. Diwan Purnaiya (Tipu's former minister) ran the administration as regent. The Mysore princely state under the restored Wodeyars lasted until 1947 — under nineteenth-century reforming maharajas (Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, Chamarajendra X, Krishnaraja IV) it became among the most administratively progressive princely states, with universal primary education from the 1840s onwards.

caused_by.gloss: The 1792 dismemberment had not eliminated Mysore as a strategic problem; Tipu's continued military preparation and his approaches to revolutionary France made the 1799 final settlement inevitable, and the Wodeyar restoration was its political form.

sources.label: James Manor, Political Change in an Indian State: Mysore 1917–1955 (1977) — backgrounder ch. 1

events.title: Vellore Mutiny
events.tooltip: Sepoys mutiny at Vellore Fort, 10 July 1806; predates 1857 by 51 years
events.summary: Madras sepoys revolted against new Christian-style headgear and grooming rules, killed 200 EIC officers in three hours, and were suppressed by morning.
events.detail: On 10 July 1806 sepoys of the EIC's Madras Native Infantry stationed at Vellore Fort revolted in the predawn hours, killing some 200 EIC officers and European troops within three hours and seizing the fort. The trigger was new Madras Army regulations (November 1805) prescribing turbans modelled on European hats, restrictions on caste marks and beards, and replacement of brass earrings — read by the sepoys as preparatory to forced Christianisation. Behind the regulations stood the political background of Tipu Sultan's family: his sons (Fateh Hyder, Abdul Khaliq, others) were held at Vellore Fort after the 1799 fall of Srirangapatna; some sepoys later said they had heard the family promise reward for restoration. Colonel Robert Rollo Gillespie's relief force arrived from Arcot before noon, retook the fort, and ordered approximately 350 sepoys executed — one detachment by being blown from cannon. The dress regulations were withdrawn and the Madras Army's commander, General John Cradock, was recalled. The Vellore Mutiny is the structural rehearsal for 1857.

sources.label: James W. Hoover, Men Without Hats: Dialogue, Discipline and Discontent in the Madras Army 1806–1807 (2007)
K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (1955), ch. on the EIC period

events.title: Tipu Sultan's Khwabnama (Book of Dreams)
events.tooltip: Tipu Sultan records 37 dreams, Srirangapatna, 1786–1798
events.summary: Tipu's personal Persian record of 37 dreams across twelve years — intimate, religiously freighted, never intended for public reading.
events.detail: Tipu Sultan kept a small octavo manuscript at Srirangapatna in which he recorded dreams in his own hand, in Persian, between 1786 and 1798 — thirty-seven entries across twelve years. Each is dated and most are interpreted, often referencing military prospects or divine sanction for ongoing campaigns against the Marathas, the Nizam, and the East India Company. The manuscript was discovered in his bedchamber after his death at the British storming of Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799 and deposited in the Mysore palace records. Unlike Mughal court chronicles or formal autobiographies, the Khwabnama is utterly private — a ruler's interior religious life captured without performance. Mahmud Husain published a partial English translation in 1957 (The Dreams of Tipu Sultan) from the Calcutta manuscript. Among the few first-person dream-records by a sovereign anywhere in 18th-century world.

sources.label: Mahmud Husain, The Dreams of Tipu Sultan (Pakistan Historical Society, 1957)
Kate Brittlebank, Tipu Sultan's Search for Legitimacy: Islam and Kingship in a Hindu Domain (1997), ch. 4
Irfan Habib (ed.), State and Diplomacy under Tipu Sultan (2001)

events.title: Moplah (Mappila) Rebellion
events.tooltip: Mappila tenant rebellion across Malabar, August 1921 – early 1922
events.summary: Mappila tenants rose against Hindu landlords and the Madras government during the Khilafat-Non-Cooperation period — six months of rebellion, 10,000 dead.
events.detail: The August 1921 Mappila rebellion in Malabar grew out of a long agrarian crisis: Mappila Muslim tenant cultivators worked land owned by Hindu Namboodiri and Nair janmis under the Malabar tenancy system, with no security and rising rents. Khilafat and Non-Cooperation organising in 1920–21 politicised the tenants. After police arrested Mappila leaders at Tirurangadi mosque on 20 August 1921, riots became insurrection: jails attacked, telegraph cut, district treasury looted, parallel khilafat administration declared at Eranad with Variankunnath Kunjahammed Haji as 'sultan'. From October the rebellion took a communal turn — forced conversions and Hindu reprisals — that broke the Khilafat-Non-Cooperation alliance and gave Gandhi reason to question the entire programme. Suppression by Madras infantry took six months. Government counts: roughly 2,300 rebels killed in operations, 1,650 wounded, 5,690 captured, 38,000 arrested. The November 1921 Wagon Tragedy — 67 prisoners suffocated in a sealed railway wagon between Tirur and Coimbatore — became the rebellion's emblem. Total Mappila deaths estimated at 10,000.

sources.label: K.N. Panikkar, Against Lord and State: Religion and Peasant Uprisings in Malabar 1836–1921 (1989)
Robert L. Hardgrave Jr., 'The Mappilla Rebellion 1921: Peasant Revolt in Malabar', Modern Asian Studies 11:1 (1977)
Stephen Dale, Islamic Society on the South Asian Frontier: The Mappilas of Malabar 1498–1922 (1980)

events.title: Rampa Rebellion under Alluri Sitarama Raju
events.tooltip: Alluri Sitarama Raju leads Rampa hill tribes, 1922–1924
events.summary: A 27-year-old ascetic-revolutionary led Konda Reddi and Koya tribals in two years of guerrilla raids on EIC police outposts across the Eastern Ghats.
events.detail: The 1882 Madras Forest Act had criminalised traditional podu (shifting cultivation) across the Agency hill tracts, and the Madras government's road-building used coerced tribal labour. Alluri Sitarama Raju (1897/98–1924), a Telugu Brahmin who had taken sannyasa and lived among the Konda Reddi and Koya tribals, organised a guerrilla force that on 22 August 1922 attacked the police station at Chintapalle, seizing weapons. Over two years they raided some twelve police outposts — Krishnadevipeta, Rajavommangi, Addatigala, Rampachodavaram — across the Visakhapatnam and East Godavari hill agencies, killing British and EIC officers (notably Scott Coward and Heron, who shot prisoners). The Madras government deployed Assam Rifles and the Malabar Special Force; Major Goodall took overall command. Raju was captured at Chintapalle on 7 May 1924, tied to a tree and shot on the spot — no trial. Roughly 100 Reddi-Koya rebels were killed in the campaign. Raju's combination of religious authority and tribal organisation prefigured the post-independence Naxalite turn in the same Eastern Ghats geography.

sources.label: M. Venkatarangaiya (ed.), The Freedom Struggle in Andhra Pradesh, vol. III (1968)
David Arnold, 'Rebellious Hillmen: The Gudem-Rampa Risings 1839–1924', in Subaltern Studies I (1982)

events.title: Vaikom Satyagraha
events.tooltip: Vaikom temple-road satyagraha, Travancore, 1924–1925
events.summary: Twenty months of satyagraha at Vaikom won the right of avarna (lower-caste) Hindus to walk the temple road — the first organised caste-rights mass action.
events.detail: The roads around the Mahadeva Temple at Vaikom in Travancore were closed to avarna (untouchable) castes — Ezhavas, Pulayas, Parayas — under Brahminical custom backed by princely-state law. T.K. Madhavan (Ezhava reformer), K.P. Kesava Menon, and K. Kelappan launched satyagraha on 30 March 1924, with mixed-caste batches deliberately walking the prohibited roads. Travancore police arrested participants daily for sixteen months; Periyar (E.V. Ramasamy) came from Tamil Nadu to lead, was jailed, returning twice. Gandhi visited in March 1925 and negotiated with the regent Maharani Sethu Lakshmi Bayi. The satyagraha ended on 23 November 1925 with the regent opening three of the four prohibited road-stretches; full temple entry was granted only with the Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936. Vaikom is the structural model — disciplined non-violent occupation, daily arrests, sustained organisation, sympathetic press — that Ambedkar's Mahad satyagraha (1927) and Kalaram (1930) would refine.

sources.label: T.K. Ravindran, Vaikkam Satyagraha and Gandhi (Sri Narayana Institute, 1975)
Robin Jeffrey, The Decline of Nayar Dominance: Society and Politics in Travancore 1847–1908 (1976) — context

events.title: Second Battle of Tarain
events.tooltip: Muhammad of Ghor defeats Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain, 1192
events.summary: Muhammad of Ghor's cavalry defeats the Chauhan confederation under Prithviraj III — the defeat that opens the Delhi Sultanate fourteen years later.
events.detail: After a humiliating defeat at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191, Muhammad of Ghor returned in 1192 with a reorganised cavalry-heavy force estimated at 120,000. Prithviraj Chauhan III, ruler of the Chauhan kingdom centred at Ajmer-Delhi, fielded a Rajput confederation of similar nominal size but slower in mobility. Ghor's mounted archers feigned retreat through the day; the Chauhans pursued, broke formation, and were destroyed in the late afternoon counter-attack. Prithviraj was captured and executed; the Chauhan kingdom collapsed within months. Ghor placed his slave-general Qutb-ud-din Aibak in charge of the conquered territory at Delhi. The Tarain defeat is the conventional opening of subcontinental sultanate-era history; the Mamluk dynasty Aibak founded fourteen years later is its institutional legacy.

sources.label: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanate to the Mughals — Part One (1997), ch. 1
Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate: A Political and Military History (1999), ch. 1

events.title: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate
events.tooltip: Qutb-ud-din Aibak crowned at Lahore, 1206; Mamluk dynasty established
events.summary: After Muhammad of Ghor's assassination, his slave-general Aibak crowned himself sultan at Lahore — the first of the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty rulers.
events.detail: Muhammad of Ghor was assassinated near the Indus on 15 March 1206 by Khokhar tribesmen. His Indian conquests went to his most senior slave-general (mamluk), Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who had administered the Delhi territory since Tarain. Aibak was formally crowned at Lahore on 25 June 1206 — a careful political act, since slave-generals were not conventionally enthroned and Aibak needed to claim succession by election among the Ghorid mamluks rather than by inheritance. The Sultanate's institutional shape — Persian-Turkic court, mamluk military elite, iqta land grants in lieu of salaries — was set in this first decade. Aibak began the Qutb Minar at Delhi (continued by Iltutmish) and the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque on the site of demolished Hindu and Jain temples in Mehrauli. He died at Lahore in 1210 in a polo accident.

caused_by.gloss: Tarain made Aibak's Delhi viceroyalty possible; Ghor's death made his independent sultanate inevitable.

sources.label: K.A. Nizami, Studies in Medieval Indian History and Culture (1966), ch. 2
Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999), ch. 2

events.title: Iltutmish consolidates the Sultanate
events.tooltip: Iltutmish accedes at Delhi, 1211; consolidates Mamluk rule
events.summary: Aibak's son-in-law and slave-general Iltutmish defeats rivals and consolidates the Sultanate — the real architect of its institutional shape.
events.detail: Aibak's son Aram Shah (1210–1211) lacked the military authority to hold the Mamluk coalition. Iltutmish — Turkic slave, son-in-law to Aibak, governor of Badaun — marched on Delhi in 1211, defeated Aram Shah at the battle of Jud (near Delhi), and took the throne. His twenty-five year reign (1211–1236) is the Sultanate's institutional founding period: the iqta system was systematised, the silver tanka and copper jital coinage standardised, the Turkic 'Forty' (Chahalgani) inner council established, the Qutb Minar completed, and the Sultanate received formal recognition from the Abbasid Caliph at Baghdad in 1229. He absorbed Sind and Bengal as tributaries and maintained a careful neutrality during Genghis Khan's Indus campaign of 1221, avoiding direct Mongol confrontation that would have ended the still-fragile state.

caused_by.gloss: Aibak's mamluk-elective succession framework collapsed under his son; Iltutmish's military takeover institutionalised what Aibak's coronation had only sketched.

sources.label: Satish Chandra, Medieval India — Part One (1997), ch. 2
Sunil Kumar, The Emergence of the Delhi Sultanate, 1192–1286 (2007)

events.title: Genghis Khan reaches the Indus
events.tooltip: Genghis Khan pursues Jalal ad-Din to the Indus, 1221
events.summary: Pursuing the Khwarezmian prince Jalal ad-Din, Genghis Khan reached the Indus — the closest Mongol approach to the Delhi Sultanate, deliberately not pursued.
events.detail: Genghis Khan's destruction of the Khwarezmian Empire (1219–1221) ended at the Battle of the Indus on 24 November 1221, when his force trapped Jalal ad-Din Mingburnu's army on the river. Jalal ad-Din famously escaped by leaping his horse from a cliff into the Indus and swimming to the Punjab side. Iltutmish, asked by Jalal ad-Din for refuge, refused — calculating that hosting the Mongols' enemy would invite a Mongol invasion the Sultanate could not survive. Genghis sent envoys to Delhi but withdrew in early 1222 rather than crossing the Indus, citing the climate. The decision spared the Sultanate the fate of Khwarezm, Bukhara, and Samarkand. Mongol pressure on the northwest frontier would persist for two centuries — the Sultanate maintained a permanent army of 300,000 in part to guard against renewed invasion.

location.name: Indus river crossing (near modern Kalabagh, Punjab)

sources.label: Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017), ch. 3
Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999), ch. 4 on Mongol relations

events.title: Reign of Razia Sultan
events.tooltip: Razia Sultan reigns at Delhi, 1236–1240; first woman ruler of Delhi
events.summary: Iltutmish's nominated daughter Razia held the Delhi throne for three and a half years before Turkic slave nobles deposed and killed her.
events.detail: Iltutmish nominated his daughter Razia as successor in 1236, having found his sons unfit. The Turkic slave-noble council (Chahalgani) initially passed her over for her brother Ruknuddin, but Ruknuddin's incompetence — and his mother's cruelty toward rival nobles — provoked a Delhi uprising that put Razia on the throne in November 1236. She ruled directly, dispensing with the veil at court, riding in male dress, and conducting durbar publicly. She promoted the Abyssinian slave Yaqut over Turkic noble objections; the resulting backlash, led by the governor of Bhatinda Malik Altunia, deposed her in April 1240. She married Altunia, raised an army, and was killed near Kaithal in October 1240 attempting to retake Delhi. The first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; the next would be Sultan Jahan Begum of Bhopal, seven hundred years later.

caused_by.gloss: Iltutmish's deathbed nomination of Razia over his sons set the conflict that defined her short reign — the Turkic 'Forty' would not accept a woman the council had not chosen itself.

sources.label: Minhaj-i-Siraj, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (c. 1260; trans. H.G. Raverty, 1881)
Rafiq Zakaria, Razia, Queen of India (1966)

events.title: Balban accedes to the Sultanate
events.tooltip: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban crowned at Delhi, 1266
events.summary: Former regent and slave-general Balban took the throne and broke the power of the Turkic slave-noble council that had run the Sultanate for fifty years.
events.detail: Balban — Turkic slave, son-in-law to Sultan Nasir-ud-din Mahmud, regent and effective ruler from 1246 — formally took the throne in 1266 after Mahmud's death. His twenty-year reign was a deliberate authoritarian reorganisation: the 'Forty' Turkic slave-noble council (Chahalgani) that had made and unmade the previous five sultans was systematically dismantled by execution, demotion, and selective promotion of non-Turkic loyalists. The court adopted Persian Sasanian protocols — sijda (prostration) and paibos (kissing the foot) became compulsory; the king-as-shadow-of-God doctrine was promulgated. Balban built a permanent army centred on Mongol-trained cavalry, reorganised intelligence under a network of barids (informers), and systematically destroyed the Mewati and Doab forest robbers who had been raiding Delhi. The model of personalised, centralised, ceremonially exalted sultanate rule that the Khaljis and Tughlaqs would inherit was Balban's design.

sources.label: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (c. 1357; partial Eng. trans. Elliot & Dowson)
Satish Chandra, Medieval India — Part One (1997), ch. 3

events.title: Alauddin Khalji's coronation
events.tooltip: Alauddin Khalji crowned at Delhi after killing his uncle, 1296
events.summary: Alauddin Khalji murdered his uncle Jalal-ud-din at Kara, then bribed his way to the Delhi throne — opening the Sultanate's most expansionist phase.
events.detail: The Khalji 'revolution' of 1290 had replaced the Mamluk Turks with a related but distinct Afghan-Turkic Khalji clan; the founder, Jalal-ud-din Firoz Khalji, was a moderate ruler in his late sixties. His nephew and son-in-law Alauddin, governor of Kara, returned from a successful Devagiri raid (1294) with vast plunder, invited Jalal-ud-din to a meeting at Kara on 19 July 1296, and had him murdered. Alauddin marched on Delhi, distributed the Devagiri treasure to nobles and soldiery, and was crowned in October 1296. His twenty-year reign (1296–1316) is the high water of Sultanate territorial reach: market price controls, currency and revenue reforms, repulse of six Mongol invasions, the southern campaigns of Malik Kafur, the sack of Chittor and Madurai. The Sultanate Alauddin built — directly administered, militarily formidable, fiscally dirigiste — was not equalled in centralised power until the Mughals.

sources.label: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh (c. 1311; trans. Mohammad Habib, 1931)
Banarsi Prasad Saksena, 'The Khaljis', in A Comprehensive History of India, vol. V (1970)

events.title: Alauddin's market price-control reforms
events.tooltip: Alauddin Khalji enforces price controls in Delhi, 1297–1305
events.summary: Three administered markets fixed prices on grain, cloth, slaves, and horses — funding a permanent army of 475,000 cavalry on stable wages.
events.detail: Alauddin Khalji's reforms set fixed prices for staples (wheat, barley, rice, pulses), cloth, sugar, slaves, horses, and cattle in three administered Delhi markets — the grain market, the cloth and luxury market, and the slave-and-horse market. Each market had a controller (shahna), price registers, surprise inspections, and harsh penalties for short measure (including, per Barani, removal of underweight quantities of flesh from the cheating merchant). Grain was procured from the Doab at fixed state-set prices and sold in Delhi at the same. The reforms were enforced rigorously enough that Barani records prices stayed stable through famine years. The political purpose was military: stable low prices let Alauddin pay 475,000 cavalry on a wage that would otherwise have required either inflation or land grants. The reforms collapsed within a year of Alauddin's death (1316) when his successor Mubarak Shah dismantled the controls and disbanded the army.

caused_by.gloss: The standing-army-on-cash-wages model required the price controls; without them the wages would not have purchased adequate provisions.

sources.label: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (c. 1357; partial Eng. trans. Elliot & Dowson)
Irfan Habib, 'The Price Regulations of Alauddin Khalji — A Defence of Zia Barani', Indian Economic and Social History Review 21:4 (1984)

events.title: Mongol siege of Delhi repulsed
events.tooltip: Alauddin holds Delhi against Targhi's Mongol force, 1303
events.summary: Alauddin held Siri Fort against a two-month Mongol siege under Targhi; the closest the Mongols ever came to taking Delhi.
events.detail: The sixth and most serious Mongol invasion of Alauddin's reign came in late 1303 under the Chagatai general Targhi, with a force estimated at 120,000. Alauddin was returning from the Chittor campaign, his army exhausted; he took refuge in the partly-built Siri fort outside Delhi rather than attempting battle in the open. Targhi besieged Siri for two months. The Mongols devastated the Doab countryside, but the fort held; their cavalry was unsuited to siege work and supply lines were stretched. Targhi withdrew in early 1304 without taking the city. Alauddin used the close-call to refortify Delhi, push the frontier outposts forward to Multan and Samana, and place the experienced general Ghazi Malik (later Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) in charge of the northwest frontier. After 1306 the Mongols stopped invading the Sultanate; the threat that had defined northwestern Indian politics for eighty years receded.

caused_by.gloss: Mongol pressure on the Sultanate's northwest persisted from the 1221 Indus campaign onwards; the 1303 siege was the high water of that pressure before it receded.

sources.label: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999), ch. 8
Iqtidar Husain Siddiqui, Indo-Persian Historiography up to the Thirteenth Century (2010)

events.title: Siege of Chittor
events.tooltip: Alauddin Khalji takes Chittor from Ratnasimha, 1303
events.summary: Alauddin's eight-month siege of Chittor ended in the fortress's fall and the jauhar of its women — the campaign that produced the Padmini legend.
events.detail: Alauddin Khalji marched on Chittor in January 1303, besieging the Mewar fortress of Rana Ratnasimha (the Rajput Ratan Singh of later legend). The siege lasted eight months; Chittor fell on 26 August 1303. The defending garrison performed saka — a final suicidal sortie — while the women including the queen, in Rajput tradition, performed jauhar (mass self-immolation). The campaign is the principal subject of Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Awadhi-language Padmavat (1540), which centred the campaign on Alauddin's desire for Ratnasimha's queen Padmini — a story for which there is no contemporary evidence and which Amir Khusrau (who accompanied Alauddin) does not mention. Chittor became part of the Sultanate's directly-administered territory under Alauddin's son Khizr Khan, then was retaken by Hammir Singh of Mewar in 1326 after Khalji collapse. The Padmini story would shape Hindu-Muslim communal historiography from the late 16th century onwards.

caused_by.gloss: Alauddin's expansionist reign required the elimination of the western Rajput powers as a precondition for the southern campaigns; Chittor was the fortress that controlled the Mewar approach.

sources.label: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh (c. 1311)
Ramya Sreenivasan, The Many Lives of a Rajput Queen: Heroic Pasts in India, c. 1500–1900 (2007)

events.title: Malik Kafur sacks Madurai
events.tooltip: Malik Kafur reaches Madurai for Alauddin Khalji, 1311
events.summary: Alauddin's slave-general Malik Kafur reached Madurai — the southernmost Sultanate raid, returning to Delhi with 612 elephants and 96,000 maunds of gold.
events.detail: Malik Kafur (Hazar-Dinari) — Alauddin Khalji's eunuch slave-general, captured at the Gujarat campaign of 1297 — led four southern campaigns between 1307 and 1311 that brought the entire peninsula under tribute. The first two extracted treaty payments from the Yadavas of Devagiri and the Kakatiyas of Warangal. The 1310 campaign defeated the Hoysalas at their capital Dwarasamudra. The 1311 final campaign reached Madurai under the Pandyas, sacked the city and the Meenakshi temple, and returned to Delhi with reportedly 612 elephants, 96,000 maunds of gold (about 241 tonnes), and 20,000 horses. None of these southern kingdoms were annexed — they remained tributary, a model the Mughals would later follow. The Khalji southern campaigns established the convention that subcontinental empires extract tribute from the Deccan rather than directly administering it. Within five years all of it had unravelled: by 1316 the Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas, and Pandyas had stopped paying.

caused_by.gloss: The southern campaigns paid for themselves and replenished the treasury that funded the standing army; the price-control state needed a steady inflow of plunder to sustain the wage bill.

sources.label: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh (c. 1311)
K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (1955), ch. on the Pandyas

events.title: Tughlaq dynasty founded
events.tooltip: Ghazi Malik takes Delhi as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, 1320
events.summary: Ghazi Malik, frontier governor and veteran of the Mongol wars, killed the usurper Khusrau Khan and founded the Tughlaq dynasty.
events.detail: After Alauddin Khalji's death (1316) the Khalji line collapsed in four years of court intrigue. Mubarak Shah (1316–1320) was murdered by his lover Khusrau Khan, an ennobled Hindu convert, who briefly held the throne as Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah (1320). The Turkic-Afghan nobility refused to accept his rule. Ghazi Malik — Punjabi Turk, governor of Dipalpur, veteran of twenty-eight battles against the Mongols — marched on Delhi with his son Muhammad (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq), defeated Khusrau at the battle of Saraswati on 5 September 1320, and was crowned as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq. The Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1413) is the Sultanate's high imperial phase under its first three rulers (Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad, Firuz Shah) and its long disintegration after Firuz Shah's death (1388).

sources.label: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (c. 1357)
Mahdi Husain, Tughluq Dynasty (1963)

events.title: Capital shifted to Daulatabad
events.tooltip: Muhammad bin Tughlaq orders capital shift to Daulatabad, 1327
events.summary: Muhammad bin Tughlaq ordered Delhi's administrative class to march 1,100 km south to Devagiri — renamed Daulatabad — and reversed the order within two years.
events.detail: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reasoning for the 1327 capital shift was partly strategic — Devagiri was central to his Deccan tribute network, defensible, and out of Mongol raid range — and partly that he wanted Delhi's Persian-Turkic elite incorporated into a southern administration he was building from converts and lower-caste military entrepreneurs. The order required the entire administrative class — nobles, scholars, ulama, merchants — to relocate 1,100 kilometres. Barani, who hated the policy, records that the order was enforced ruthlessly: a blind man and a lame man were dragged from their homes; the lame man's body fell apart on the road. Within two years Muhammad reversed the order — Devagiri's water supply could not sustain the population, the southern revenue was insufficient, and Delhi was being overrun by Mongol raids. The reverse migration killed many of the survivors of the first one. The episode became the canonical case in Sultanate historiography of imperial overreach.

caused_by.gloss: The Tughlaq dynasty's centralised tribute model required a southern administrative base; Devagiri was the obvious geographical centre for the deccan revenue stream Malik Kafur had inaugurated.

sources.label: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (c. 1355; trans. H.A.R. Gibb, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1929)
Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (c. 1357)
Mahdi Husain, The Rise and Fall of Muhammad bin Tughluq (1938)

events.title: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency
events.tooltip: Muhammad bin Tughlaq issues copper token currency, 1329–1332
events.summary: Token copper coins issued at silver-tanka face value to fund expansion, withdrawn within four years after mass forgery destroyed their acceptance.
events.detail: In 1329 Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued copper coins valued at the silver tanka (the standard Sultanate currency) — a fiduciary token currency unprecedented in subcontinental practice. The motivation was fiscal: the southern campaigns and capital-shift had drained the treasury, the Mongol frontier needed funding, and Muhammad's planned Khurasan campaign required cash. Token currency would let him meet these obligations without depleting silver reserves. The system collapsed because the state failed to monopolise minting: counterfeiting was easy (copper was cheap and abundant), and within months parallel circulation of forged tokens made the official issue worthless. Hindu zamindars, Barani records, paid their land tax in counterfeit while keeping silver tankas in their treasuries. Muhammad withdrew the issue in 1332, redeeming all tokens — including the forgeries — at face value, which devastated the treasury he had hoped to refill. The episode is the second canonical case (after Daulatabad) in Sultanate-era historiography of administrative overreach.

caused_by.gloss: The capital-shift's fiscal damage made the token-currency expedient appear necessary; the two episodes together are usually read as a unit in Tughlaq historiography.

links.label: Wikipedia: Muhammad bin Tughluq — Token currency

sources.label: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (c. 1357)
Irfan Habib, 'Currency System of the Mughal Empire (1556–1707)', Medieval India Quarterly 4 (1961) — historical context section

events.title: Bahmani Sultanate breaks away
events.tooltip: Hasan Gangu founds the Bahmani Sultanate at Daulatabad, 1347
events.summary: Deccan amirs revolted against Tughlaq rule and founded the Bahmani Sultanate — the first independent Muslim kingdom in the south.
events.detail: The Tughlaq Daulatabad project collapsed into rebellion. In 1345 the southern amirs of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Deccan administration revolted; in August 1347 the rebel commander Hasan Gangu was crowned at Daulatabad as Alauddin Bahman Shah, founding the Bahmani Sultanate. Capital moved to Gulbarga in 1347 and to Bidar in 1429. Bahmani rule lasted until 1527, when the kingdom fragmented into the five Deccan Sultanates (Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Berar, Bidar, Golconda) — the same kingdoms Akbar's grandson Aurangzeb would spend his reign annexing. The Bahmani breakaway is the structural turning point in Sultanate history: from 1347 onward the Delhi Sultanate is a north-Indian power, never again the subcontinental tribute-extractor of the Khalji-Tughlaq high period. The Vijayanagara empire (founded 1336) had already established the Hindu-ruled south; Bahmani gave the Deccan its own Muslim political tradition, distinct from Delhi.

caused_by.gloss: The capital shift placed Tughlaq elites in the Deccan; their later revolt against the failed administration produced the Bahmani breakaway from the same geography.

sources.label: H.K. Sherwani, The Bahmanis of the Deccan (1985)
Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300–1761 (2005)

events.title: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's accession
events.tooltip: Firuz Shah Tughlaq crowned, 1351; reign of consolidation and decline
events.summary: Firuz Shah's 37-year reign abandoned expansionism, restored orthodox patronage, and presided over the Sultanate's contraction to a north-Indian regional power.
events.detail: Muhammad bin Tughlaq died on campaign in Sind in March 1351. His cousin Firuz Shah was crowned at Thatta and brought the army back to Delhi after settling Sind. His reign (1351–1388) is conventionally read as the Sultanate's contraction-and-stabilisation phase. Firuz abandoned the southern claims, commuted many cash-revenue obligations to in-kind levies, restored land grants (waqfs and madad-i-maash) the previous reigns had resumed, founded several new towns (Hisar, Firuzabad, Jaunpur), built irrigation canals from the Yamuna and Sutlej, and codified the jizya tax with new severity — the first systematic application of jizya to Brahmins, who had previously been exempt. He patronised orthodox Sunni ulama including Barani in his retirement. The reign was prosperous and culturally productive but politically static; the centralised imperial machine of the Khaljis and early Tughlaqs was not rebuilt. After Firuz's death in 1388 the Sultanate fragmented quickly.

caused_by.gloss: Firuz's reign was a deliberate retreat from his cousin's expansionism and fiscal experimentation; the contrast was the political identity of the new regime.

sources.label: Shams-i Siraj Afif, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (late 14th c.; partial Eng. trans. Elliot & Dowson)
Mahdi Husain, Tughluq Dynasty (1963)

events.title: Ziauddin Barani writes Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi
events.tooltip: Barani writes Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi at Delhi, c. 1357
events.summary: At seventy, exiled and impoverished after Muhammad bin Tughlaq's death, Barani writes the most opinionated chronicle of the Delhi Sultanate.
events.detail: Ziauddin Barani spent seventeen years as nadim (court companion) to Muhammad bin Tughlaq before falling from favour after the sultan's death in 1351. Stripped of office and lands, in his late sixties he wrote the Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (c. 1357), a Persian chronicle of the Delhi Sultanate from Balban's accession (1266) through Firuz Shah Tughlaq's reign. The text is reactionary in argument — Barani believed the older Turkic-Persian aristocracy should govern, against Muhammad bin Tughlaq's promotion of converts and lower-caste men — and extraordinarily candid as autobiography of an elite class watching its world dissolve. Read alongside his Fatawa-i Jahandari (a treatise on kingship), the Tarikh is the most ideologically explicit Sultanate text. Modern historians use it both as source and as window into 14th-century elite anxieties.

caused_by.gloss: Firuz Shah's restoration of orthodox patronage gave the disgraced Barani both an audience for his Sultanate-restorationist ideology and a reigning sultan to dedicate the work to.

sources.label: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (ed. Sayyid Ahmad Khan, 1862; partial Eng. trans. H.M. Elliot, History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, vol. III)
Mohammad Habib & Khaliq Ahmad Nizami, A Comprehensive History of India, Vol. V: The Delhi Sultanate (1970), ch. on historiography
Peter Hardy, Historians of Medieval India (1960), ch. 2

events.title: Timur sacks Delhi
events.tooltip: Timur sacks Delhi, December 1398; Sultanate effectively destroyed
events.summary: Timur's three-day sack killed an estimated 100,000 and ended Tughlaq central authority — the collapse the Sayyids and Lodis would briefly hold.
events.detail: Timur (Tamerlane) crossed the Indus in September 1398, citing the religious laxity of the Tughlaq state — a transparent pretext for plunder. He defeated Mahmud Tughlaq's force outside Delhi on 17 December 1398 and entered the city the next day. The sack lasted three days; Timur's chronicler Sharaf ad-Din Yazdi records that 'every soldier obtained more than twenty persons as slaves' and that the heads of the dead built a pyramid outside the gates. Modern estimates range from 100,000 to 200,000 killed in Delhi alone. Timur withdrew in January 1399 with the Sultanate's accumulated treasure, the entire skilled artisan class (taken as slaves to Samarkand), and one thousand stonemasons used to build the Bibi-Khanym Mosque. The Tughlaq central authority never recovered; the Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451) and the Lodi dynasty (1451–1526) ruled an empire reduced from subcontinental to north-Indian.

sources.label: Sharaf ad-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama (c. 1424; partial trans. Elliot & Dowson)
Beatrice Forbes Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

events.title: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi dynasty
events.tooltip: Bahlul Lodi takes Delhi, 1451; first Afghan dynasty of Sultanate
events.summary: Bahlul Lodi, the Sirhind-based Afghan governor, took Delhi from the last Sayyid sultan and founded the Sultanate's first Afghan-tribal dynasty.
events.detail: The Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451) — claiming descent from the Prophet through their founder Khizr Khan — never extended its writ much beyond the Delhi-Doab region after Timur's destruction. The last Sayyid sultan Alam Shah (1445–1451), demoralised, retired voluntarily to Badaun. Bahlul Lodi, the Afghan governor of Sirhind from a Pashtun military family that had served the Tughlaqs, marched on Delhi in April 1451 and was crowned on 19 April. The Lodi dynasty (1451–1526) is the Sultanate's last and the first ruled by a frankly Afghan-tribal elite rather than Turkic-Persian one — a difference that would matter to Babur's calculation seventy-five years later. Bahlul's thirty-eight-year reign re-extended Sultanate authority over Jaunpur (1483) and the Doab and Punjab; his son Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) shifted the capital to Agra. The dynasty ended at Panipat in 1526 when Ibrahim Lodi fell to Babur.

caused_by.gloss: Timur's destruction of central Tughlaq authority created the post-Sultanate vacuum the Sayyids and Lodis successively filled — neither rebuilding the imperial apparatus.

sources.label: K.S. Lal, Twilight of the Sultanate (1963)
Iqtidar Husain Siddiqui, Afghan Despotism in India (1969)

events.title: Ibrahim Lodi's accession
events.tooltip: Ibrahim Lodi crowned at Agra, 1517; tensions with Afghan nobility set up Panipat
events.summary: Ibrahim Lodi's centralising policies and humiliations of senior Afghan nobles drove rebellions that culminated in Daulat Khan Lodi inviting Babur to invade.
events.detail: Sikandar Lodi died in November 1517; his son Ibrahim was crowned at Agra (which Sikandar had made the capital in 1504) on 22 November. Ibrahim's nine-year reign (1517–1526) is the Sultanate's last. He attempted to centralise power against the Afghan tribal nobility his grandfather and father had relied on — demanding strict court protocol, refusing to share authority, executing senior amirs on suspicion. The result was rebellion: the Punjab governor Daulat Khan Lodi and Ibrahim's own uncle Alam Khan Lodi separately conspired to bring in Babur from Kabul as a counterweight. Ibrahim defeated Alam Khan's bid (1524) but Babur, after his fifth Hindustan raid, met Ibrahim at Panipat on 21 April 1526. Ibrahim died on the field — the first sultan of Delhi to die in battle since Iltutmish's wars three centuries earlier. The Sultanate ended at Panipat; the Mughal Empire began on the same field on the same day.

caused_by.gloss: The Lodi reliance on Afghan-tribal nobility was the regime's organising principle; Ibrahim's attempt to centralise against it broke the political settlement his grandfather had built.

sources.label: Babur, Baburnama (trans. Wheeler M. Thackston, 1996)
K.S. Lal, Twilight of the Sultanate (1963)

events.title: Battle of Chausa
events.tooltip: Sher Shah Suri defeats Humayun, Chausa, 1539
events.summary: Sher Khan's Afghan forces routed Humayun on the bank of the Karmanasa, ending Mughal rule in north India for fifteen years.
events.detail: Humayun had pursued the rising Afghan chief Sher Khan into Bihar, expecting a quick suppression. Sher Khan instead drew the Mughals into the rains, struck their camp on the night of 26 June 1539, and broke the army at the Karmanasa river. Humayun escaped only because a water-carrier named Nizam floated him across on an inflated buffalo-skin — a debt the emperor honoured years later by seating Nizam on the throne for a day. Sher Khan now styled himself Sher Shah, took Delhi the next year, and ruled an empire stretching from Bengal to the Indus until his death by gunpowder accident at Kalinjar in 1545.

sources.label: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals — Part Two (1999)
Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi (c. 1580)

events.title: Sher Shah's administrative reforms
events.tooltip: Rupee, Grand Trunk Road, land revenue (Sur), 1540–1545
events.summary: Sher Shah's five-year reign rebuilt the post road, standardised silver coinage as the rupiya, and codified a land-revenue system Akbar would later inherit.
events.detail: Sher Shah took an empire he had won by force and ran it as an administrator. The silver rupiya he minted at 178 grains became the unit of account that survived through the Mughal, Maratha, EIC, British, and Republic regimes — the modern rupee descends directly from it. He repaved and extended the Sadak-e-Azam from Sonargaon in Bengal to Kabul, with caravan-sarais at every stage and shaded trees along the verge. His revenue system, based on direct measurement of cultivated land and fixed cash rates, gave the cultivator a written entitlement and the state a predictable yield. Akbar's vizier Todar Mal would build the entire Mughal zabt system on this scaffolding.

location.name: Sur empire (capital at Delhi; tomb at Sasaram)

sources.label: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals — Part Two (1999)
Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India 1556–1707 (1963; rev. 1999)

caused_by.gloss: Chausa won Sher Shah the empire; the reforms were how he held it.

events.title: Battle of Wandiwash
events.tooltip: Battle of Wandiwash, 22 January 1760 — Coote defeats Lally; ends French India
events.summary: Eyre Coote's EIC force routed Lally-Tollendal at Wandiwash — end of French ambitions on the subcontinent; British monopoly of European expansion.
events.detail: The Third Carnatic War (1756–63), the Indian theatre of the Seven Years' War, pitted Joseph François Dupleix's successor Thomas-Arthur de Lally-Tollendal against the EIC under Eyre Coote. Lally had taken Fort St David from the British in 1758 and besieged Madras 1758–59 unsuccessfully. Coote, with 1,900 European and 2,100 sepoy troops, met Lally's 2,250 European and 1,300 sepoy force outside Wandiwash (Vandavasi) on 22 January 1760. The French line broke after Lally's cavalry withdrew without engaging; ~600 French casualties to Coote's 200. The Wandiwash defeat was followed by the British siege of Pondicherry (May 1760 – January 1761) which capitulated to Coote on 16 January 1761. The Treaty of Paris (1763) returned Pondicherry to France but stripped it of fortifications and limited it to commercial functions only — a permanent demilitarisation that ended any French ambition to a sub-continental territorial presence. Pondicherry survived as a four-enclave commercial holding until 1954. After Wandiwash the EIC had no European rival on Indian soil; the field was open for the post-1761 expansion through Bengal, the Carnatic, and the Anglo-Mysore wars.

sources.label: G.J. Bryant, The Emergence of British Power in India 1600–1784 (2013)
S.P. Sen, The French in India: First Establishment and Struggle (1947)

events.title: Battle of Mahidpur — Third Anglo-Maratha War closure
events.tooltip: Battle of Mahidpur, 21 December 1817 — closes the Third Anglo-Maratha War
events.summary: Hislop defeated Holkar's army at Mahidpur on the Sipra — the decisive engagement of the Third Anglo-Maratha War that ended the Confederacy as a sovereign power.
events.detail: The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) was Lord Hastings's deliberate dismantling of the surviving Maratha Confederacy — Peshwa Bajirao II at Pune, Sindhia at Gwalior, Holkar at Indore, Bhonsle at Nagpur. The proximate cause was the Pindari raids (free-booting Maratha-affiliated cavalry that had ravaged EIC territory through the 1810s). Three coordinated EIC armies under Hastings, Hislop, and Malcolm advanced from Bengal, the Deccan, and Gujarat. Mahidpur on 21 December 1817 — Sir Thomas Hislop with 5,500 EIC troops against Malhar Rao Holkar III's 35,000 Maratha-Pindari force on the Sipra river — was the decisive set-piece engagement: ~3,000 Maratha dead, ~800 EIC casualties. Subsequent campaigns — the Peshwa's defeat at Koregaon (1 January 1818), the surrender of Bajirao II at Mhow (3 June 1818), the captures of Asirgarh and Trimbakji's Berar — completed the dismantling. The Treaty of Mandsaur (Holkar, January 1818) and the formal extinction of the Peshwa office (June 1818) ended the Maratha Confederacy as a sovereign Indian power. Bajirao II was pensioned at Bithoor (UP) — where his adopted son Nana Sahib would later figure as a 1857 leader.

sources.label: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600–1818 (1993)
John Malcolm, A Memoir of Central India (1823)

events.title: First Anglo-Afghan War — retreat from Kabul
events.tooltip: Retreat from Kabul, January 1842 — annihilation of Elphinstone's army
events.summary: Elphinstone's 16,500-strong EIC force was annihilated retreating Kabul to Jalalabad through the passes — one survivor, Dr Brydon, reached Jalalabad alive.
events.detail: The First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42) was Lord Auckland's pre-emptive intervention in Afghanistan to install Shah Shuja over Dost Mohammed Khan, framed by the Russian-threat anxieties of the Great Game. The Army of the Indus took Kabul in August 1839; Shah Shuja was installed; an EIC garrison of 4,500 troops and ~12,000 camp followers under Elphinstone settled in. By autumn 1841 anti-Shuja Afghan resistance under Akbar Khan (Dost Mohammed's son) had taken Kabul's outskirts. The British envoy William Macnaghten was murdered at a December parley with Akbar. On 6 January 1842 Elphinstone began the withdrawal under safe-conduct guarantees that Akbar's tribal allies did not honour. The 90-mile retreat through the Khurd Kabul, Tezeen, and Jagdalak passes in winter snow saw the column annihilated by sniping, ambush, and exposure. Of ~16,500 who left Kabul, one combatant — assistant surgeon William Brydon — reached Jalalabad on 13 January (about 100 captives plus families were later released). The Army of Retribution returned to Kabul in autumn 1842 to recover prisoners and bazaar-burn the city, then withdrew. The Auckland intervention was a strategic catastrophe and the formative imperial-overreach lesson of the early Victorian Raj.

sources.label: William Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
Lady Florentia Sale, Journal of the Disasters in Afghanistan 1841–42 (1843)

events.title: Battle of Gujrat — Second Anglo-Sikh War closure
events.tooltip: Battle of Gujrat, 21 February 1849 — Hugh Gough defeats the Khalsa Army
events.summary: Hugh Gough defeated the Khalsa Army on the Chenab at Gujrat — annexation of Punjab followed. The last independent indigenous Indian state fell.
events.detail: Ranjit Singh's Sarkar-i-Khalsa unravelled in the seven-year succession bloodletting that followed his 1839 death. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) ended with the Treaty of Lahore (March 1846) ceding Jullundur Doab and (sold separately to Gulab Singh) Kashmir, but leaving a residual Sikh state under Maharani Jind Kaur's regency for Duleep Singh. The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–49) was triggered by the Multan revolt under Diwan Mulraj and joined by Sher Singh Attariwala's Sikh army. After the bloody, indecisive Battle of Chillianwala (13 January 1849) — Sir Hugh Gough's costly assault on the Sikh position that produced ~2,400 EIC casualties to ~3,500 Sikh — Gough reorganised and met the Sikh army at Gujrat on the Chenab on 21 February 1849. The artillery duel and infantry assault routed the Khalsa; ~5,000 Sikh casualties to ~800 EIC. The Sikh forces surrendered at Rawalpindi on 14 March 1849, ceremonially laying down arms with the cry 'Today Ranjit Singh has died.' Dalhousie's annexation proclamation of 29 March 1849 brought the Punjab under EIC sovereignty; Duleep Singh, ten years old, surrendered the Koh-i-Noor and was sent to England under the guardianship of Dr John Login. The Punjab annexation closed the EIC's territorial expansion — the last sovereign indigenous Indian state had fallen.

sources.label: Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs vol. II (1966)
J.D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (1849)

events.title: Third Anglo-Burmese War — annexation of Upper Burma
