events.tooltip: Third Anglo-Burmese War, 7–29 November 1885 — annexation of Upper Burma
events.summary: Three-week campaign deposed King Thibaw at Mandalay; Upper Burma was annexed to British India 1 January 1886, completing the EIC-and-Crown absorption of Burma.
events.detail: Britain had taken Lower Burma in two earlier wars (1824–26 Treaty of Yandabo: Arakan and Tenasserim; 1852: Pegu and the Irrawaddy delta). Upper Burma under the Konbaung dynasty remained sovereign until November 1885. The proximate British casus belli was the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation logging dispute and Burmese moves towards a French commercial-and-military treaty. Lord Dufferin (Viceroy 1884–88) ordered the invasion. Major-General Sir Harry Prendergast's Burma Field Force of 11,000 troops sailed up the Irrawaddy in 55 transports; Mandalay fell on 28 November 1885 with minimal resistance. King Thibaw and Queen Supayalat were deposed and exiled to Ratnagiri (Maharashtra) where Thibaw lived until 1916. Upper Burma was annexed by proclamation 1 January 1886 and added to British India as a province administered from Rangoon. The post-annexation Burmese resistance — the Pacification campaign through 1890, the long Burma underground — would persist through the colonial period; Aung San and the Thirty Comrades' alliance with Japan in 1942 was the long answer. Burma was separated from India under the GOI Act 1935 (effective 1937) and became independent 4 January 1948.

sources.label: Thant Myint-U, The Making of Modern Burma (2001)
Sudha Shah, The King in Exile: The Fall of the Royal Family of Burma (2012)

people.name: Raja Rammohan Roy
people.tooltip: Rammohan Roy (1772–1833), founder of Brahmo Sabha; campaigner against sati
people.summary: Bengali polyglot reformer; founded the Brahmo Sabha 1828; campaigned for the abolition of sati (1829); died at Bristol on a mission for the Mughal emperor.

track.tooltip: Tuhfat al-Muwahhidin ('Gift to Monotheists') in Persian and Arabic, c. 1803
track.summary: First treatise — Persian-Arabic monotheist tract attacking image-worship, polytheism, and supernatural claim across all religious traditions.
track.note: Anonymous publication. Drew on Mu'tazila rationalist Islam, the Vedantic monism he had absorbed from his father's Vaishnava household, and Sufi pluralism. Already at thirty he had a comparative-religion vocabulary unusual in early-nineteenth-century India.

track.tooltip: Service in the EIC revenue establishment, 1805–1814
track.summary: Worked in the EIC's Bhagalpur and Rangpur revenue offices under John Digby — learning English, Company administration, Christian-rationalist literature.
track.note: Digby was his patron and a key influence — gave him a Western-philosophy reading list including the Unitarians. Roy retired with a private fortune in 1814; from 1815 ran his reform programme from Calcutta until his 1830 departure for England.

track.tooltip: Vedanta translations and the Atmiya Sabha, 1815–1820
track.summary: Translated the Upanishads (Kena, Isha, Katha) into Bengali and English; founded the Atmiya Sabha 1815 — first Calcutta Hindu-monotheist reform society.
track.note: His Bengali Upanishad translations are the first vernacular Bengali Vedanta — argued the Upanishads taught a single formless God consistent with rational monotheism, and that image-worship was a later corruption. The argument prefigured Dayananda Saraswati's Arya Samaj a half-century later.

track.tooltip: Anti-sati campaign — petitions, tracts, Bentinck's 1829 ban
track.summary: Twelve-year campaign through tracts, petitions, testimony. Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 4 December 1829 banned the practice; Roy's framing was the vehicle.
track.note: His sister-in-law had been forced onto her husband's pyre in 1812 — the personal experience he cited as the campaign's origin. Petitioned Lord Hastings, then Lord Bentinck. The orthodox Hindu Dharma Sabha petitioned the Privy Council against the ban; Roy travelled to England in 1830 partly to defend the ban there.

track.tooltip: Publishes The Precepts of Jesus, 1820
track.summary: Published The Precepts of Jesus — gospel moral teachings stripped of supernatural claim. Triggered Trinitarian–Unitarian controversy with Serampore Baptists.
track.note: Joshua Marshman of Serampore attacked the work as Socinianism. Roy's three Appeal to the Christian Public defenses are sustained Sanskrit-and-Greek scriptural exegesis from a non-Christian author. The English Unitarian Mission (Adam, Yates) and the Bengali reform movement converged through the 1820s.

track.tooltip: Memorial to Lord Amherst on English-language education, 11 December 1823
track.summary: Petitioned Amherst against the proposed Sanskrit College — argued for English-and-modern-sciences education over classical schooling. Macaulay 1835 echoed.
track.note: His position — that Sanskrit revival would 'load the minds of youth with grammatical niceties and metaphysical distinctions of little or no practical use' — became the Indian-modernist position in the Anglicist-Orientalist controversy. Macaulay's 1835 Minute on Indian Education and the Bentinck Resolution 1835 implemented it. The Hindu College (1817) and the Sanskrit College (1824) became the two-pole institutional outcome.

track.tooltip: Founds the Brahmo Sabha at Chitpur, Calcutta, 20 August 1828
track.summary: Founded the Brahmo Sabha (later Brahmo Samaj) for monotheist Hindu worship — no images, no priestly mediation, scriptural Vedanta in Sanskrit and Bengali.
track.note: Liturgy: Vedantic recitation, devotional song, prayer to a formless God. Membership initially small, drawn from Calcutta bhadralok families (Tagores, Mukherjees). Debendranath Tagore (Rabindranath's father) reorganised the Sabha as Brahmo Samaj 1843 and gave it the institutional form that ran through Keshub Chunder Sen's reforms to its modern survival.

track.tooltip: Sent to England as envoy of Mughal emperor Akbar II, November 1830
track.summary: Akbar II conferred the title 'Raja' and sent him to England to petition for restoration of Mughal pension — first Indian Hindu envoy to Europe.
track.note: Met Bentham, Macaulay, the Unitarian intellectuals; testified before the parliamentary Select Committee on the EIC charter renewal in 1832. Died at Stapleton Grove, Bristol, on 27 September 1833 of meningitis. Buried at Arnos Vale Cemetery, Bristol — the first Indian Hindu reformer buried in England, the chhatri (canopy memorial) at Arnos Vale erected by Dwarakanath Tagore in 1843.

track.tooltip: Death at Stapleton Grove, Bristol, 27 September 1833
track.summary: Died at Bristol of meningitis at sixty-one. Buried at Arnos Vale Cemetery — the chhatri memorial erected by Dwarakanath Tagore 1843 still stands.
track.note: Brahmo Samaj continued under Debendranath, then Keshub Chunder Sen, then the post-1880 schism into the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj. The intellectual lineage runs through Dayananda's Arya Samaj, Vivekananda's Vedanta, Tagore's Visva-Bharati, and indirectly into the Indian liberal-modernist tradition that Nehru would lead.

people.name: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
people.tooltip: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820–1891), Bengali reformer and Sanskritist
people.summary: Sanskrit College Principal; campaigned for the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856; rebuilt Bengali prose; founded ~35 girls' schools across rural Bengal.

track.tooltip: Vidyasagar title from Sanskrit College, 1839; teaching post 1841
track.summary: Conferred 'Vidyasagar' by Sanskrit College examination 1839 at nineteen. Joined Fort William College as head pandit 1841; Sanskrit College 1846.
track.note: Master of every Sanskrit literary and philosophical genre. Bengali Romantic prose owes its modern register to his Bodhoday (1851), Betal Panchabingsati (1847), Sitar Banobash (1860), and Akhyan Manjari (1862) — primers and adapted-classical retellings that became standard Bengali school texts for a century.

track.tooltip: Sanskrit College Principal — opens admission to lower castes, 1851
track.summary: Made Principal at thirty; opened Sanskrit College admission to non-Brahmin castes (1851) — radical departure. Resigned 1858 over EIC interference.
track.note: Reformed the curriculum: introduced English, Western philosophy, mathematics. The lower-caste admission decision broke with two thousand years of Brahmin monopoly on Sanskrit learning at premier institutions. The 1858 resignation followed his refusal to accept the EIC director's interference; he never returned to government service.

track.tooltip: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act XV of 1856, 26 July 1856
track.summary: Drafted and saw through the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act XV of 1856 — legalised remarriage of Hindu widows. Sanskrit-textual defences ran 1854–56.
track.note: Two Bengali tracts (1855, 1856) — Hindu Vidhava Vivah Hayoa Uchit Kina ('Should Hindu Widow Remarriage Be Legal?') — built the case from Parashara-smriti citations against orthodox Sanskrit-textual opposition. He personally underwrote and funded ~25 widow remarriages over the next two decades, including his only son Narayan Chandra's 1870 marriage to a Brahmin widow.

track.tooltip: Founds 35 girls' schools across rural Bengal, 1857–58
track.summary: Founded 35 model girls' schools across Hooghly, Burdwan, Midnapore, Nadia in 1857–58 — district-level institutional density unprecedented for girls.
track.note: The schools were funded substantially out of his own pocket and from the Bethune School Fund. The provincial education department later assumed the schools — but underfunded them. Most closed by the 1870s. Vidyasagar's correspondence with Bethune (founder of the parallel Bethune College for women in Calcutta 1849) documents the institutional precariousness of mid-Victorian Bengali women's education.

track.tooltip: Anti-Kulin polygamy tracts, 1871–1873
track.summary: Campaigned against Kulin Brahmin polygamy through two Bengali tracts (1871, 1873). Petitioned the Bengal government for an Act; the orthodox lobby blocked it.
track.note: Kulin Brahmin polygamy — where a single Kulin man might be ritually married to dozens of women across his lifetime, with the women returning to natal households as effective grass-widows — was the second great Bengali women's-rights campaign after widow remarriage. The campaign failed legislatively but documented the practice for the first time. The 1955 Hindu Marriage Act made monogamy the legal default seventy years after Vidyasagar's case.

track.tooltip: Retreat to Karmatar (Jharkhand), 1880–1891
track.summary: Withdrew from Calcutta to Karmatar in the Santhal hills 1880; spent the last decade among Santhal villagers, ran a dispensary, taught village children.
track.note: The withdrawal was framed by his disillusionment with bhadralok Calcutta orthodoxy — the same orthodoxy that had blocked widow-remarriage reform on the ground despite the 1856 Act. The Santhal years are documented in his nephew's biography and in Rabindranath's elegiac 1891 Bengali essay 'Vidyasagar Charit'. He died at Karmatar of cancer 29 July 1891.

people.name: Swami Vivekananda
people.tooltip: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), founder of Ramakrishna Mission
people.summary: Bengali Brahmo-turned-Vedantin; principal disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa; Chicago Parliament of Religions 1893; founded the Ramakrishna Mission 1897.

track.tooltip: First meets Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar, November 1881
track.summary: Eighteen-year-old Brahmo college student met Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar Kali temple. Five years of intermittent visits ended with Ramakrishna's 1886 death.
track.note: Born Narendranath Dutta in a Calcutta Kayastha household — father Vishwanath Dutta a Calcutta High Court attorney. Brahmo Samaj education; rationalist, sceptical, drawn to Western philosophy. The Ramakrishna encounter was the formative confrontation — the rationalist who could not dismiss the saint.

track.tooltip: Sannyas at Baranagar after Ramakrishna's death, 1886
track.summary: Took sannyas with Ramakrishna's inner circle after the master's death (16 August 1886). Established the Baranagar Math as the brotherhood's first house.
track.note: Twelve disciples took the vows on Christmas Eve 1886 around a fire at Antpur. The Baranagar Math (December 1886 onward) was funded by Surendranath Mitra; the brotherhood lived in extreme poverty for the next four years before Vivekananda's wandering-monk years began.

track.tooltip: Parivrajaka — wandering-monk years across India, 1888–1892
track.summary: Four years walking the subcontinent as a parivrajaka — Banaras, Brindavan, the Himalayas, Rajputana, Khetri, Madras, finally Kanyakumari.
track.note: Met Maharaja Ajit Singh of Khetri 1891 (lifelong patron) who suggested the title 'Vivekananda'. The three-day meditation on a rock off Kanyakumari (24–26 December 1892) crystallised the resolve to address the Parliament of Religions. Funds for the journey were raised by Madras admirers (Subramania Iyer, Manmatha Bhattacharya) and Khetri.

track.tooltip: Chicago Parliament of Religions, 11 September 1893
track.summary: Chicago Parliament of Religions, 11 September 1893: 'Sisters and Brothers of America' — five-minute standing ovation. Three-year US/UK lecture tour followed.
track.note: Sailed from Bombay 31 May 1893; reached Chicago via Yokohama, Vancouver, then by rail. The Parliament address put Hindu Vedanta into the global comparative-religion conversation as a coherent philosophical position rather than as exotic curiosity. The US tour 1893–96 produced the Vedanta Societies of New York (1894), Boston, San Francisco — institutional vehicles that survive.

track.tooltip: London lectures and the Vedanta movement in Britain, 1895–96
track.summary: London lectures at Princes' Hall and the Brewery 1895–96. Margaret Noble (Sister Nivedita) became a disciple and accompanied him to India 1898.
track.note: Met Max Müller at Oxford (1896), Paul Deussen at Kiel — major nineteenth-century European Indologists. Margaret Noble — Belfast-born Anglo-Irish teacher — became Sister Nivedita in 1898 at Belur Math, ran the Bagbazar girls' school in Calcutta, was politically active in the swadeshi years. She died at Darjeeling 1911.

track.tooltip: Return to India and Colombo–Madras–Calcutta address tour, January 1897
track.summary: Returned to Colombo 15 January 1897; the Madras-and-Bengal addresses that spring — the Lectures from Colombo to Almora — established his all-India presence.
track.note: The Madras–Hyderabad–Calcutta–Almora circuit produced the Lectures from Colombo to Almora — the canonical statement of Vivekananda's Practical Vedanta and his programme of national religious-and-civic regeneration. The addresses framed Hinduism as civilisationally coherent, doctrinally rational, and capable of national-political mobilisation — the discursive ground on which both Aurobindo and the later cultural nationalist movements would build.

track.tooltip: Founds the Ramakrishna Mission at Belur, 1 May 1897
track.summary: Founded the Ramakrishna Mission at Calcutta, 1 May 1897. Belur Math 1898 as monastic headquarters. Welfare-and-service-as-worship the operative principle.
track.note: The Mission's combination of monastic order and civic-welfare arm — schools, hospitals, famine and plague relief — was institutionally novel for Hindu monasticism. The 1899 Calcutta plague relief operation under Sister Nivedita and Brahmananda made the Mission's public reputation. The Mission today operates ~200 centres globally.

track.tooltip: Second Western tour and California Vedanta work, 1899–1900
track.summary: Second Western tour June 1899 – December 1900: California, New York, Paris Exposition, Vienna, Constantinople, Cairo, Athens. Tubercular health failing.
track.note: Founded the Shanti Ashrama in California (1900) — the first Vedanta retreat centre in the US. Health was visibly failing through 1900; diabetes and asthma compounded by the inherited tubercular constitution. Returned to Belur Math December 1900; never travelled abroad again.

track.tooltip: Death at Belur Math, 4 July 1902, age 39
track.summary: Died at Belur Math 4 July 1902 at thirty-nine, probably of cerebral aneurysm — he had predicted he would not live past forty. Funeral pyre on the Hooghly bank.
track.note: His Complete Works (8 volumes, edited by Mayavati Math 1907 onward) became one of the most-printed Indian-author bodies of work of the twentieth century. The intellectual influence runs through Aurobindo's nationalist mysticism, Gandhi (who said he was first introduced to the political possibility of religion by Vivekananda), Subhas Bose, and the post-Independence Hindu cultural nationalist tradition.

people.name: Kabir Das
people.tooltip: Kabir (c. 1440–1518), Banaras weaver-mystic poet
people.summary: Banaras Julaha (weaver-caste) poet-mystic; nirguni Bhakti devotee; ~3,000 surviving verses; rejected Hindu-Muslim institutional religion equally.

track.tooltip: Born to a Julaha (weaver-caste) family at Banaras, c. 1440
track.summary: Born to a Julaha Muslim weaver family at Banaras — caste tradition holds them descended from Hindu converts. The weaver origin centres the verse imagery.
track.note: Early tradition (Bhaktamal, Anantadas) tells the story of the infant Kabir being found floating on Lahartara pond and adopted by Niru and Nima. The historicity is uncertain; the Julaha-weaver origin is consistent across all early sources. Kabir's verse imagery — the loom, the warp and weft, the cloth of breath — is grounded in the daily craft.

track.tooltip: Discipleship under Ramananda at Banaras, c. 1465
track.summary: Tradition has Kabir tricking Ramananda into giving him the Ram-mantra. Whether literal or symbolic, the Ramananda-Kabir lineage links him to the Bhakti silsila.
track.note: Ramananda was the heterodox Vaishnav teacher who broke with the Sri Sampradaya tradition over caste — admitted disciples regardless of birth. The Julaha-Brahmin discipleship was itself a heretical act in late-15th-century Banaras. Kabir's later teacher-tradition includes 12 named principal disciples across caste and confession.

track.tooltip: Banaras poetic period — bijak, sakhi, ramaini, c. 1470–1500
track.summary: Three-decade Banaras period producing the corpus — pads (devotional songs), sakhis (couplets), ramainis (rhymed quatrains). Oral recitation; later compilations.
track.note: The corpus is preserved in three principal recensions: the Bijak (Kabir Panthi tradition), the Adi Granth (Sikh tradition, 224 verses included by Guru Arjan), and the Rajasthani Pancavani (Dadu Panth tradition). Total ~3,000 verses with substantial overlap and variation. The textual-critical work on the corpus (Charlotte Vaudeville, Linda Hess) remains foundational.

track.tooltip: Tradition of confrontation with Sikander Lodi, c. 1495
track.summary: Tradition holds Sikander Lodi summoned Kabir for blasphemy; Kabir's anti-orthodox poems offended both the qazi and the pandit establishment of Banaras.
track.note: The tradition appears in the Anantadas Parichai and the Mughal-era Persian sources. Kabir's poems lampooning Brahminical priesthood ('Pandit, what is your reading? You read all your life and never know yourself') and Islamic orthodoxy ('You who fast and pray and walk to Mecca, what use? Search within') made enemies in both establishments.

track.tooltip: Death at Maghar (near Gorakhpur), c. 1518
track.summary: Tradition holds he chose to die at Maghar — orthodox Hindus held it as a place of cursed rebirth — to refuse the Banaras-death moksha bargain.
track.note: The Maghar choice is consistent with his lifelong polemic against death-place superstition. Two communities — Hindu and Muslim — both claimed his body; on lifting the shroud they found only flowers, half buried (Muslim), half cremated (Hindu). The story is among the canonical Bhakti hagiographies. The Maghar dargah-and-samadhi complex remains contested between communities.

people.name: Mirabai
people.tooltip: Mirabai (c. 1498–1547), Mewar Krishna-bhakta princess-poet
people.summary: Princess of Merta and married into the Mewar royal house; renounced court life for Krishna-bhakti; ~1,500 attributed pads in Rajasthani-Brajbhasha.

track.tooltip: Krishna-bhakti as a child at Merta court, c. 1505
track.summary: Granddaughter of Rao Dudaji of Merta; Vaishnav upbringing. Tradition: her Krishna-as-bridegroom devotion dates from a childhood encounter with a sadhu.
track.note: Father Ratan Singh died young; raised by grandfather Rao Dudaji. The childhood Krishna-image story (a sadhu gives the infant Mira a Krishna idol; she takes it as her bridegroom) is the canonical hagiographic origin in Nabhadas's Bhaktamal. Whether literal or symbolic, the Krishna-as-bridegroom devotional frame structured her later poetry.

track.tooltip: Marriage to Bhojraj, heir to Sisodia Rana Sanga of Mewar, c. 1516
track.summary: Married to Bhojraj of the Sisodia royal house at eighteen — Mewar's first political marriage with the Merta Rathores. Bhojraj died c. 1521, possibly at Khanwa.
track.note: The widowed Mira refused to commit sati or to retreat into widow-seclusion; she continued public Krishna-bhakti devotion at the Chittor court, scandalising the orthodox Sisodia household. Rana Vikramaditya (her brother-in-law) and the queen-mother are the canonical antagonists. The poison-cup story (Vikramaditya sends Mira a cup of poison disguised as charanamrita; she drinks; Krishna saves her) entered hagiography from this period.

track.tooltip: Returns to Merta and then leaves court life entirely, 1530s
track.summary: Returned to Merta court; the Rathore household also rejected her devotion. By the late 1530s she had left court — a wandering devotee on the bhakti circuit.
track.note: The 1535 Mughal-Rajput Bahadur Shah of Gujarat campaign and the Mewar succession instability through the 1530s would have reinforced the political untenability of her Chittor position. The Brindavan visit (where she is said to have engaged Jiva Goswami in theological debate that produced his concession to woman-as-spiritual-equal) is from this period.

track.tooltip: Final years and death at Dwarka, c. 1546–47
track.summary: Tradition has her final years at Dwarka in the Krishna temple; merged with the idol on the day of her death. Dwarka temple still bears her image.
track.note: The Mewar court had sent emissaries (per Nabhadas) to bring her back; she refused and went to Dwarka. The merging-with-the-idol story (she walks into the sanctum and is absorbed) is the canonical hagiographic close. Her ~1,500 attributed pads survive in the Bhakti corpus across Rajasthani, Brajbhasha, and Gujarati linguistic strands; the textual-critical question of which are authentically hers remains live (cf. Nancy Martin, Hawley).

people.name: Sant Tukaram
people.tooltip: Tukaram (1608–1650), Pandharpur Varkari Vaishnav poet
people.summary: Kunbi-caste Vaishnav poet of Dehu (Pune district); the abhang corpus is the apex of the Marathi Varkari tradition; one of the four 'pillars'.

track.tooltip: 1630 Deccan famine — household devastation
track.summary: The 1630–32 Deccan famine took his first wife, son, and substantial part of the family land at Dehu. The crisis-and-loss is the canonical biographical hinge.
track.note: The 1630–32 Shah Jahan-era Deccan famine that killed an estimated 7.4 million in Gujarat extended into Maharashtra; Dehu was on the famine line. Tukaram's biographical accounts (Mahipati's Bhaktalilamrita) date his renunciation-and-bhakti turn from this disaster. The destitution he wrote about thereafter was lived experience.

track.tooltip: Vithoba vision at Bhandara hill, c. 1633
track.summary: Solitary fast on the Bhandara hill above Dehu produced the vision-experience that anchored his abhang composition for the next 17 years.
track.note: The Vithoba (Vitthal of Pandharpur) vision is the canonical Sant tradition mystical-encounter formula — Jnaneshwar at Alandi, Namdev at Pandharpur, Eknath at Paithan all have parallel hill-or-temple vision moments. The Tukaram poems date from after this experience: ~5,000 abhangs in the Marathi devotional corpus, the longest single-author body in the Varkari tradition.

track.tooltip: Brahmin orthodox attack — manuscripts thrown in the Indrayani, c. 1640
track.summary: Rameshwar Bhatt led a Brahmin orthodox petition; ordered Tukaram's manuscripts thrown in the Indrayani river. Tradition: they surfaced after 13 days.
track.note: Rameshwar Bhatt was the local Wagholi Brahmin orthodox authority; the petition objected to a Kunbi-caste Sudra composing Marathi-language devotional verse on Sanskrit theological themes. The manuscripts-resurfacing story enters Mahipati and the Varkari hagiographic tradition; Rameshwar later becomes Tukaram's disciple. The episode is the canonical case of orthodox-Brahmin opposition to vernacular Bhakti and its eventual capitulation.

track.tooltip: Encounter with Shivaji at Lohgad, c. 1649
track.summary: Tradition has Shivaji visiting Dehu c. 1649 as a young Maratha chieftain; received Tukaram's blessing and returned to politics, refusing renunciation.
track.note: Shivaji was nineteen, in the early phase of his Sahyadri fort-capture campaign (Torna 1646, Rajgad 1648). The visit is a canonical Maratha-tradition encounter — the political founder seeks the spiritual sanction. Whether literal or post hoc, the Tukaram-Shivaji affirmation became central to the Maratha state's later ideological self-presentation.

track.tooltip: Disappearance from Dehu — 'departure to Vaikuntha', 1650
track.summary: Tradition has him taken bodily to Vaikuntha by Vithoba's vimana; Varkari accounts give 9 March 1650. No body, no death-rites — disappearance is the close.
track.note: The bodily-ascension framing is unusual in Sant Marathi tradition (most other Sants died documented natural deaths). Modern scholarly speculation has included murder, suicide, or political escape — none with documentary support. The Dehu shrine remains the Varkari tradition's principal pilgrimage site after Pandharpur; the annual Wari procession from Dehu and Alandi to Pandharpur continues unbroken since the seventeenth century.

people.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
people.tooltip: Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948)
people.summary: Lawyer, activist, architect of mass non-violent resistance — the political method that made the freedom movement.

track.tooltip: Called to the bar at Inner Temple, 1891
track.summary: Three years in London. Vegetarian Society, theosophy, and a quiet shy man learning courtroom English.
track.note: Returns to India weeks later. Briefs are scarce; he sails for Durban in 1893 to argue a single case for Dada Abdulla & Co.

track.tooltip: Thrown off the train at Pietermaritzburg, 1893
track.summary: First-class ticket holder ejected for being non-white. The night Gandhi later cited as the moment he committed to political action.
track.note: Twenty-one years in South Africa follow. The satyagraha method is invented in those years, before any of it reaches India.

track.tooltip: Returns to India, lands at Apollo Bunder, 1915
track.summary: Forty-five years old. Gokhale tells him to spend the first year travelling India in third-class trains and saying nothing.
track.note: He more or less obeys. The political year begins in 1917 at Champaran.

track.tooltip: Champaran satyagraha, 1917
track.summary: Bihar's indigo planters had locked tenants into ruinous contracts for a century. Gandhi's first Indian campaign broke them.
track.note: Arrested for refusing a magistrate's order to leave the district. The local court had to dismiss the case after thousands of peasants assembled. Provincial recognition of his method follows.

track.tooltip: Sabarmati Ashram founded, 1917
track.summary: An ashram on the banks of the Sabarmati outside Ahmedabad, run on satyagraha and self-spun cloth. The political base for the next 13 years.
track.note: He vows not to return until India is free. He never does — leaves on the Salt March in 1930 and the ashram is shut down by the Raj that year.

track.role: Architect of the campaign; surrendered his Kaiser-i-Hind medal and built the boycott machinery.
track.note: His first claim on the entire national movement. Most senior Congress leaders had wanted to wait for Dyer to be punished. Gandhi did not.

track.tooltip: First Yerwada imprisonment, 1922
track.summary: Six-year sentence for sedition after Chauri Chaura. Released in 1924 for an appendicitis operation; spends the rest of the decade out of mass politics.
track.note: Trial speech at Ahmedabad: 'I am here to invite and submit cheerfully to the highest penalty.' Judge Broomfield called it the proudest day of his career.

track.role: Led the march from Sabarmati to Dandi at sixty-one — 78 satyagrahis, 24 days, 240 miles.
track.note: The deliberate slowness was the strategy. Twelve miles a day to maximise press coverage and recruit walkers from villages along the route. Photographed daily for the world's papers.

track.tooltip: Poona Pact, signed at Yerwada, 1932
track.summary: Ended his fast-unto-death against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Negotiated with Ambedkar through Yerwada's prison bars.
track.note: A reserved-seat compromise rather than separate electorates. Ambedkar always treated it as a settlement under duress; Gandhi treated it as a moral correction.

track.tooltip: Sevagram Ashram founded, 1936
track.summary: Moves from Sabarmati to a tiny village near Wardha. Deliberately central, deliberately remote. Stays nearly a decade.
track.note: Run more austerely than Sabarmati. Visiting senior Congress leaders had to fetch their own water and clean their own latrines.

track.role: 'Do or die' at Gowalia Tank Maidan; arrested before dawn the next morning along with the entire Congress leadership.
track.note: Spends the rest of the war at the Aga Khan Palace, Pune. Kasturba dies there in 1944, four months before his release.

track.tooltip: Noakhali peace tour, 1946–47
track.summary: Walked barefoot through villages where the previous month's communal killings had emptied the houses. He was 77.
track.note: Forty-seven villages on foot in four months. While the Congress in Delhi negotiated partition, he was trying to remind Bengal what it had been before October.

track.tooltip: Assassinated at Birla House, 30 January 1948
track.summary: Shot at point-blank range during the evening prayer meeting. He was on a fast for communal harmony at the time of his death.
track.note: Three bullets from a Beretta. Nehru on All India Radio: 'The light has gone out of our lives.' India observed 13 days of mourning. Five months later, the Republic was a year and a half away.

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.tooltip: Jawaharlal Nehru (1889–1964)
people.summary: Congress president, prime minister, principal architect of the Indian republic and its first seventeen years.

track.tooltip: Harrow School, 1905
track.summary: Sent to England at fifteen. Two years at Harrow, three at Trinity Cambridge, two at the Inner Temple.
track.note: He read science at Trinity. The political education was incidental — Sinn Féin pamphlets, Fabian lectures, the Russian revolution of 1905 read in the Cambridge papers.

track.tooltip: First meets Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress, 1916
track.summary: Twenty-six and looking for a politics. Gandhi was already forty-six and three years into Champaran preparation.
track.note: Underwhelmed initially. Three years later at Champaran the method made sense. By 1921 he was running Non-Cooperation in the United Provinces.

track.role: Provincial leader for the United Provinces; first imprisonment Lucknow Jail 1921.
track.note: Shed the Theosophical-Society polish; came out of jail a recognisable Congress nationalist.

track.tooltip: Brussels: League Against Imperialism, 1927
track.summary: First sustained contact with the international anti-colonial Left. Returns convinced India's freedom is part of a wider settlement.
track.note: Meets Sun Yat-sen's widow, Albert Einstein's correspondence, and the African delegations. The internationalism shaped his later non-aligned line as prime minister.

track.role: Congress president, the youngest in its history. Unfurled the tricolour at midnight on 31 December.
track.note: His father Motilal handed him the chair. Seen at the time as nepotism; in retrospect it was the moment Congress committed to Purna Swaraj rather than dominion status.

track.role: Arrested at the start of the campaign; spent two of the next four years in Naini Jail.
track.note: Did not march himself. The pattern of long imprisonments was set: nine years in jail, total, before independence.

track.tooltip: The Discovery of India written at Ahmednagar Fort, 1942–46
track.summary: Three years in a princely-state fort with twelve other Congressmen. The book that defined the post-independence vision was written there in pencil.
track.note: Published 1946. The middle chapters — on syncretism, on what India had been before colonial rule — became the secular republic's founding myth.

track.role: Delivered 'Tryst with Destiny' to the Constituent Assembly hours before midnight on 14 August.
track.note: The speech does not mention partition. Mountbatten was sworn in as Governor-General the next morning; Nehru as the first Prime Minister.

track.tooltip: Death at Teen Murti House, 1964
track.summary: Died in office, prime minister for nearly seventeen continuous years. The country had not known another.
track.note: The building became the Nehru Memorial Museum in 1966 and remained that for fifty-seven years. Renamed Prime Ministers' Museum in 2023.

people.name: Bhagat Singh
people.tooltip: Bhagat Singh (1907–1931)
people.summary: Revolutionary, theorist, and martyr at twenty-three. Argued Marxism in jail and went to the gallows reading Lenin.

track.tooltip: National College, Lahore — left Congress for revolution, 1923
track.summary: Left Khalsa High School after his family's mortgage went to the British. National College was the polemical cousin of Lahore's Government College.
track.note: Read Bakunin, Trotsky, the Irish brigade. The college was a recruiting ground for the Hindustan Republican Association.

track.tooltip: HSRA founded at Firoz Shah Kotla, Delhi, 1928
track.summary: The Hindustan Republican Association becomes the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. The 'S' was Bhagat Singh's insertion.
track.note: First Indian revolutionary group to declare a socialist economic programme. The shift from anti-colonial nationalism to anti-capitalism made it dangerous to Congress as much as to the Raj.

track.tooltip: Saunders shooting, Lahore, 17 December 1928
track.summary: Killed assistant superintendent J.P. Saunders to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai. Their target had been the senior officer Scott; they shot the wrong man.
track.note: Posters appeared the next morning: 'Lala Lajpat Rai has been avenged.' The HSRA had carried out a political execution; the Raj read it as terrorism.

track.tooltip: Bombs the Central Legislative Assembly, Delhi, 8 April 1929
track.summary: Two non-lethal bombs into an empty corner of the chamber, plus leaflets, plus a deliberate refusal to escape. The trial was the point.
track.note: Inspired by Auguste Vaillant's bombing of the French Chamber. 'It takes a loud voice to make the deaf hear.' Arrested at the scene by choice.

track.tooltip: 63-day hunger strike, Lahore Jail, 1929
track.summary: Demanded political-prisoner status — books, newspapers, decent food. Co-prisoner Jatin Das died on day 63.
track.note: The strike turned a terrorism trial into a national movement. Provincial assemblies adjourned. Congress paid for Das's funeral procession to Calcutta — half a million walked.

track.tooltip: Hanged at Lahore Central Jail, 23 March 1931
track.summary: Executed eleven hours ahead of schedule, an act the colonial state did not bother to explain. Bodies cremated secretly on the Sutlej.
track.note: Gandhi's silence on the executions during the Gandhi–Irwin negotiations cost him with the Punjab youth for a decade. Bhagat Singh's last book request: Lenin's State and Revolution.

people.name: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
people.tooltip: B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956)
people.summary: Jurist, economist, principal drafter of the Indian Constitution, and the most consequential anti-caste theorist of the twentieth century.

track.tooltip: Elphinstone College, Bombay, 1907
track.summary: First Mahar to matriculate from Elphinstone. Sat outside the classroom for fear his caste would defile its interior.
track.note: Sponsored by Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda. The Maharaja's scholarship took him to Columbia three years later.

track.tooltip: Columbia University, New York, 1913
track.summary: MA and PhD in economics under John Dewey. The lasting influence — democracy as a method of associated living, not a constitutional form.
track.note: The Columbia thesis became 'Castes in India' (1916), his first published anti-caste work. Dewey's influence is visible in every later constitutional speech.

track.tooltip: London School of Economics, 1916
track.summary: Doctorate in economics, called to the bar at Gray's Inn. The full apparatus a colonial subject could acquire.
track.note: Returned to India in 1917, ran out of scholarship money, taught at Sydenham College, returned to London in 1920 to finish. The compressed schedule produced a DSc, a barrister's qualification, and twenty pounds in pocket on arrival back.

track.tooltip: Mahad Satyagraha — Chavdar Tank, 1927
track.summary: Led ten thousand Mahars to drink from the public tank at Mahad. The first organised Dalit assertion of access to a shared resource.
track.note: The tank's water was 'purified' by upper-caste rituals after the satyagraha. In December he returned and burnt the Manusmriti — the public renunciation of Hindu scriptural authority.

track.tooltip: Round Table Conferences, London, 1930–32
track.summary: Represented the Depressed Classes against Gandhi's Congress. Fought for separate electorates as constitutional protection.
track.note: The Communal Award of 1932 granted separate electorates. Gandhi began his fast-unto-death from Yerwada in protest. Ambedkar conceded under duress at the Poona Pact.

track.tooltip: Poona Pact, Yerwada, 24 September 1932
track.summary: Reserved seats inside a joint electorate, in exchange for ending Gandhi's fast. Ambedkar always read it as a settlement at gunpoint.
track.note: He wrote later: 'There was nothing noble in the fast. It was a foul and filthy act.' The reserved-seat compromise has shaped Indian electoral arithmetic ever since.

track.tooltip: Annihilation of Caste, drafted at Bombay, 1936
track.summary: An undelivered speech that became the canonical anti-caste text. The Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal cancelled the lecture rather than hear it.
track.note: Self-published when no Hindu reformist body would print it. Gandhi's response, and Ambedkar's reply to Gandhi, are appended in later editions.

track.role: Chair of the drafting committee of the Constitution; law minister in the first Cabinet.
track.note: Drafted in two years and eleven months. He called it 'a beautiful piece of paper' and said in 1953 he would be the first to burn it if it failed Dalits.

track.tooltip: Conversion to Buddhism, Diksha Bhoomi, 14 October 1956
track.summary: Took the refuges and the precepts at Nagpur with 380,000 Mahars. Twenty-two vows rejecting the Hindu pantheon.
track.note: He had announced the conversion intent in 1935 ('I was born a Hindu, but I shall not die a Hindu'). Took twenty-one years to find the form. He died fifty-three days later.

track.tooltip: Death at Alipur Road, New Delhi, 6 December 1956
track.summary: Died at home in his sleep, six weeks after the conversion at Nagpur. The Buddha and His Dhamma was published posthumously the next year.
track.note: Cremation at Dadar Chowpatty, Bombay. Bharat Ratna conferred posthumously in 1990, thirty-four years late.

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.tooltip: Muhammad Ali Jinnah (1876–1948)
people.summary: Lawyer, Congress moderate, Muslim League president, and architect of partition. Founder and first Governor-General of Pakistan.

track.tooltip: Lincoln's Inn, London, 1893–96
track.summary: Bar at sixteen, the youngest Indian called in his year. Watched Dadabhai Naoroji's election to the Commons.
track.note: Returned to Bombay 1896 to a slow practice. The legal style — meticulous, dispassionate, English-coded — became the lifelong manner.

track.tooltip: Joins the Indian National Congress, 1906
track.summary: Calcutta session, the moderate wing under Naoroji. Speeches in flawless English on civil-service reform.
track.note: Naoroji's private secretary at the session. For the next fifteen years the most prominent Muslim figure in Congress, often called 'the ambassador of Hindu–Muslim unity'.

track.tooltip: Lucknow Pact, 1916
track.summary: Negotiated joint Congress–League demands for self-government. The high-water mark of his Hindu–Muslim coalition politics.
track.note: League accepted Congress's larger numbers; Congress accepted separate Muslim electorates. The bargain Gandhi's later mass politics rendered illegible to both sides.

track.tooltip: Resigns from Congress at Nagpur, 1920
track.summary: Walked out over Non-Cooperation. Booed off the stage when he addressed Gandhi as 'Mister' rather than 'Mahatma'.
track.note: He read mass agitation as ungovernable. 'Your way is the wrong way.' Two decades of constitutional politics follow before he reaches the Lahore Resolution.

track.tooltip: Self-imposed London exile, 1931–34
track.summary: Practised at the Privy Council. Treated India as a closed file. Returned only when Liaquat Ali Khan persuaded him the League needed him.
track.note: He kept a Bombay flat for the eventual return. The years of distance gave him the political detachment to refuse Gandhi's later coalition offers.

track.tooltip: Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution, Minto Park, 1940
track.summary: Demanded 'independent states' in the Muslim-majority regions. The constitutional position that became Pakistan.
track.note: The resolution did not name Pakistan; that came in journalism that month. The text spoke of 'states' (plural) in the east and west. The two-nation theory had its constitutional vehicle.

track.role: Issued the call. The League's response to the failed Cabinet Mission Plan.
track.note: He framed it as constitutional protest. The Calcutta provincial League read it as licence. The Great Calcutta Killings followed within hours of the date.

track.tooltip: Inaugural address to Pakistan Constituent Assembly, 11 August 1947
track.summary: 'You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques.' The secular speech the new state never made canonical.
track.note: The text was suppressed in Pakistani textbooks for decades. Reads in retrospect as an abandoned constitutional path — religion as private matter, citizenship as universal. He died thirteen months later.

track.tooltip: Death at the Governor-General's House, Karachi, 11 September 1948
track.summary: Tuberculosis the British knew about and Jinnah hid through the partition negotiations. Died thirteen months after Pakistan's founding.
track.note: Lord Wavell wrote in 1946 that he would have refused partition had he known how ill Jinnah was. The British did know. The political timing was made to fit a man too ill to manage delay.

people.name: Subhas Chandra Bose
people.tooltip: Subhas Chandra Bose (1897–1945), 'Netaji'
people.summary: Bengali nationalist who broke with Gandhi over methods, raised the Indian National Army from Axis-held Asia, died in a 1945 Taipei plane crash.

track.tooltip: Resigns from the Indian Civil Service, April 1921
track.summary: Stood fourth in the 1920 ICS exam at Cambridge — the highest by an Indian to that date. Resigned within months of qualifying.
track.note: Letter to brother Sarat: 'A nation reared in slavery cannot be saved by a man who has accepted slavery as a profession.' Returns to Calcutta and joins C.R. Das.

track.tooltip: Chief Executive Officer, Calcutta Corporation, 1924
track.summary: C.R. Das as Mayor; Bose as CEO at twenty-seven. Six months in, the Raj jails him under Bengal Regulation III without trial.
track.note: Held first at Alipore, then deported to Mandalay in Burma — the same prison that had held Tilak. Returns ill in 1927; tuberculosis he never fully shakes.

track.tooltip: Tripuri Congress presidency split with Gandhi, March 1939
track.summary: Re-elected Congress President against Gandhi's nominee Pattabhi Sitaramayya by 1,580 votes to 1,377. Resigned within months under Working Committee pressure.
track.note: Gandhi: 'After all Sitaramayya's defeat is more mine than his.' Bose's plan was to issue a six-month ultimatum to the Raj over war participation. The Working Committee refused to let him form a Cabinet. He resigned, founded the Forward Bloc.

track.tooltip: Escape from Calcutta house arrest, 16–17 January 1941
track.summary: Slipped out of 38/2 Elgin Road past the watching CID disguised as a Pathan insurance agent — Calcutta to Peshawar to Kabul to Berlin overland.
track.note: His nephew Sisir Kumar Bose drove the car. Reached Kabul through the tribal areas; Italian and German diplomatic help got him onward to Moscow and then Berlin by 2 April. The CID realised he was missing 27 January.

track.tooltip: Berlin years — Free India Centre and Azad Hind Radio, 1941–43
track.summary: Met Hitler once (May 1942). Founded the Free India Centre, Azad Hind Radio, and the Indian Legion (3,000 Wehrmacht-Indian POWs).
track.note: The Hitler meeting disappointed him — Hitler wanted Indians to fight Russia, not Britain. The 'Jai Hind' greeting and the title 'Netaji' were both coined here. Married Emilie Schenkl in Berlin (1937, formalised secretly); daughter Anita born November 1942.

track.tooltip: U-180 submarine transfer Berlin to Singapore, February–May 1943
track.summary: Three-month submarine voyage Kiel to off Madagascar, transferred to Japanese I-29, on to Sabang and Tokyo. Took over INA at Singapore in July.
track.note: Took command of the Indian National Army from Rash Behari Bose on 4 July at Cathay Building. INA strength rose from ~16,000 to over 40,000 under his leadership, including the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of women combatants under Lakshmi Sahgal.

track.tooltip: Provisional Government of Azad Hind proclaimed, Singapore, 21 October 1943
track.summary: Bose as Head of State, Prime Minister, and Defence Minister of the Provisional Government of Free India — recognised by nine Axis-aligned states.
track.note: Declared war on Britain and the United States. The Andaman and Nicobar islands (Japanese-occupied since March 1942) were nominally transferred to Azad Hind in December 1943 — Bose visited Port Blair and renamed them Shaheed and Swaraj.

track.role: Marched the INA's three divisions with the Japanese Fifteenth Army to the Indian frontier under the slogan 'Chalo Delhi' — broken at Imphal–Kohima.
track.note: His personal command was at Maymyo and then on the front; the rout exposed the strategic mismatch between Japanese logistics and Bose's political objectives. The INA never recovered.

track.tooltip: Plane crash at Taipei, 18 August 1945 (disputed)
track.summary: Mitsubishi Ki-21 bomber crashed on take-off from Taipei airfield three days after Japan's surrender. Officially died of burns at Nanmon Military Hospital.
track.note: Three official commissions of inquiry — Shah Nawaz (1956), Khosla (1970), Mukherjee (2005) — split: the first two affirmed the crash, the third disputed it. Ashes have remained at Renkō-ji Temple, Tokyo, since September 1945. The denial of his death sustained a half-century of Bengali political mythology.

people.name: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur
people.tooltip: Babur (1483–1530), founder of the Mughal empire
people.summary: Timurid prince of Ferghana who, after losing Samarkand twice, founded the Mughal empire from a Kabul base in 1526.

track.role: Inherits Ferghana at eleven, on his father Umar Sheikh Mirza's death in a pigeon-coop fall at Akhsi.
track.note: The Baburnama opens with this moment. Everything in the next thirty-six years is shaped by the smallness of what he started with.

track.tooltip: Babur first takes Samarkand at fourteen, 1497
track.summary: First of three Samarkand captures. Held the city for a hundred days before losing it to a Ferghana rebellion that forced him to choose.
track.note: His first taste of the imperial Timurid capital — the city of his great-great-great-grandfather Timur. Lost not in battle but because rebellion at home meant he couldn't hold both Andijan and Samarkand at once.

track.role: Defeated by Muhammad Shaybani Khan at Sar-e-Pul; loses Samarkand for the second and final time at eighteen.
track.note: The formative defeat of his life. Spent the next ten years roaming the Hindu Kush as a stateless Timurid prince before taking Kabul.

track.role: Crosses the Hindu Kush with three hundred horsemen, takes Kabul from the Arghun governor Muqim Beg without major resistance.
track.note: Twenty-two years in Kabul follow — the city he loved most, the one in which he wrote much of the Baburnama, and the city to which his body would eventually be returned.

track.role: Retakes Samarkand with Safavid Persian backing under Shah Ismail; loses it the next year after the Persians are defeated at Ghazdivan.
track.note: Third and final Samarkand failure. Ends his Central Asian ambitions; turns south to Hindustan.

track.role: Leads his first raid east of the Indus into Bhera in Punjab — reconnaissance of the Lodi frontier rather than conquest.
track.note: Three more raids follow in 1520, 1524, 1525, each one a step deeper than the last.

track.role: Takes Lahore at Daulat Khan Lodi's invitation; Daulat Khan turns against him within months.
track.note: The dress rehearsal for Panipat. Returns briefly to Kabul, then comes back the next year for the final invasion.

track.role: Defeats Ibrahim Lodi with twelve thousand horsemen against ~one hundred thousand, using gunpowder artillery and tulghuma cavalry envelopment.
track.note: The founding battle. Enters Delhi three days later; his reign in Hindustan begins. He has four and a half years left to live.

track.role: Defeats Rana Sanga of Mewar's Rajput coalition with the same gunpowder line; takes the title Ghazi.
track.note: Without Khanwa, Panipat would have been a raid, not a founding. The Rajput defeat lets him hold Delhi.

track.role: Defeats the Afghan-Bengal alliance at the Ghaghra–Ganges confluence; secures the eastern frontier.
track.note: Third great battle in three years. Returns to Agra and dies eighteen months later.

track.role: Dies at Agra after a short illness; passes the empire to his eldest son Humayun.
track.note: Reputedly vowed to take on his ailing son Humayun's fever in his own body. The empire he leaves is held together by his reputation alone — Humayun loses it within nine years.

track.tooltip: Babur reburied at Bagh-e-Babur, Kabul, c. 1539
track.summary: Per Babur's own wish recorded in the Baburnama, his body was moved from Agra to the garden he had built at Kabul about nine years after his death.
track.note: He lived twenty-two years in Kabul before founding the Mughal empire in Hindustan. By his explicit instruction his body was returned to it. The garden survives, restored after the Afghan civil wars; the cenotaph is open to the sky as he asked.

people.name: Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar
people.tooltip: Akbar (1542–1605), third Mughal emperor; consolidator of the empire
people.summary: Third Mughal emperor; ascended at thirteen after Panipat 1556; built the empire from Hindu Kush to Deccan; codified mansabdari and Rajput-marriage alliance.

track.tooltip: Born at Umarkot Fort in Sindh, 15 October 1542
track.summary: Born at Umarkot in Sindh during Humayun's flight to Persia after Sher Shah's defeat at Chausa. Spent his first thirteen years in Persian and Afghan exile.
track.note: Father Humayun was a fugitive from the Sur Empire; mother Hamida Banu Begum gave birth in the Hindu Sodha Rajput chief Rana Prasad's hospitality. The early Persian-Afghan exile years (Kandahar, Kabul, Mashhad) shaped Akbar's later cross-confessional politics.

track.role: Acceded to the Mughal throne days before; Bairam Khan as regent commanded the field. Hemu's defeat opened Hindustan to the second Mughal consolidation.
track.note: Akbar was thirteen and present at the battle. Bairam Khan's victory over Hemu Vikramaditya restored Mughal authority over the Delhi-Agra heartland that Sher Shah had taken from Humayun.

track.role: Coronated at fourteen at Kalanaur (Punjab) under Bairam Khan's regency, 14 February 1556 — eleven days after Humayun's death at Delhi.
track.note: Bairam Khan ran the empire as regent until 1560 when Akbar dismissed him. The 1560 'transfer of power' was the moment Akbar emerged as the operational sovereign.

track.tooltip: Marriage to Harkha Bai (Jodha Bai) of Amber, January 1562
track.summary: Marriage to Harkha Bai of the Kachhwaha Rajputs at Sambhar — the founding political alliance with the Rajputs and the model for Mughal-Rajput integration.
track.note: Raja Bharmal of Amber's daughter — mother of the future Jahangir. The marriage gave the Kachhwaha Rajputs imperial-ally status (Bhagwan Das, Man Singh as Mughal generals) and inaugurated the Mughal-Rajput political fusion that lasted till Aurangzeb's reversal.

track.role: Founded the new capital at Sikri to commemorate the birth of son Salim (the future Jahangir) at the saint Salim Chishti's hermitage.
track.note: The Sikri-as-capital experiment ran 1571–85; abandoned thereafter, probably due to water scarcity. The intact red-sandstone architectural complex survives — among the most legible expressions of Mughal-Hindu-Sufi architectural synthesis.

track.role: His Mughal army under Man Singh fought Maharana Pratap of Mewar at Haldighati — Mughal tactical victory; Mewar resistance continued for two more decades.
track.note: Akbar was not personally present; Man Singh commanded. Pratap escaped the battlefield and retained guerrilla resistance from the Aravallis until his death in 1597 — the one major Rajput house to refuse the Mughal-Rajput integration.

track.role: Codified the mansabdari ranks system that organised the Mughal nobility into 33 grades — the structural innovation of Mughal imperial administration.
track.note: Mansabdari converted feudal-style holdings into a centrally-graded service system — recruitment, pay, and military obligation administered through the central diwan. The system held until late Aurangzeb when it broke under Deccan-war fiscal pressure.

track.role: Promulgated the Din-i-Ilahi at the Ibadat Khana — synthetic monotheist court religion drawing on Sufi, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, and Christian elements.
track.note: Never more than ~19 disciples in his lifetime; effectively died with him in 1605. The doctrinal experiment is less important than the inter-religious court culture it framed — Akbar's reign as the high-water mark of Mughal religious eclecticism, deliberately reversed by Aurangzeb a century later.

track.role: Commissioned Abul Fazl to begin the Akbarnama — the official three-volume reign-history that became the canonical Mughal historiographical model.
track.note: Abul Fazl, the chief ideologue of Akbar's later reign, was murdered in 1602 on Salim's instruction. The Akbarnama and the parallel Ain-i-Akbari (administrative-statistical compendium) are the central sources for sixteenth-century Mughal India.

track.role: Died at Agra Fort 27 October 1605 of dysentery, aged 63. Salim succeeded as Jahangir; the Salim-Akbar father-son tension had structured the last decade of the reign.
track.note: Buried at Sikandra outside Agra in a tomb whose architecture deliberately combined Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Christian, and Islamic motifs — the architectural statement of his eclectic religious project. The empire he left covered ~3.2 million sq km from Kabul to the Krishna river.

people.name: Muhi-ud-din Muhammad Aurangzeb Alamgir
people.tooltip: Aurangzeb (1618–1707), sixth Mughal emperor; reigned 49 years
people.summary: Sixth Mughal emperor; took the throne after the 1658 war of succession; reigned 49 years; spent the last 26 in Deccan; reversed Akbar's eclecticism.

track.tooltip: Born at Dahod, Gujarat, 3 November 1618
track.summary: Third son of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal. Spent ages 8–12 (1626–28) as a hostage at Jahangir's court during Shah Jahan's rebellion against his father.
track.note: Mumtaz Mahal — Shah Jahan's favourite wife — died in 1631 giving birth to Aurangzeb's youngest sister Gauhara Begum. The Taj Mahal at Agra was built (1632–53) as her mausoleum. The succession-relevant Shah Jahan children: Dara Shukoh (eldest), Shah Shuja, Aurangzeb, Murad Bakhsh.

track.tooltip: Appointed Viceroy of the Deccan, 1636 (aged 17)
track.summary: Appointed Viceroy of the Mughal Deccan at seventeen — Aurangabad capital. Two terms (1636–44, 1652–58); learnt the theatre that defined his later reign.
track.note: Renamed Khirki as Aurangabad. The 1636 appointment came after the Mughal-Ahmednagar war's conclusion (Shah Jahan's first Deccan campaign). Aurangzeb's Deccan governance experience — Bijapur and Golconda diplomacy, Maratha-frontier tensions — shaped his post-1681 strategic decision to relocate the imperial court south.

track.tooltip: War of Succession against Dara Shukoh, 1657–58
track.summary: Shah Jahan's illness Sep 1657 triggered the four-brother war. Aurangzeb defeated Dara at Samugarh 8 June 1658; imprisoned Shah Jahan; executed Dara 1659.
track.note: The four sons: Dara Shukoh (heir-presumptive), Shah Shuja (Bengal), Aurangzeb (Deccan), Murad Bakhsh (Gujarat). Aurangzeb allied with Murad to defeat Dara, then turned on Murad and imprisoned him at Gwalior (executed 1661). Shah Shuja fled to Arakan and disappeared. Dara was captured, paraded through Delhi in chains, tried for apostasy, beheaded.

track.role: Crowned at the Shalimar Gardens, Delhi, 31 July 1658 — title 'Alamgir' ('World-Seizer'). Held a second formal coronation at Delhi June 1659 after Dara's defeat was complete.
track.note: The succession war and Shah Jahan's imprisonment at Agra Fort (where the deposed emperor lived for eight more years until his death 1666) defined Aurangzeb's reign as legally suspect from its founding moment — the Sunni orthodox-jurisprudence framing he later cultivated was partly a response.

track.tooltip: Reimposition of the jaziya tax on non-Muslims, 2 April 1679
track.summary: Reimposed the jaziya tax on non-Muslim subjects, 2 April 1679 — abolished by Akbar 1564. Reversal of a century-old Mughal religious settlement.
track.note: The reimposition triggered Hindu and Rajput protests in Delhi (the Jama Masjid demonstration of April 1679 was suppressed); Mewar, Marwar, and the Bundela Rajputs revolted. The jaziya was withdrawn briefly during the Deccan campaigns and finally abolished by Bahadur Shah I in 1712. Aurangzeb's reversal of Akbar's religious policy is the central point of historiographical contestation about his reign.

track.tooltip: Departure for the Deccan, September 1681 — never to return
track.summary: Left Delhi Sep 1681 with the largest Mughal field army ever — to crush the Marathas and absorb Bijapur and Golconda. Never returned to Hindustan.
track.note: The Deccan campaign was the longest sustained military operation in Mughal history — 26 years from departure to death at Ahmadnagar. The fiscal drain (estimated at 100 crore rupees over the campaign) hollowed out the imperial treasury; the army's continuous southern deployment opened northern frontiers to the Sikh and Jat resistance movements that would fragment the empire after Aurangzeb's death.

track.role: Annexed Bijapur (1686) then Golconda (1687) — extinguishing the two surviving Bahmani-successor sultanates and bringing the Deccan to within reach of imperial integration.
track.note: The Bijapur and Golconda treasuries (Golconda alone surrendered ~6 crore rupees) financed the next decade of the Maratha campaign. The administrative absorption of these sultanates added 33 new mansabs and the Bahmani administrative class to the Mughal nobility — partly relieving the fiscal pressure but doubling the patronage demands.

track.role: Captured Sambhaji at Sangameshwar February 1689; executed at Tulapur 11 March 1689 after refusing to convert. The Maratha succession passed to Rajaram, then to Tarabai.
track.note: Sambhaji's execution was meant to break the Maratha resistance; instead it produced two decades of intensified guerrilla war under Rajaram, then Tarabai. The Mughal-Maratha war from 1689 onward is the operational reason Aurangzeb could never withdraw from the Deccan.

track.tooltip: Receives Guru Gobind Singh's Zafarnamah at Ahmadnagar, 1706
track.summary: Received Guru Gobind Singh's Persian-verse Zafarnamah from Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh at Ahmadnagar — the moral indictment of his last year.
track.note: The Zafarnamah was Guru Gobind Singh's response to Wazir Khan of Sirhind's breach of safe-conduct at Anandpur and the murder of his children. Mughal accounts say Aurangzeb read it; Sikh accounts say it shook him. The exchange — the Sikh tenth Guru and the dying Mughal emperor — is one of the iconic moments of late-Mughal religious-political history.

track.role: Died at Ahmadnagar 3 March 1707 aged 88. Buried in a simple grave at Khuldabad as he had specified — no marble, no inlay, his own income from Quran-copying paying for it.
track.note: His will divided the empire among three surviving sons; Bahadur Shah I's accession after the war of succession (Battle of Jajau, June 1707) opened the rapid imperial fragmentation of the eighteenth century. The Maratha, Sikh, Jat, and Awadh successor states were operational within a generation.

people.name: Jyotirao Govindrao Phule
people.tooltip: Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890), anti-caste reformer of Pune
people.summary: Mali (gardener-caste) reformer of Pune. Co-founded the first girls' school 1848; founded the Satyashodhak Samaj 1873; published Gulamgiri the same year.

track.tooltip: Married Savitribai at thirteen, 1840
track.summary: Married Savitribai Khandoba (b. 1831) at thirteen — she was nine. The lifelong educational and political partnership begins from this marriage.
track.note: Phule taught Savitribai to read at home — Mali-caste girls had no formal access to literacy. By the late 1840s she was teaching alongside him; by 1851 she was India's first woman headmistress. The intellectual collaboration is rare in nineteenth-century reform marriages.

track.tooltip: Opens India's first girls' school at Bhide Wada, Pune, 1 January 1848
track.summary: Opened a girls' school at Bhide Wada, Pune — first run by Indians, open across caste. Savitribai was the first teacher; Brahmin opposition was immediate.
track.note: Father Govindrao Phule expelled the couple from the family home in 1849 under Brahmin pressure. They moved into the home of friend Usman Sheikh — the school was supported by Sheikh's sister Fatima Sheikh, who became Savitribai's first colleague and one of India's first Muslim women teachers. By 1852 they had opened five girls' schools.

track.tooltip: Opens a school for Mahar and Mang 'untouchable' children, 1851
track.summary: Opened a separate school for Mahar and Mang 'untouchable' children — among the first explicitly cross-caste schools in colonial India.
track.note: The Phules' household drinking water was made available to 'untouchables' from this period — directly inverting the caste prohibition that defined village water access. Two grain-of-Brahmin caste-violation acts: educating girls, and educating untouchables. The orthodox Pune response was sustained social and physical attack.

track.tooltip: Founds the Satyashodhak Samaj ('Truth-Seekers' Society'), 24 September 1873
track.summary: Founded the Satyashodhak Samaj as the institutional vehicle of non-Brahmin organising — anti-priestly, anti-ritual, reformist marriage, direct theism.
track.note: Provided non-Brahmin officiants for marriages and life-cycle ceremonies, undercutting the Brahmin priestly economy. The Samaj's network in Maharashtra and Bombay provided the institutional ground for the later non-Brahmin movement and for Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur's reservation policy at Kolhapur.

track.tooltip: Publication of Gulamgiri ('Slavery'), 1873
track.summary: Polemical treatise comparing Brahmin caste rule to American slavery, dedicated to American abolitionists. Argued the Aryan-conquest origin of caste hierarchy.
track.note: The Aryan-invasion theory entered Indian political polemic through Phule. He read the Brahmin-Shudra binary as a conqueror-vs-indigenous frame; the Bali Raja-Vamana mythology was retold as an indigenous king's defeat by Aryan trickery. The book foreshadowed Periyar's Self-Respect critique by half a century.

track.tooltip: Publication of Shetkaryacha Asud ('The Cultivator's Whipcord'), 1883
track.summary: Treatise on agrarian distress under colonial revenue and moneylender exploitation — argued for cultivator credit; foreshadowed Deccan Riots critique.
track.note: Written four years after the 1879 Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act and five years after the 1875 Deccan Riots in Pune-Ahmednagar. Phule's diagnosis — Brahmin moneylender plus colonial revenue plus monopoly priesthood — bridged caste and economic critique. M.G. Ranade's later moderate Deccan Sabha drew on parts of it.

track.tooltip: Conferred title of 'Mahatma' by Bombay public meeting, 11 May 1888
track.summary: Conferred the title 'Mahatma' at a Bombay public meeting — three decades before Tagore did the same for Gandhi. The honorific had non-Brahmin origin.
track.note: Conferred by V.R. Shinde, Narayan Lokhande and a meeting of working-class Bombay non-Brahmin associations. The title 'Mahatma' had a Maharashtrian non-Brahmin lineage that the Gandhi-Tagore later use does not always acknowledge.

track.tooltip: Death at Pune, 28 November 1890
track.summary: Died at sixty-three of a stroke. Savitribai lit the funeral pyre — refusing the orthodox prohibition on women cremators. Satyashodhak Samaj continued.
track.note: Ambedkar would later list Phule as one of his three intellectual gurus (alongside the Buddha and Kabir). The Phule-Ambedkar lineage of anti-caste politics — institutionally distinct from the Congress reformist tradition — runs from Pune 1848 through Mahad 1927 to the Constitution of 1950.

people.name: Savitribai Phule
people.tooltip: Savitribai Phule (1831–1897), India's first woman headmistress
people.summary: Mali-caste teacher; co-founded India's first girls' school at Bhide Wada 1848; first Indian woman headmistress; died of plague nursing the sick, 1897.

track.tooltip: Begins literacy under husband Jyotirao's tuition, c. 1841
track.summary: Married at nine, illiterate. Jyotirao taught her at home; trained at the American Mission, Ahmednagar and at Cynthia Farrar's Normal School, Pune.
track.note: The American Mission at Ahmednagar under the Reverend John Murdoch and Cynthia Farrar's Pune Normal School were among the only institutions in 1840s western India training women teachers. She trained at both. The pedagogical formation was as much American Protestant as it was Marathi reformist.

track.tooltip: First woman headmistress at the Bhide Wada girls' school, January 1848
track.summary: Took charge of Bhide Wada school as headmistress at seventeen — India's first woman teacher and headmistress. Stones and cow dung thrown on the school walk.
track.note: Carried two saris to school — one to change into after orthodox men in the Brahmin neighbourhood threw cow dung and stones at her on the walk. The records of the Bombay Presidency Educational Department list her as the first woman to hold the headmistress title in any Indian school.

track.tooltip: Forms teaching partnership with Fatima Sheikh, 1849
track.summary: After expulsion from Phule home, taught alongside Fatima Sheikh — likely India's first Muslim woman teacher — from the Sheikh home in Ganj Peth, Pune.
track.note: Fatima Sheikh and her brother Usman Sheikh sheltered the Phule household; Fatima trained at the Pune Normal School alongside Savitribai. Their joint teaching covered Muslim, Brahmin, and untouchable girls in the same classroom — an arrangement without precedent in 1840s Indian schooling.

track.tooltip: Publishes Kavya Phule poetry collection, 1854
track.summary: Marathi poetry — anti-caste verse, the long poem 'Go, Get Education' addressed to Shudra and Ati-Shudra women. First published Marathi woman poet.
track.note: Bawan Kashi Subodh Ratnakar (1892) was the second collection — a verse history of Indian women's oppression. Her surviving prose includes a series of letters to Jyotirao from Naigaon between 1856 and 1868 documenting school inspections, household finance, and political polemic at twenty-five-and-up.

track.tooltip: Founds Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha (infanticide-prevention shelter), 1863
track.summary: Set up an infanticide-prevention home in Pune for Brahmin widows pregnant outside marriage — adopted son Yashwant born to such a resident in 1873.
track.note: Phule social reform around widow remarriage and infanticide pre-dated the more famous Bengal reformist work of Vidyasagar (1856 Widow Remarriage Act in Bengal). The Phules' own adopted son Yashwantrao — whose mother had taken refuge at the home — became a doctor and continued the family reform work.

track.tooltip: Officiates Satyashodhak inter-caste marriages from 1873
track.summary: Conducted Satyashodhak marriages — no Brahmin priest, Marathi vernacular, bride-groom equality oath. Persistent orthodox legal harassment followed.
track.note: Satyashodhak marriages were repeatedly challenged in court for legal validity through the 1880s; the Bombay High Court upheld them as valid Hindu marriages in a series of judgments through the 1890s. The institutional precedent for non-Brahmin officiation in Maharashtrian Hindu weddings dates here.

track.tooltip: Lights Jyotirao Phule's funeral pyre, 28 November 1890
track.summary: Lit her husband's funeral pyre — a public violation of the orthodox prohibition on women cremators. Took over the Satyashodhak Samaj presidency.
track.note: Ran the Satyashodhak Samaj as president for the remaining seven years of her life. Adopted son Yashwantrao Phule became its secretary. The Samaj's organisational network across the Deccan held up through the 1900s and fed into Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur's reservation policies.

track.tooltip: Dies of bubonic plague while nursing the sick, 10 March 1897
track.summary: Set up a plague clinic in Hadapsar; contracted plague nursing a Mahar boy; died at sixty-six. The Pune plague was a major colonial-era urban outbreak.
track.note: The 1896–97 Pune plague killed an estimated 50,000 in the city; the colonial Plague Committee under W.C. Rand was assassinated by the Chapekar brothers in June 1897, three months after Savitribai's death. The Indian women's history canon began to recover her in the 1980s; her birthday (3 January) is now recognised as a state day in Maharashtra.

people.name: Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati
people.tooltip: Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), Sanskritist and Mukti Mission founder
people.summary: Maharashtrian-Brahmin Sanskritist; conferred 'Pandita' by Calcutta scholars; converted to Christianity; founded the Mukti Mission for famine widows.

track.tooltip: Pilgrim childhood with father Anant Shastri Dongre, 1858–1878
track.summary: Father Anant Shastri taught Sanskrit to wife and daughter — heterodox; the family lived as wandering pilgrims. Parents died in the 1876–78 Madras famine.
track.note: Anant Shastri's tuition was extraordinary for his time — Sanskrit and Puranic learning given to women. The family walked between pilgrim sites for two decades. The Madras famine of 1876–78 — one of the great Victorian holocausts — killed both parents at Tirumala. Ramabai walked with her brother Srinivas across the subcontinent for the next two years, arriving at Calcutta in 1878.

track.tooltip: Calcutta Senate confers the Pandita title, 1878
track.summary: Examined by Calcutta University Senate Sanskrit pundits at twenty. Conferred 'Pandita' and 'Sarasvati' for grammar and Vedanta — first woman so honoured.
track.note: The Senate examination was unprecedented — Sanskrit Pandita titles had not been conferred on women in the orthodox tradition. Bengali reformist intelligentsia (Keshub Chunder Sen's Brahmo circle, Calcutta University Sanskrit faculty) sponsored the test. The titles followed her for the next forty years.

track.tooltip: Marriage to Bipin Behari Das Medhavi 1880; widowed sixteen months later, 1882
track.summary: Married inter-caste to a Bengali Shudra-caste lawyer at twenty-two — itself a reformist act. Widowed sixteen months later when he died of cholera at twenty-six.
track.note: Daughter Manorama born April 1881. Widow at twenty-three with a year-old daughter — and a Sanskritist Brahmin widow no orthodox marriage rules accommodated, having broken caste with the marriage. Returned with daughter to Pune in 1882; the experience of her widowhood became the political ground of her women's-reform writing.

track.tooltip: Founds Arya Mahila Samaj at Pune, 1 May 1882
track.summary: Founded Arya Mahila Samaj for women's education and against child marriage. Testified to the 1882 Hunter Commission on Indian education.
track.note: Hunter Commission testimony recommended women teachers for girls' schools and women medical officers for women patients. The recommendation produced the Lady Dufferin Fund (1885) for women's medical education in India — Ramabai's intervention is the documented direct origin.

track.tooltip: Travels to England; baptised at Wantage Sisterhood, 29 September 1883
track.summary: Travelled to England 1883 to study medicine; baptised at the Anglican Wantage Sisterhood. Conversion broke with the Pune reform circle.
track.note: The conversion split Pune reformist opinion — Tilak's Kesari attacked it; Ranade defended her. She rejected the Sisterhood's request that she abandon Hindu philosophy and remained a heterodox Indian-vernacular Christian — translating the Bible into Marathi over twenty years (printed at Mukti Press 1924).

track.tooltip: Publishes The High-Caste Hindu Woman in Philadelphia, 1887
track.summary: Published The High-Caste Hindu Woman in Philadelphia — first Indian-authored English-language indictment of Brahmin widow oppression in the West.
track.note: Travelled to the United States 1886–88 on the proceeds and lecture circuit; the Ramabai Association was founded in Boston, December 1887, to fund her widows' work in India. The book's reception in American women's-rights circles (Frances Willard, Susan B. Anthony) made her the first Indian woman to be a public intellectual figure in American Christian-feminist networks.

track.tooltip: Founds Sharada Sadan widows' home at Bombay, 11 March 1889
track.summary: Opened Sharada Sadan ('House of Learning') for child widows at Chowpatty, Bombay — moved to Pune the next year. Sanskrit, Marathi, English, and a craft.
track.note: First Indian institutional home for high-caste child widows — a population structurally barred from remarriage and from inheritance, often abandoned by natal and marital households. Twelve years of running it gave her the operational platform for the larger Mukti Mission.

track.tooltip: Founds the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon, 1898
track.summary: Founded the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon during the 1896–97 famine. Within five years housed ~2,000 widows and abused girls — schools, farms, printing press.
track.note: Toured the Central Provinces and Berar famine zone in 1896–97 personally collecting destitute widows; ~300 women and girls walked back to Kedgaon with her. The 1905 'Mukti revival' Pentecostal episode placed Mukti at the origin of Pentecostal Christianity in India. Mukti operates today with continuous institutional life since 1898 — among the longest-running Indian women's-welfare institutions.

track.tooltip: Death at Mukti Mission, Kedgaon, 5 April 1922
track.summary: Died at sixty-three — nine months after daughter Manorama's death (1921). Mukti Mission successor leadership held the institution through the 1920s and beyond.
track.note: Government of India 1989 commemorative postage stamp; nominated to the Maharashtra government's pantheon of social reformers; recovered as a major figure in 1980s–90s feminist Indian history. The institution she founded survives — and her writings, dispersed across English, Marathi, and Sanskrit, remain only partially edited.

track.tooltip: Marathi Bible translation completed at Mukti, 1924 (posthumous)
track.summary: Spent twenty years translating the Bible into Marathi from Hebrew and Greek originals — printed at Mukti Press; published in 1924, two years posthumously.
track.note: The first Marathi Bible done from original-language sources rather than English-translation intermediary. Mukti Press also printed her Marathi-language histories of the Old and New Testaments and her commentaries — a body of vernacular Christian scholarship by an Indian woman that the academic study of Indian Christianity has only partially recovered.

people.name: Periyar E.V. Ramasamy
people.tooltip: Periyar E.V. Ramasamy (1879–1973), Self-Respect Movement and Dravidar Kazhagam
people.summary: Erode reformer who broke with the Congress over caste; founded the Self-Respect Movement 1925, Dravidar Kazhagam 1944 — anti-caste, anti-Brahmin, anti-religion.

track.tooltip: Pilgrimage to Kashi (Banaras) and the temple-feed exclusion, c. 1904
track.summary: Refused entry to a free temple meal at Kashi for being non-Brahmin — Tamil Naidu pilgrim. The canonical origin of his lifelong anti-Brahmin politics.
track.note: He told the story repeatedly through his life — fed scraps from the temple kitchen meant for animals after being refused the Brahmin-only feed. The trip was meant as ritual purification; came back instead with the operational diagnosis of the next seven decades.

track.tooltip: Erode Municipal Council chairmanship and Congress entry, 1919
track.summary: Erode merchant; Municipal Council chairman from 1917. Joined Congress under Rajaji's persuasion 1919; rose rapidly within Tamil Nadu Congress.
track.note: Brought commercial competence and organisational skill to a Tamil Nadu Congress short on both. Rose within five years to Tamil Nadu Congress secretary; jailed twice (1921 toddy-shop picketing, 1922 non-cooperation). The Congress phase ran until the Vaikom and Kanchipuram disputes of 1924–25.

track.role: Travelled to Vaikom in March 1924 to lead the satyagraha against caste exclusion at the Mahadeva temple roads; jailed twice for participation; called 'Vaikom Veerar' on release.
track.note: The Vaikom episode established him as an all-India anti-caste activist beyond the Tamil Congress. His refusal to abandon the movement when the Travancore administration arrested its Kerala leadership built the personal cross-regional network that the later Self-Respect Movement drew on.

track.tooltip: Walks out of the Kanchipuram Tamil Nadu Congress, November 1925
track.summary: Walked out of the Tamil Nadu Congress at Kanchipuram after it refused communal-representation reservations and reaffirmed Brahmin domination of office.
track.note: The break was clean and final. He never rejoined Congress and spent the next half-century constructing a politics explicitly opposed to it — a politics whose lasting electoral organisation became Tamil Nadu's defining political fact after 1967.

track.tooltip: Launches the Self-Respect Movement (Suya Mariyathai Iyakkam), 1925
