track.summary: Launched the Self-Respect Movement — anti-caste, anti-Brahmin-priest, anti-Sanskritic ritual. First Self-Respect marriage without a Brahmin priest, 1928.
track.note: Kudi Arasu (Republic), the Tamil weekly he founded in 1925, became the movement's theoretical organ — pamphlet polemic, satirical anti-Brahmin commentary, women's-rights advocacy. It ran continuously through colonial-era state harassment until the early 1950s.

track.tooltip: Russian and European tour, 1932
track.summary: Travelled the Soviet Union, Germany, Spain, Britain. Returned arguing for socialist economics alongside the cultural Self-Respect programme.
track.note: The Soviet trip introduced explicit Marxist vocabulary into the Self-Respect lexicon. The 1934 Erode programme combined Self-Respect cultural critique with collectivist economic positions; the synthesis broke under colonial-government repression of communist-affiliated organisations from 1934 on, and Periyar pivoted back to cultural-political work alone.

track.tooltip: President of the Justice Party, December 1938
track.summary: Took over the South Indian Liberal Federation (Justice Party) — the non-Brahmin parliamentary vehicle since 1916. Renamed it Dravidar Kazhagam, 1944.
track.note: Fused the older Justice Party institutional shell with the Self-Respect ideological body. The Anti-Hindi Imposition Agitation of 1937–40 against Rajaji's Hindi-compulsory order in Madras schools — three students died, Periyar jailed for a year — was the political event that consolidated Tamil mass support around the Justice / Dravidar platform.

track.tooltip: Founds the Dravidar Kazhagam at Salem, 27 August 1944
track.summary: Renamed the Justice Party as the Dravidar Kazhagam at Salem. Demanded Dravida Nadu — a Dravidian republic for the four southern linguistic regions.
track.note: Dravida Nadu as a constitutional demand was never realised; it became, after the 1962 Sino-Indian War and the Sixteenth Amendment 1963 banning secessionism, a cultural-political claim rather than an electoral one. Anna's 1949 split formed the DMK on a sub-set of the platform; the DK–DMK lineage is the durable institutional legacy.

track.tooltip: C.N. Annadurai's split — DMK formed, 17 September 1949
track.summary: Periyar's late marriage to Maniammai precipitated C.N. Annadurai's split. Anna founded the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam at Robinson Park, Madras.
track.note: Anna's DMK chose the electoral path Periyar disdained; entered the Madras Legislative Assembly in 1957, won it in 1967, and has alternated with the AIADMK in Tamil Nadu government ever since. The DK remained Periyar's instrument as a propagandist movement, never an electoral party. Both lineages claim him.

track.tooltip: Death at Vellore, 24 December 1973, age 94
track.summary: Died at ninety-four. State funeral by the DMK government in Madras. His anti-caste, Tamil-autonomy platform shaped state politics for half a century.
track.note: His birthday (17 September) is the Tamil Nadu government's 'Social Justice Day'. His samadhi at Periyar Thidal in Madras is a state-protected site. The DK pamphlet output continues; the political-cultural framework — affirmative action, women's property rights, Tamil-language pride, anti-Sanskritic ritual reform — is institutionalised in Tamil Nadu state policy in ways no other regional reformer's programme is.

people.name: Rabindranath Thakur (Tagore)
people.tooltip: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941), Bengali polymath and Nobel laureate
people.summary: Bengali polymath. Nobel for Gitanjali 1913; renounced knighthood after Jallianwala 1919; founded Visva-Bharati 1921; broke with Gandhi over non-cooperation.

track.tooltip: Years at Shilaidaha managing the family zamindari estate, 1890s
track.summary: Sent to manage the Tagore zamindari at Shilaidaha (East Bengal) in his late twenties. A decade on the Padma houseboat — his greatest short-fiction output.
track.note: Galpaguchchha — the canonical Bengali short-story collection (~84 stories, mostly written 1891–1901) — emerged from the Padma riverside life. The encounter with rural Bengal poverty and East Bengal Muslim peasant life shaped the political consciousness that broke with the urban Hindu-bhadralok orthodoxy of the partition years.

track.tooltip: Founds the Santiniketan ashram-school, 22 December 1901
track.summary: Founded the Brahmacharya Ashram school at Santiniketan with five pupils. Open-air pedagogy, no walls, no caste — a break with Macaulayan schooling.
track.note: His father Debendranath Tagore had bought the Santiniketan land in 1862 as a Brahmo retreat. Rabindranath turned it into a working school; in 1921 raised the school to Visva-Bharati University, the international centre for Asian and humanist studies. Ravi Shankar, Indira Gandhi, Satyajit Ray, and Amartya Sen are among its later associates.

track.tooltip: Breaks with the Bengal swadeshi movement over communal violence, 1907
track.summary: Withdrew from Bengal Swadeshi after the 1906–07 communal flashpoints in East Bengal. Wrote Gora and the rural-Muslim short stories from this withdrawal.
track.note: His novel Gora (serialised 1907–09) is the long Bengali interrogation of bhadralok cultural-religious chauvinism. The withdrawal from active swadeshi was the first of his three major political breaks — the others being with Gandhi (over non-cooperation 1921) and with Bose (over fascism 1937).

track.tooltip: Nobel Prize in Literature for Gitanjali, 13 November 1913
track.summary: First Asian Nobel laureate in any field — for Gitanjali (English version, translated by Tagore with Yeats's editing). The Bengali original appeared 1910.
track.note: The Nobel transformed his international reputation while complicating the Indian one. World tours from 1916 — Japan, the United States, Argentina, Italy, the USSR — made him India's first global cultural ambassador, and gave him a platform from which to critique Western nationalism (lectures collected in Nationalism, 1917) before Indian nationalism even peaked.

track.tooltip: Renounces knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 31 May 1919
track.summary: Renounced his 1915 knighthood by letter to Viceroy Chelmsford after Dyer's Jallianwala Bagh massacre — first major Indian intellectual to break ranks.
track.note: Letter to Chelmsford: 'The time has come when badges of honour make our shame glaring in their incongruous context of humiliation, and I for my part wish to stand, shorn of all special distinctions, by the side of those of my countrymen who, for their so-called insignificance, are liable to suffer a degradation not fit for human beings.'

track.tooltip: Public debate with Gandhi over non-cooperation, 1921
track.summary: Series of Modern Review essays disputing Gandhi's non-cooperation programme — argued boycott was destructive negation, advocated cooperation on terms.
track.note: Tagore's essay 'The Call of Truth' (1921) and Gandhi's reply 'The Great Sentinel' framed two distinct visions of the freedom struggle — Tagore's universalist-cooperative-internationalist position against Gandhi's national-ascetic-mass-mobilisation. Both ran in Modern Review and Young India through that year. The disagreement remained respectful and was never patched.

track.tooltip: Visva-Bharati University founded at Santiniketan, 23 December 1921
track.summary: Raised the Santiniketan ashram-school into Visva-Bharati — international university, motto 'Yatra Visvam Bhavatyekanidam' (where the world meets in one nest).
track.note: Sylvain Lévi, the French Indologist, was the first visiting professor; the institution attracted a sustained international Asian-studies faculty (Patrick Geddes, Leonard Elmhirst, Romain Rolland). Visva-Bharati became a Central University by Act of Parliament in 1951; one of the few institutions of his life whose architecture survived him.

track.tooltip: Sriniketan rural-reconstruction institute founded, 6 February 1922
track.summary: Founded Sriniketan as the rural-reconstruction sister institute to Visva-Bharati — agriculture, cooperative credit, weaving, women's literacy.
track.note: The first systematic Indian-led rural-reconstruction project — predating Gandhi's Sevagram by fourteen years. Elmhirst, the Cornell-trained agronomist, anchored the work for a decade before founding Dartington Hall on the same model in Devon (1925). The cooperative-credit and women's-literacy components fed into Indian rural-development design through the post-Independence Community Development Programme (1952).

track.tooltip: Public letter to Bose disputing fascism, 1937
track.summary: Wrote publicly against Bose's flirtation with fascist Italy — 'fascism is the political form of barbarism, more dangerous than colonial rule'. The break held.
track.note: Bose had been to Italy in 1933–34 and met Mussolini; Tagore (who had refused even to meet Mussolini on his 1925 Italian trip after first being misled into a Fascist-government reception) refused to support Bose's strategic logic of the enemy-of-my-enemy. The letter ran in Modern Review. The Tagore-Bose-Gandhi triangle of late 1930s Bengali politics never fully reconciled.

track.tooltip: Final lecture 'Crisis in Civilisation', 14 April 1941
track.summary: Final public address at Santiniketan four months before death. A despairing assessment of the European war, colonial brutality, and human prospects.
track.note: 'And yet I shall not commit the grievous sin of losing faith in Man.' The address closed with a refusal to despair even as the analysis was bleak. The text stands as the major Indian intellectual statement of 1941 — written between Hitler's Russian invasion (June) and the Atlantic Charter (August).

track.tooltip: Death at Jorasanko Thakurbari, Calcutta, 7 August 1941
track.summary: Died at eighty in the family Jorasanko house in north Calcutta. The funeral was the largest Bengali public mourning since Vivekananda's in 1902.
track.note: Two of his compositions — Jana Gana Mana (1911) and Amar Sonar Bangla (1905) — became the national anthems of independent India and Bangladesh respectively, the only person to have authored two national anthems. Sri Lanka's anthem also draws on a Tagore composition translated by his student Ananda Samarakoon. Visva-Bharati and Sriniketan continue to operate.

people.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Bhonsle
people.tooltip: Shivaji (1630–1680), founder of the Maratha kingdom
people.summary: Bhonsle Maratha chieftain who built a sovereign kingdom from the Western Ghats out of Bijapuri and Mughal territory; crowned at Raigad, 1674.

track.tooltip: Capture of Torna fort from Bijapur, 1646
track.summary: First fort taken at sixteen — bought off the Bijapuri commandant. The seed of a string of fort captures across the Sahyadri.
track.note: Treasure found at Torna funded the construction of Rajgad — the Maratha headquarters for the next quarter-century before Raigad.

track.tooltip: Killing of Afzal Khan at Pratapgad, 10 November 1659
track.summary: Bijapur sent Afzal Khan with 10,000 troops to crush the rebellion. Shivaji met him alone in a parley tent under Pratapgad and killed him with the bagh nakh.
track.note: The Bijapuri force, ambushed in the forested approaches by Maratha infantry, was routed within hours. The bagh nakh (tiger claws) and the wagh nakhi tale entered Maratha legend; the underlying point was a five-year guerrilla campaign that broke Bijapuri authority in the western Konkan.

track.tooltip: First sack of Surat, January 1664
track.summary: Four-day raid on the Mughal empire's richest port. Carried off an estimated one crore of bullion and trade goods; English and Dutch factories spared.
track.note: Surat was Aurangzeb's customs revenue capital. The raid was both a financial blow and a deliberate humiliation; the Mughal response was to send Mirza Raja Jai Singh.

track.tooltip: Treaty of Purandar with Mirza Raja Jai Singh, 11 June 1665
track.summary: After Jai Singh's siege of Purandar, Shivaji surrendered 23 of 35 forts and accepted nominal Mughal vassalage — buying time, not submission.
track.note: Murarbaji Deshpande's defence of Purandar — refusing surrender to the last — became the standard against which later Maratha garrison commanders were measured. Jai Singh persuaded Shivaji to attend the Mughal court at Agra. It was a trap.

track.tooltip: Escape from Aurangzeb's Agra court, 17 August 1666
track.summary: Insulted at the Agra darbar, placed under house arrest. Escaped concealed in a basket of sweets — twenty-five days back to Raigad via Mathura.
track.note: His son Sambhaji escaped with him. The escape became, with the killing of Afzal Khan, the second great theatrical episode of the Shivaji legend — and a permanent personal grievance for Aurangzeb whose Deccan campaign of 1681 onwards is partly its long answer.

track.tooltip: Second sack of Surat, October 1670
track.summary: Three-day repeat raid on Surat, six years after the first. The Mughal governor had not improved the defences.
track.note: Followed up by the Battle of Salher in February 1672 — the first set-piece Maratha victory over a Mughal army in the open field. Aurangzeb's Deccan policy hardened from this point.

track.tooltip: Rajyabhishek coronation at Raigad, 6 June 1674
track.summary: Crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in a Vedic ceremony presided over by Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi — a sovereign Hindu kingdom on the western coast.
track.note: The coronation needed a Brahmin sanction Shivaji had been refused by the Maharashtrian Brahmin establishment; Gaga Bhatt was brought from Varanasi to confer kshatriya status. New currency (the Shiva-rai), a new Sanskritised administrative vocabulary, an Ashtapradhan council. The Hindavi Swarajya frame becomes operational.

track.tooltip: Karnataka campaign — Jinji, Vellore, southern conquests, 1677–78
track.summary: Eighteen-month southern campaign carried Maratha authority to Tanjore — Jinji, Vellore, Tirumalavadi forts taken; alliance with the Qutb Shahi at Golconda.
track.note: Jinji became the Maratha southern stronghold — the same fort to which Rajaram fled in 1689 after Sambhaji's execution and from which the Marathas held out against Aurangzeb's pursuit for eight years.

track.tooltip: Death at Raigad, 3 April 1680
track.summary: Died at fifty of fever — possibly typhoid. Kingdom passed to Sambhaji; the long Deccan war with Aurangzeb that defined a generation began.
track.note: Aurangzeb left for the Deccan in September 1681 with the largest Mughal field army ever assembled — and never returned to Hindustan. Shivaji's polity outlasted Aurangzeb's by half a century.

people.name: Tipu Sultan, Sultan of Mysore
people.tooltip: Tipu Sultan (1751–1799), 'Tiger of Mysore'
people.summary: Mysore sovereign across four Anglo-Mysore wars; killed defending Srirangapatna, 4 May 1799 — the EIC's last serious Indian rival south of the Krishna.

track.tooltip: Battle of Pollilur, 10 September 1780 — Second Anglo-Mysore War
track.summary: Twenty-eight-year-old Tipu's cavalry annihilated Colonel Baillie's column near Conjeevaram — the EIC's worst Indian defeat to that date.
track.note: The battle was depicted in mural form on the walls of the Daria Daulat Bagh at Srirangapatna — Tipu's commemorative wallpaper of British humiliation. ~3,800 EIC troops killed or captured. Many British officers were imprisoned at Srirangapatna for years; some forcibly converted.

track.tooltip: Accession on death of Hyder Ali, 7 December 1782
track.summary: Inherited the Mysore throne mid-war on Hyder Ali's death from cancer at Chittoor. Closed the Second Anglo-Mysore War with the 1784 Treaty of Mangalore.
track.note: The Treaty of Mangalore (March 1784) restored pre-war boundaries and is the last treaty in which the EIC negotiated as an equal — not a sovereign — with an Indian power. Cornwallis arrived in 1786 with instructions to break Mysore.

track.role: Begins the dream-journal that would track 37 numbered dreams over a decade — political, military, and personal anxieties recorded as rebus.
track.note: The Khwabnama is one of the most unusual personal documents from any Indian ruler — a reigning sovereign's working dream-record, kept in his own hand.

track.tooltip: Third Anglo-Mysore War, 1790–92 — Cornwallis's siege of Srirangapatna
track.summary: Cornwallis-led EIC, Maratha, and Nizam coalition besieged Srirangapatna; Tipu sued for peace, ceded half of Mysore, sent two sons as hostages.
track.note: Indemnity of 33 million rupees and territorial cessions to all three coalition partners. The hostage-sons (Abdul Khaliq, Muiz-ud-din) were held at Madras for two years. Tipu rebuilt the army through the 1790s, sought French support, and corresponded with revolutionary Paris.

track.role: Signed the Treaty of Seringapatam ceding half of Mysore — the territorial settlement that closed the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
track.note: The half ceded included Coorg, Malabar, Baramahal, and Dindigul — strategic and revenue-rich. Mysore was reduced from a regional empire to a defensible Cauvery-valley kingdom.

track.tooltip: Jacobin Club at Srirangapatna and tree of liberty, 5 May 1797
track.summary: Planted a tree of liberty at Srirangapatna; took the title Citoyen Tipoo. Sought French expeditionary support against the EIC through Mauritius.
track.note: The Mauritius proclamation of January 1798 inviting French volunteers reached Wellesley as casus belli for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. Napoleon's Egyptian expedition that summer made the threat plausible to London.

track.tooltip: Fall of Srirangapatna and death in defence, 4 May 1799
track.summary: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. EIC stormed the Water Gate breach; Tipu died fighting at the Hoally Gateway. Mysore reverted to Wodeyar rule under the EIC.
track.note: Body identified after the storming by Major Allan and Colonel Wellesley (the future Duke of Wellington). The Wodeyar dynasty was restored as a princely state under EIC subsidiary alliance — Mysore's last serious sovereignty in the south extinguished. The looted Tipu's Tiger automaton sits in the V&A to this day.

people.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
people.tooltip: Ranjit Singh (1780–1839), 'Sher-e-Punjab'
people.summary: Sukerchakia misl chief who consolidated the Sikh misls into a single Khalsa Sarkar from Lahore — Punjab from the Sutlej to the Khyber for forty years.

track.tooltip: Becomes Sukerchakia misl chief on father's death, age 12, 1792
track.summary: Mahan Singh died of fever; Ranjit inherited the Sukerchakia misl at twelve. Smallpox in childhood had blinded his left eye and pitted his face.
track.note: Mother Raj Kaur and mother-in-law Sada Kaur (Kanhaiya misl) were the regents. The misl confederacy of twelve Sikh kindred-chieftains had governed Punjab since the 1760s; Ranjit's project was to break the misl boundaries and forge a single state.

track.tooltip: Takes Lahore from Bhangi misl with Sada Kaur's troops, 7 July 1799
track.summary: Marched on Lahore with 25,000 Kanhaiya troops. The Bhangi sardars opened the Lohari Gate; the city was taken without battle.
track.note: Zaman Shah Durrani had nominally appointed him governor of Lahore the previous year in return for retrieving Afghan artillery — the appointment Ranjit converted into possession. Lahore became the Khalsa capital.

track.tooltip: Anointed Maharaja of the Punjab on Baisakhi, 12 April 1801
track.summary: Anointed Maharaja of the Sarkar-i-Khalsa by Sahib Singh Bedi (descendant of Guru Nanak) at Lahore Fort. Refused a crown — the Khalsa was the sovereign.
track.note: Coinage was struck in the names of the Gurus, not of the Maharaja. The state was framed as the temporal arm of the Khalsa Panth — a constitutional fiction that gave the Sikh polity its distinctive theocratic-secular hybrid character.

track.tooltip: Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC, 25 April 1809
track.summary: Sutlej fixed as the Khalsa-EIC boundary. Cis-Sutlej Sikh chiefs accepted EIC protection; Ranjit's eastward expansion ended.
track.note: Negotiated by Charles Metcalfe for the EIC. With the eastern frontier closed, Ranjit turned westward — Multan, Kashmir, and Peshawar. The treaty held until his death; the EIC moved across the Sutlej only in 1845.

track.tooltip: Capture of Multan from the Saddozai Afghan governor, 2 June 1818
track.summary: Six-month siege ended when Misr Diwan Chand's troops stormed the citadel. Multan's Afghan governor Muzaffar Khan died with his sons defending the citadel.
track.note: First major reduction of Saddozai-Durrani territory by the Khalsa. Opened the route to Sindh and the lower Indus; brought the Zamzama gun (later Kim's Gun) to Lahore.

track.tooltip: Conquest of Kashmir from the Afghans, 5 July 1819
track.summary: Misr Diwan Chand defeated Jabbar Khan, Afghan governor of Kashmir, at Shopian. Five centuries of intermittent Afghan-Mughal Kashmir ended.
track.note: Kashmir came under direct Sikh administration; Ranjit's nominee governors managed the valley until 1846. After his death and the First Anglo-Sikh War, Kashmir was sold to Gulab Singh of Jammu under the Treaty of Amritsar 1846 — the genealogy of the Dogra rule that lasted to 1947.

track.tooltip: Annexation of Peshawar from the Barakzai, May 1834
track.summary: Hari Singh Nalwa took Peshawar from the Barakzai brothers — the Khalsa frontier reached the Khyber. Persistent Pashtun-Khalsa frontier war for the next decade.
track.note: Nalwa fortified the Khyber with the Jamrud fort; he died at Jamrud in 1837 holding off Dost Mohammed Khan's counter-attack. The Khalsa's Pashtun frontier was the only Indian polity ever to push back permanently into Afghan country.

track.tooltip: Death at Lahore Fort, 27 June 1839
track.summary: Died after a final stroke at fifty-nine. The Khalsa Sarkar he had built unravelled within seven years; the EIC annexed Punjab in 1849.
track.note: Four sons and three regents in seven years of succession bloodletting; Hari Singh Nalwa already dead at Jamrud (1837); the Khalsa Army's panchayats turned political. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) and the Second (1848–49) followed. The Koh-i-Noor — which Ranjit had taken from Shah Shuja in 1813 — was surrendered by his minor son Duleep Singh to Lord Dalhousie in 1849.

people.name: Birsa Munda
people.tooltip: Birsa Munda (1875–1900), 'Dharti Aba'
people.summary: Munda adivasi prophet of Chotanagpur; led the Ulgulan ('Great Tumult') of 1899–1900 against colonial land settlement and missionary encroachment.

track.tooltip: Enters German Mission school at Burju, c. 1886
track.summary: Family converted to Lutheran Christianity; Birsa attended the Burju mission school, then the Chaibasa GEL Mission school. Withdrew in his teens.
track.note: The mission encounter shaped his later religious vocabulary — Birsait theology drew on Christian millenarian forms even as it rejected the missions politically. He left the church in his early teens after a dispute about adivasi land grievances; the missionaries had sided with the zamindars.

track.tooltip: Tutelage with Vaishnav guru Anand Pandey at Bandgaon, c. 1893
track.summary: Two years with a Vaishnav teacher exposed Birsa to Hindu cosmology, mantras, and the bhakti vocabulary he later turned to indigenous prophetic use.
track.note: His religious synthesis — monotheist, abstemious, anti-Christian and anti-missionary, but also anti-traditional adivasi spirit-worship — drew on the Vaishnav years. The result was unrecognisable to the orthodox of any of those traditions.

track.tooltip: Proclaims himself 'Dharti Aba' (Father of the Earth), 1895
track.summary: At Chalkad, declared himself the Munda prophet sent by Singbonga. Called for return to khuntkatti land tenure and the end of dikku (outsider) rule.
track.note: First religious gathering drew thousands. Birsait followers — Birsaits — abstained from alcohol, wore the sacred thread, kept Thursday as a sabbath. The colonial state read it as a Christian-style movement; the missions read it as syncretic; both missed the political programme on land.

track.tooltip: First imprisonment, Hazaribagh Central Jail, 1895–97
track.summary: Arrested August 1895 on rioting charges; sentenced to two years' rigorous imprisonment at Hazaribagh. Released 1897 under the Diamond Jubilee amnesty.
track.note: The two-year jail term hardened the movement. On release Birsa moved between forest hideouts in the Singhbhum and Khunti hills; the Birsait network grew through 1898 in preparation for the Ulgulan.

track.role: Proclaimed the Ulgulan ('Great Tumult') on Christmas Eve 1899; led coordinated attacks on police stations, churches, and zamindari outposts across Khunti and Tamar.
track.note: The military phase ran from 24 December 1899 to early February 1900. ~400 Mundas killed in the suppression; Birsa was captured at Sentra hill on 3 February 1900.

track.tooltip: Death in Ranchi Central Jail, 9 June 1900, age 24
track.summary: Officially died of cholera in jail awaiting trial. Munda oral tradition records poisoning. The 1908 Chotanagpur Tenancy Act was the colonial answer.
track.note: His mausoleum at Distillery Bridge, Ranchi, became the Munda movement's pilgrimage site. The Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908 — protecting adivasi land from non-tribal alienation — is the direct legislative legacy of the Ulgulan; the principle was extended to the Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act 1949 and to Schedule V of the post-Independence Constitution. Jharkhand state, founded 2000, took its centenary year as a deliberate echo.

people.name: Krishnadevaraya, Vijayanagara Emperor
people.tooltip: Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529), Tuluva-dynasty emperor of Vijayanagara
people.summary: Tuluva emperor of Vijayanagara at its apex; defeated the Bahmani successors at Raichur 1520; patron of Telugu and Sanskrit poetry from Hampi.

track.tooltip: Coronation at Vijayanagara, 8 August 1509
track.summary: Crowned at twenty-two on the death of half-brother Vira Narasimha Raya — the Tuluva accession that began two decades of consolidation and expansion.
track.note: Inherited a war on three fronts — Bahmani successors to the north, Gajapatis of Orissa to the east, Portuguese settlement at Goa to the west. The reign would resolve all three by force or treaty within fifteen years.

track.tooltip: Defeats Adil Shahi at Diwani, 1510 — opening the Bahmani-successor war
track.summary: Defeated Yusuf Adil Shah of Bijapur at Diwani in his first major campaign — establishing the Krishna river as the contested northern frontier.
track.note: The Bahmani Sultanate had fragmented into five successor sultanates after 1490. Krishnadevaraya played them against each other for two decades; the strategic logic broke only after his death, when they united for Talikota in 1565.

track.tooltip: Capture of Udayagiri from the Gajapati Pratapa Rudra, 1514
track.summary: Eighteen-month siege of the Udayagiri hill-fort ended Gajapati Orissa's southern claim. Brought the Krishna Vishnu image to Hampi as war trophy.
track.note: Followed by the captures of Kondavidu (1515), Kondapalli (1515), and finally Cuttack itself. The 1518 settlement with Pratapa Rudra fixed the Krishna as the Vijayanagara-Gajapati boundary; sealed by the marriage of Krishnadevaraya to Pratapa Rudra's daughter Tukka Devi.

track.tooltip: Composes the Amuktamalyada, a Telugu poetic epic, c. 1515
track.summary: Composed in his own hand a five-canto Telugu mahakavya on the Vaishnava saint Andal — the only major literary work by a reigning South Indian sovereign.
track.note: The Telugu Ashtadiggajas — eight poets who anchored the literary court — wrote within his patronage. Allasani Peddana, Nandi Thimmana, and Tenali Ramakrishna are the names that survived. Telugu literary historiography dates a 'classical age' to this court.

track.tooltip: Battle of Raichur against Ismail Adil Shah, May 1520
track.summary: Defeated Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur at Raichur after a fifty-day siege. Krishnadevaraya led the cavalry charge in person; Portuguese musketeers tipped it.
track.note: The doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra changed hands repeatedly through the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. Raichur 1520 is the single set-piece victory that fixed it under Vijayanagara for the rest of the reign — and the moment Portuguese-supplied artillery enters the South Indian battlefield as decisive.

track.tooltip: Formalised horse-trade alliance with Portuguese Goa, post-Raichur 1521
track.summary: Formalised the Goa horse-trade alliance with Portugal after Raichur — the Arabian horse imports that fed Vijayanagara cavalry through the rest of the reign.
track.note: Vijayanagara had no native horse-breeding country; cavalry remounts came by sea via Hormuz–Goa. Krishnadevaraya's grain-for-horse settlement with the Portuguese gave Vijayanagara a strategic edge over the inland Deccan sultanates that lacked direct Portuguese access.

track.tooltip: Death at Vijayanagara, 17 October 1529
track.summary: Died in his late fifties — possibly poisoned amid succession intrigue. Half-brother Achyuta Devaraya succeeded; the empire held three more decades to Talikota.
track.note: The Battle of Talikota (26 January 1565) by the combined Deccan sultanates — exactly the alliance Krishnadevaraya's diplomacy had prevented for two decades — destroyed Vijayanagara as an imperial centre. Hampi was sacked over six months and never rebuilt. The empire's southern remnants survived as the Aravidu rump until 1646.

people.name: Guru Gobind Singh
people.tooltip: Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708), tenth and final Sikh Guru
people.summary: Tenth Sikh Guru. Founded the Khalsa at Anandpur on Baisakhi 1699; lost four sons to Aurangzeb's Mughals; closed the Guru lineage in the Adi Granth.

track.tooltip: Becomes tenth Guru on father Tegh Bahadur's execution, 11 November 1675
track.summary: Father Guru Tegh Bahadur beheaded by Aurangzeb at Chandni Chowk for defending Kashmiri Pandits' right to their religion. Gobind Rai succeeded at nine.
track.note: Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom at the Sis Ganj site at Chandni Chowk is the central memory of late-Mughal Sikh-state relations. Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayal Das were executed alongside him.

track.tooltip: Battle of Bhangani against Hill Rajas, September 1688
track.summary: First armed engagement at twenty-one — defeated Bhim Chand of Bilaspur and the Sirmur-Garhwal allied hill chiefs near Paonta Sahib on the Yamuna.
track.note: Composed the Chandi di Var and parts of the Dasam Granth at Paonta Sahib in this period. The Sikh-Pahari Hill State antagonism through the 1690s set the stage for Anandpur's siege a decade later.

track.tooltip: Founding of the Khalsa at Anandpur, Baisakhi 1699
track.summary: Initiated the Panj Pyare ('Five Beloved') with khande di pahul amrit at Anandpur — the founding of the Khalsa Panth as a casteless martial fraternity.
track.note: The Five Beloved came from across caste lines (Khatri, Jat, Chhimba, Ghumar, Nai) and from across regions (Lahore, Delhi, Dwarka, Jagannath Puri, Bidar). The Five Ks (kesh, kara, kanga, kachera, kirpan), the surname Singh for men and Kaur for women, and the formal Khalsa creed all date to this initiation.

track.tooltip: Siege and evacuation of Anandpur, 1704–05
track.summary: Eight-month siege by Sirhind Mughals plus Hill Rajas. Evacuated under safe-conduct that was immediately broken at the Sarsa river crossing.
track.note: Family separated at the Sarsa crossing in flood. Mother Mata Gujri and the two younger sons (Zorawar Singh, 9; Fateh Singh, 6) were captured by the Sirhind faujdar Wazir Khan and bricked alive into a wall in Sirhind on 12 December 1705 for refusing conversion.

track.tooltip: Battle of Chamkaur Sahib, 21–22 December 1704
track.summary: Defended the Chamkaur haveli with forty Sikhs against a Mughal force in the tens of thousands. Two elder sons (Ajit Singh 17, Jujhar Singh 14) killed.
track.note: Escaped at the Five Beloved's insistence on the night of 22 December disguised as Uchh-da-Pir, with Bhai Daya Singh, Bhai Dharam Singh, and Bhai Maan Singh. Reached the Machhiwara forest on foot. Within days all four of Guru Gobind Singh's sons (the Char Sahibzade) were dead.

track.tooltip: Composition of the Zafarnamah ('Epistle of Victory') to Aurangzeb, 1705
track.summary: Persian-verse letter written from Dina (Punjab) addressed to Aurangzeb in the Deccan, charging him with breach of solemn oath and the murder of children.
track.note: Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh carried the epistle south to Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar. The Mughal emperor died at Ahmadnagar in March 1707 having (per several reports) read it. Stanza 22: 'When all means of redress have failed, it is righteous to draw the sword.'

track.tooltip: Installs the Adi Granth as eternal Guru, Nanded, October 1708
track.summary: On his deathbed at Nanded, ended the personal-Guru lineage by investing the Adi Granth (Guru Granth Sahib) as the eternal Sikh Guru in perpetuity.
track.note: Stabbed by two Pathan assassins (sent, per tradition, by Wazir Khan of Sirhind) at Nanded the previous month; the wound reopened. Banda Singh Bahadur, met at Nanded that summer, was sent north to Punjab as Guru-appointed military commander — the Sirhind avenger and founder of the first Sikh statehood under arms.

people.name: Maharani Tarabai Bhonsle
people.tooltip: Tarabai (1675–1761), Maratha regent during Aurangzeb's Deccan war
people.summary: Maratha regent for her son Shivaji II from 1700; held the Maratha resistance against Aurangzeb's last Deccan campaign and ran the southern war from Panhala.

track.tooltip: Marriage to Rajaram Chhatrapati, 1683
track.summary: Daughter of senapati Hambirao Mohite. Married Rajaram, Shivaji's younger son, at eight; he was twelve. Politically central from her teens.
track.note: The Mohite family had served Shahji Bhonsle. Rajaram's first wife Jankibai was from the Shirke family; Tarabai was his second. Sambhaji's execution in 1689 made Rajaram the second Chhatrapati at twenty-two, in flight from Aurangzeb's army.

track.tooltip: Flight to Jinji with Rajaram, 1689
track.summary: After Sambhaji's execution and the fall of Raigad, fled south with Rajaram to the Jinji fort in Tamil country — held out eight years against Aurangzeb.
track.note: Zulfiqar Khan's eight-year siege of Jinji is the longest set-piece campaign of Aurangzeb's Deccan war. Rajaram escaped Jinji in 1697 by sea-and-land; Tarabai and the household evacuated overland. Their son Shivaji II was born at Jinji in 1696.

track.tooltip: Becomes regent for Shivaji II on Rajaram's death, 12 March 1700
track.summary: Rajaram died at twenty-nine of fever at Sinhagad. Tarabai assumed the regency for four-year-old Shivaji II and ran the Maratha war for seven years.
track.note: Khafi Khan, the Mughal court historian who saw her in action, wrote that she 'set herself up as regent during her son's minority, taking on the management of the army and the affairs of the state.' Aurangzeb's last seven years in the Deccan were spent fighting this woman's commanders.

track.tooltip: Resistance from Panhala fort against Aurangzeb's siege wars, 1700–07
track.summary: Ran the Maratha war from Panhala while Aurangzeb's army besieged Sahyadri forts one by one. Forts retaken nearly as fast as lost — the strategy held.
track.note: Aurangzeb's siege army took Satara (1700), Parli (1700), Panhala (1701), Vishalgad, Khelna, Rajmachi, Sinhagad — and by the time he had finished the southern third, Tarabai's commanders Dhanaji Jadhav, Santaji Ghorpade, and Parashuram Trimbak had retaken most of them. The Mughal financial drain became unsupportable.

track.tooltip: Split with Shahu after Aurangzeb's death, 1707
track.summary: Aurangzeb died March 1707; Bahadur Shah released Sambhaji's son Shahu to split the Marathas. Tarabai backed Shivaji II; Shahu won at Khed, October 1707.
track.note: Balaji Vishwanath, the Peshwa-to-be, switched from Tarabai's faction to Shahu's at Khed and tipped the battle. The Maratha state split into a senior Satara line under Shahu and a junior Kolhapur line under Tarabai's son. The Peshwa office she had inadvertently empowered would soon eclipse the Chhatrapati institution itself.

track.tooltip: Deposed and imprisoned by co-wife Rajasbai, 1714
track.summary: Rajasbai (Rajaram's other widow) deposed Tarabai and Shivaji II in a coup at Kolhapur; held her in confinement at Panhala then Satara for three decades.
track.note: Three decades of confinement. Re-emerged in the 1740s under Shahu's protection at Satara — and would, on Shahu's death in 1749, attempt one last political act: producing a grandson she claimed as legitimate Chhatrapati.

track.tooltip: Final political move under Peshwa Balaji Bajirao, 1750–61
track.summary: Produced 'Ramraja' as Shivaji II's grandson and Shahu's heir; clashed with Peshwa Balaji Bajirao for a decade. Died at Satara months after Panipat 1761.
track.note: Outlived Shahu (d. 1749), Balaji Bajirao's brother Chimaji Appa, the Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) which killed an entire generation of Peshwa commanders, and Peshwa Balaji Bajirao himself (d. June 1761). Died eight months after Panipat at eighty-six. The Chhatrapati office she had defended ended functionally with her.

people.name: Rani Gaidinliu
people.tooltip: Rani Gaidinliu (1915–1993), Naga Heraka leader and anti-colonial rebel
people.summary: Rongmei Naga spiritual-political leader. Carried the Heraka movement after Haipou Jadonang's hanging; jailed 1932–47 for armed resistance against the Raj.

track.tooltip: Joins cousin Haipou Jadonang's Heraka movement, c. 1927
track.summary: Joined cousin Haipou Jadonang's Heraka movement at thirteen — a Zeliangrong-Naga reform of traditional religion against missionary and colonial encroachment.
track.note: Heraka was a monotheist reform of Zeliangrong religion, framed against the Baptist missionary push and the colonial revenue settlement. Jadonang declared himself the Messianic king to restore Naga sovereignty across British Manipur, Naga Hills, and the Cachar plains.

track.tooltip: Cousin Jadonang hanged by the British at Imphal, 29 August 1931
track.summary: Jadonang was tried for the ritual killing of four Manipuri traders and hanged at Imphal at twenty-six. Gaidinliu inherited the Heraka leadership at sixteen.
track.note: Colonial administration treated Jadonang's execution as the end of the movement. Gaidinliu pivoted from spiritual-political to outright armed: refusal of taxes to the Raj, sheltering of fugitives, an underground network across the three districts.

track.tooltip: Armed Heraka rising and capture by the British, October 1932
track.summary: Armed Naga villages with daos and spears; ambushed Assam Rifles columns through 1932. Captured at Pulomi village 17 October; tried 1933, sentenced to life.
track.note: Defended by Mr Mills (the Deputy Commissioner who knew her from earlier negotiations) as a juvenile under-eighteen. Sentence converted from death (asked by the Manipuri durbar) to transportation for life. Held at Guwahati, Shillong, Aizawl, and Tura jails over fifteen years.

track.tooltip: Nehru visits her in Shillong jail, calls her 'Rani', 1937
track.summary: Nehru visited her at Shillong jail in 1937 during a Congress north-east tour; he named her 'Rani' in the press and campaigned through the war for her release.
track.note: Nehru's column in The Hindustan Times made the name stick. The British refused release at his request multiple times; an attempted appeal to the Privy Council failed in 1939. The 'Rani' framing brought a remote north-east figure into the all-India nationalist consciousness.

track.tooltip: Released after Independence on Nehru's order, 14 October 1947
track.summary: Released from Tura jail two months after Independence on Nehru's direct instruction, after fifteen years' imprisonment from age sixteen.
track.note: Returned to a Heraka movement that had splintered. The post-Independence years were spent navigating Naga sub-nationalist politics — opposed the Naga National Council's secessionist line under Phizo, advocated a Zeliangrong homeland within the Indian union. The political contradictions of frontier-region inclusion played out for the rest of her life.

track.tooltip: Zeliangrong homeland campaign and underground years, 1960s
track.summary: Underground from 1960 in the Zeliangrong hills against both the Indian government and the NNC, demanding a Zeliangrong region across three NE states.
track.note: Six years underground in the same hills as Phizo's Naga Federal Government and the Indian Army's counter-insurgency operations. Surrendered in 1966 to negotiate with the Government of India. The Zeliangrong autonomous district demand remains live; partial administrative recognition came through the Zeliangrong Heraka Association.

track.tooltip: Death at Lungkao village, Tamenglong, 17 February 1993
track.summary: Returned to her birth village in 1991 and died there at seventy-eight. Padma Bhushan 1982; postage stamp 1996; rare NE figure on state honour lists.
track.note: Birth-centenary commemorations in 2015 — including a Modi-government coin issue — were politically contested by Naga Christian groups who read Heraka as a Hindu-revivalist project. The contestation itself carries the unresolved religious-nationalist questions of north-eastern self-definition.

people.name: Jagadish Chandra Bose
people.tooltip: J.C. Bose (1858–1937), plant physiology and radio-wave pioneer
people.summary: Bengali physicist and biologist; demonstrated radio waves at Calcutta 1895; founded plant electrophysiology; first Indian FRS in physics.

track.tooltip: Joins Presidency College, Calcutta as Professor of Physics, 1885
track.summary: Cambridge Tripos; joined Presidency College Calcutta as Professor of Physics 1885 — paid two-thirds European salary for three years; refused, back-paid in full.
track.note: The salary protest — refusing one-third reduction — is the canonical biographical episode of his early career. The College authorities held out three years; Bose taught without pay; eventually they capitulated and back-paid him in full. The principle of equal pay for Indian and European faculty was established at Presidency from this point.

track.tooltip: Radio-wave transmission demo, Calcutta Town Hall, November 1895
track.summary: Demonstrated remote bell-ringing and gunpowder ignition by millimetre-wave radio at Calcutta Town Hall, Nov 1895. Marconi's first patent: 1896.
track.note: The 1895 demonstration preceded Marconi's 1896 patent and the 1901 transatlantic transmission. Bose declined to patent his work — 'I have refused the entreaties of friends to take out patents... [the discoveries] are the inheritance of all'. The IEEE in 1998 retroactively recognised him as one of the originators of radio. The receiver coherer he developed (1895–99) was independently used by Marconi.

track.tooltip: Royal Institution lecture and FRS election, 1896–1920
track.summary: Royal Institution lecture Jan 1897 on millimetre-wave detection; papers in Nature and Proc. Royal Society; FRS 1920 — first Indian physicist.
track.note: Lord Rayleigh, J.J. Thomson, Lord Kelvin endorsed his work; the Royal Institution lecture made his reputation in European physics. The pivot to plant physiology came after 1900 — his crescograph (high-magnification growth-recording instrument), demonstrations of plant electrical responses to stimulus, and the 1902 publication Response in the Living and Non-Living established the field.

track.tooltip: Founds the Bose Research Institute, Calcutta, 30 November 1917
track.summary: Founded the Bose Research Institute at Calcutta on his 59th birthday — first Indian-led scientific research institution; physics, plant physiology, biophysics.
track.note: Funded substantially from his own savings and from Indian patronage (Tata, Bhupendranath Basu). The Institute remains active under that name. The founding deliberately preceded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (1945) and the Indian Institute of Science (founded 1909) as the first institution conceived and funded principally by Indians for original scientific research.

people.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
people.tooltip: Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920), Madras-Cambridge mathematician
people.summary: Erode-Kumbakonam mathematical autodidact; ~3,900 results in number theory, modular forms, infinite series; Cambridge under Hardy 1914–19; FRS 1918, age 30.

track.tooltip: Discovers G.S. Carr's Synopsis at Town High School, Kumbakonam, 1903
track.summary: At fifteen, encountered Carr's Synopsis at Kumbakonam Town High — re-derived its 5,000 results from scratch; mathematical apprenticeship complete by sixteen.
track.note: Carr's Synopsis was a Victorian compilation for British university students — terse, no proofs. Ramanujan's habit of writing only results without derivation, the source of much later Hardy-Littlewood frustration, traces to this self-trained habit. The Government Arts College Kumbakonam scholarship he won 1904 was lost the following year because he failed every subject except mathematics.

track.tooltip: Clerkship at Madras Port Trust, March 1912
track.summary: Married 1909, broke and tubercular, took a Madras Port Trust clerkship under Sir Francis Spring — who recognised the notebooks and pushed Ramanujan to Hardy.
track.note: Spring read the notebooks and arranged correspondence with Cambridge. The first letter to Hardy (16 January 1913) — nine pages, ~120 results, no proofs — produced the famous Hardy-Littlewood verdict: 'They must be true; if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them.'

track.tooltip: Sails for Cambridge, March 1914
track.summary: Sailed for Cambridge March 1914 on Hardy's invitation — the four-year collaboration produced the Hardy-Ramanujan partition formula and highly composite numbers.
track.note: Brahmin orthodoxy at Kumbakonam initially refused permission to cross the kala pani; the family deity at Namakkal eventually delivered (per Ramanujan's mother) the dream-permission that allowed the voyage. Hardy and Littlewood became his collaborators; Janaki Ammal (his wife) remained in Madras through the war years and never joined him.

track.tooltip: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society and Fellow of Trinity College, 1918
track.summary: Elected FRS 2 May 1918 at thirty — second Indian. Trinity Fellow October 1918 — first Indian. Tubercular, 110 lb, often hospitalised.
track.note: FRS at thirty was unusual; the citation cited 'his investigations in the Theory of Numbers, Elliptic Functions, Continued Fractions, and Infinite Series'. The taxicab-1729 anecdote (Hardy: 'a rather dull number'; Ramanujan: 'No Hardy, it is a very interesting number — the smallest expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways') is from a 1919 hospital visit.

track.tooltip: Returns to Madras March 1919; dies at Kumbakonam April 1920
track.summary: Returned to Madras tubercular March 1919; died at Kumbakonam 26 April 1920, age 32. The 'lost notebook' (~600 results) recovered at Trinity 1976.
track.note: The 'lost notebook' — 138 pages of mock theta functions and modular form results from his final year — was recovered by George Andrews from the Trinity College Wren Library in 1976. Mock theta functions, Ramanujan's last unfinished work, became foundational to the modern theory of mock modular forms (Zagier, Bringmann, Ono). His birthday (22 December) is the National Mathematics Day in India.

people.name: Sir Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman
people.tooltip: C.V. Raman (1888–1970), Nobel laureate in physics 1930
people.summary: Tamil physicist; discovered the Raman effect 1928; Nobel Prize 1930 — first Asian science Nobel; founded the Indian Academy of Sciences 1934.

track.tooltip: Joins Indian Finance Department, Calcutta, 1907
track.summary: Top of Madras BA mathematics at sixteen; topped the 1907 Indian Finance Service exam; posted Calcutta as Assistant Accountant General; physics in evenings.

location.name: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Calcutta

track.note: The Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS) at Bowbazar — founded 1876 by Mahendralal Sircar as India's first private scientific research society — gave Raman lab space in his evenings. The decade of finance-by-day, physics-by-night produced ~30 publications on acoustics and optics before he resigned to take the Calcutta University chair 1917.

track.tooltip: Sea voyage observation of the blue Mediterranean, 1921
track.summary: On the September 1921 voyage Southampton-Bombay, observed the Mediterranean's deep blue — challenged the Rayleigh sky-reflection explanation.
track.note: Lord Rayleigh's view (1910) attributed sea-blue to sky-reflection. Raman's 1921 onboard work showed the colour persisted under conditions excluding reflection — molecular scattering by water itself. The two-page Nature paper (November 1921) opened the seven-year programme that produced the Raman effect 1928.

track.tooltip: Discovery of the Raman effect (inelastic light scattering), 28 February 1928
track.summary: Together with K.S. Krishnan, discovered the inelastic light-scattering effect — frequency-shifted scattered light reveals molecular vibration. Nobel Prize 1930.

location.name: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Calcutta

track.note: 28 February remains India's National Science Day. The discovery used a 1925 mercury arc lamp, a quartz spectrograph, and observed scattered-light frequency shifts in 60 different liquids. The Nobel Prize 1930 made him the first Asian science Nobel laureate; his speech at Stockholm referenced the ICS-and-Indian-civilian-life environment in which the work was done.

track.tooltip: Director of the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, 1933
track.summary: Director of IISc Bangalore 1933 — first Indian to head it. Resigned 1937 over admin disputes; founded Raman Research Institute Bangalore 1948.
track.note: Founded the Indian Academy of Sciences 1934 at Bangalore (the Indian National Academy of Sciences founded earlier under Saha at Allahabad gave the country two parallel academies, a duplication that has not been resolved). The Raman Research Institute (1948) at Bangalore on land donated by the Mysore government became his post-IISc base for the rest of his life.

people.name: Meghnad Saha
people.tooltip: Meghnad Saha (1893–1956), thermal-ionisation equation and astrophysics
people.summary: Bengali astrophysicist; Saha ionisation equation 1920 founded modern stellar spectroscopy; founded the Saha Nuclear Physics Institute; only scientist MP, 1952.

track.tooltip: Saha ionisation equation, Philosophical Magazine, 1920
track.summary: Published the thermal-ionisation equation in Philosophical Magazine 1920 — linking stellar spectra to atmospheric temperature; founded modern astrophysics.
track.note: Eddington called the Saha equation 'amongst the dozen most important advances in theoretical astrophysics' of the early 20th century. Saha was at UCL on the 1919 Premchand Roychand scholarship; A.S. Eddington and H.N. Russell extended the equation in the 1920s; the equation remains the textbook foundation of stellar atmospheric spectroscopy.

track.tooltip: Founds Indian National Academy of Sciences at Allahabad, 1934
track.summary: Founded the National Academy of Sciences India (NASI) at Allahabad 1934 — predating Raman's IAS Bangalore; the Saha-Raman duplication has persisted.
track.note: Saha at Allahabad University (1923-38) was the institutional rival to Raman's Calcutta-then-Bangalore. The two academies — Saha's NASI at Allahabad (later moved to delhi) and Raman's IAS at Bangalore — were founded in deliberate parallel; their merger has been proposed and rejected multiple times since. The duplication is the institutional residue of the Bengal scientific rivalry.

track.tooltip: Founds the Institute of Nuclear Physics, Calcutta, 11 January 1950
track.summary: Founded the Institute of Nuclear Physics at Calcutta 1950; renamed Saha Institute after his death. India's first nuclear institution beside Bhabha's TIFR.
track.note: Inaugurated by Madame Joliot-Curie. Saha had built the Calcutta cyclotron — first in Asia — through 1939-44 with substantial Tata Trust funding. The Saha-Bhabha relationship was tense: Bhabha's TIFR Bombay (1945) absorbed most central nuclear funding under Nehru's preference; Saha's Calcutta institute remained smaller. The split shaped Indian nuclear-science institutional geography.

track.tooltip: Lok Sabha member from North-West Calcutta, 1952–56
track.summary: Elected to the first Lok Sabha 1952 from North-West Calcutta as independent — the only practising scientist in the Constituent Assembly or first Lok Sabha.
track.note: Critic from the floor of Nehru's nuclear policy — argued for a Calcutta-based programme over Bhabha's Bombay-centred model. Drafted the calendar reform proposal that produced the 1957 National Calendar of India (the Saka Era). Died of a heart attack 16 February 1956 walking to a Planning Commission meeting at North Block — the lone scientist in the post-Independence Indian parliament.

polities.name: Maurya Empire
polities.tooltip: Maurya Empire — 322–185 BCE, the first subcontinental imperial state
polities.summary: Chandragupta's overthrow of the Nandas to Pushyamitra Sunga's coup — the Mauryas were the first to unify the subcontinent under a single political authority.
polities.framing: The Mauryan Empire is the first state to unify most of the subcontinent — at its peak under Ashoka extending from Afghanistan to Karnataka and from Gujarat to Bengal. Its institutional inheritance includes the Arthashastra (Kautilya's treatise on statecraft, the most extensive ancient Indian political text), the Mauryan provincial-administrative framework that successor states would draw on for centuries, and the Ashokan dhamma policy that produced the earliest surviving Indian inscriptions. The empire's collapse under Pushyamitra Sunga's coup left a political vacuum that lasted five centuries — no equivalent unified imperial regime emerged until the Guptas (320 CE).
rulers: Brihadratha (last emperor, killed by Pushyamitra c. 185 BCE)

sources.label: Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; rev. 2012)
Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India (2002), ch. 7–8

polities.name: Gupta Empire
polities.tooltip: Gupta Empire — c. 320–550 CE, the second subcontinental imperial state
polities.summary: Chandragupta I's founding to Hun-induced collapse — the Guptas re-unified north India and built classical antiquity's high culture.
polities.framing: The Gupta Empire was the second subcontinental imperial regime after the Mauryas, ruling from c. 320 to c. 550 CE — about 230 years that Indian historiography conventionally identifies as the classical-antiquity peak. The Guptas re-unified north India after five centuries of post-Mauryan fragmentation; their territorial reach under Samudragupta and Chandragupta II extended from the Hindu Kush to the Bay of Bengal and tributary into the Deccan. The institutional inheritance includes the formative Sanskrit literary canon (Kalidasa, Bhartrihari), foundational mathematics (Aryabhata's place-value zero, c. 499 CE), astronomy (Aryabhatiya, Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita), and the iconographic types that defined Hindu temple sculpture. The Hun (Hephthalite) invasions from the 450s onwards exhausted the empire; political-administrative continuity ended c. 550 CE. Northern India remained politically fragmented until the Delhi Sultanate (1206) — over six and a half centuries.

date_span.display: c. 320 CE (Chandragupta I) – c. 550 CE (post-Hun collapse)

sources.label: S.R. Goyal, A History of the Imperial Guptas (1967)
Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India (2002), ch. 9

polities.name: Harsha's Empire
polities.tooltip: Harsha's Empire — 606–647 CE, Pushyabhuti dynasty from Kanauj
polities.summary: Harsha's 41-year empire from Kanauj — the last unified north Indian regime before the post-Gupta fragmentation hardened into the Tripartite Struggle.
polities.framing: Harsha's Pushyabhuti-dynasty empire (606–647 CE) is the most successful single attempt at re-unifying north India between the Gupta collapse (c. 550) and the Delhi Sultanate (1206) — six and a half centuries during which no other regime achieved comparable territorial scope. The 41-year reign produced extensive court documentation (Bana's Harshacharita, Xuanzang's Records, Harsha's own three plays) that makes this among the best-documented early-medieval Indian regimes. The empire reached from Punjab to Bengal and extended south to the Narmada (where Pulakeshin II checked it). Its institutional fragility — entirely held together by Harsha's personal authority — produced the immediate post-647 fragmentation and the Tripartite Struggle for Kanauj that defined the next two centuries.

date_span.display: 606–647 CE (Harsha's reign; empire fragmented after his death)

rulers: Harsha (606–647, last great north Indian emperor before Sultanate)

sources.label: D. Devahuti, Harsha: A Political Study (3rd ed., 1998)

polities.name: Pala Empire
polities.tooltip: Pala Empire — c. 750–1161 CE, Buddhist patron dynasty of Bengal-Bihar
polities.summary: Bengal-Bihar dynasty founded by elective Gopala c. 750; last major Indian patron of Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism; ended by the Senas c. 1161.
polities.framing: The Pala Empire ruled Bengal-Bihar for over four centuries (c. 750–1161 CE) — among the longest continuous regional dynasties of early-medieval India. Its founder Gopala was elected by the Bengali nobility to end the post-Gupta matsya-nyaya chaos, an unusual non-dynastic founding legitimacy. The Palas were the last major Indian patrons of institutional Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism — Vikramashila, Somapura, Odantapuri, Jagaddala universities all flourished under successive Pala emperors. The dynasty contested Kanauj in the Tripartite Struggle (Dharmapala, Devapala) but consolidated its power in the eastern Gangetic plain rather than pursuing the symbolic-imperial centre. Atisha Dipankara left Vikramashila for Tibet in 1042 — taking the Pala-patronised Sanskrit Buddhist scholarship that became the foundation of Tibetan Buddhism. The Senas (Lakshmana Sena's dynasty) displaced the Palas c. 1161; Bakhtiyar Khilji's 1193 sack of the universities and his 1204 conquest of the Senas ended the eastern Indian Buddhist tradition the Palas had patronised.
rulers: Mahipala I (c. 988–1038; revival under late dynasty)

sources.label: R.C. Majumdar (ed.), The History of Bengal, vol. I (1943)

polities.name: Imperial Chola Empire
polities.tooltip: Imperial Cholas — 985–1279 CE, dominant South Indian regime
polities.summary: Vijayalaya's 9th-c. revival to Rajaraja-Rajendra peak to Pandya defeat 1279 — South India's longest imperial regime and its only major naval projection.
polities.framing: The Imperial Chola period (985–1279 CE) — counted from Rajaraja I's accession — is South India's longest unified imperial regime. Vijayalaya Chola (r. c. 848) had revived the older Sangam-age Chola line in the 9th century; under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I the empire absorbed most of South India, the Sri Lankan north, and (briefly) Srivijaya in Sumatra. The Brihadishvara temple at Tanjore (1010) and the Gangaikonda Cholapuram complex (after 1025) are the architectural monuments. The Chola institutional inheritance includes the most extensively documented administrative system of any pre-Mughal Indian dynasty (the Tamil land-grant inscriptions number in the thousands), the Chola bronze sculpture tradition, and the merchant-guild networks (Ainnurruvar, Manigramam) that sustained the Bay of Bengal trading economy through the 13th century. The dynasty declined under Pandya and Hoysala pressure across the 13th century; the last Chola, Rajendra III, fell to the Pandyas c. 1279.

sources.label: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Cōḷas (1935; rev. 1955)
Y. Subbarayalu, South India under the Cholas (2012)

polities.name: Delhi Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Delhi Sultanate — 1206–1526, five Turkic-Afghan dynasties
polities.summary: Three centuries of Turkic-Persian-Afghan rule from Delhi — the Mamluk-Khalji-Tughlaq imperial high water and the long Sayyid-Lodi decline.
polities.framing: The Delhi Sultanate is conventionally read as five distinct dynasties (Mamluk 1206–90, Khalji 1290–1320, Tughlaq 1320–1413, Sayyid 1414–51, Lodi 1451–1526) but ran as one institutional regime — Persian-court, Turkic-military-elite, iqta-funded, with a continuous claim to subcontinental sovereignty backed by an army permanently stationed against the Mongol northwest. The Khalji-Tughlaq high period (1296–1351) was the Sultanate's imperial peak — Alauddin's standing army of 475,000, Malik Kafur's southern campaigns reaching Madurai, the entire subcontinent under tribute. From the Bahmani breakaway (1347) onwards the Sultanate contracted to a north-Indian regional power; Timur's 1398 sack ended the imperial pretension; the Lodi successor regime fell at Panipat in 1526.
rulers: Mamluk: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210), Iltutmish (1211–1236), Razia (1236–1240), Balban (1266–1287)
Tughlaq: Ghiyasuddin (1320–1325), Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351), Firuz Shah (1351–1388)
Sayyid: Khizr Khan (1414–1421), Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah, Alam Shah (1445–1451)

sources.label: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate: A Political and Military History (1999)
Sunil Kumar, The Emergence of the Delhi Sultanate, 1192–1286 (2007)

polities.name: Bahmani Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Bahmani Sultanate — 1347–1527, Deccan breakaway from the Tughlaqs
polities.summary: Hasan Gangu's 1347 revolt produced the first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan; fragmented in 1527 into the five Deccan Sultanates.

sources.label: H.K. Sherwani, The Bahmanis of the Deccan (1985)
Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300–1761 (2005)

polities.name: Sur Empire
polities.tooltip: Sur Empire — 1540–1556, the Suri interregnum between Mughal phases
polities.summary: Sher Shah's 1540 defeat of Humayun inaugurated sixteen years of Suri rule — revenue and road reforms that the returning Mughals inherited intact.

date_span.display: 1540 (Sher Shah defeats Humayun) – 1556 (Hemu falls at Panipat)

sources.label: K.R. Qanungo, Sher Shah and His Times (1965)

polities.name: Mughal Empire
polities.tooltip: Mughal Empire — 1526–1857, Babur's Panipat to formal dissolution after 1857
polities.summary: Babur's victory at Panipat to the formal British dissolution of the empire after 1857 — the longest unified subcontinental imperial regime since the Mauryas.
polities.framing: The Mughal Empire is conventionally periodised in three phases: founding and consolidation (Babur–Humayun–Akbar, 1526–1605), high imperial rule (Jahangir–Shah Jahan–Aurangzeb, 1605–1707), and long decline punctuated by the formal end after the 1857 rebellion. Its institutional legacy — the mansab system, zabt revenue, Persian as administrative language, the Mughal court ceremonial — outlived the dynasty by decades, structuring both the late Maratha Confederacy and the early EIC's Bengal administration. Babur is buried in Kabul; Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last emperor, was exiled to Rangoon and died there in 1862.

date_span.display: 1526–1857 (formal dissolution by EIC after the 1857 rebellion)

rulers: Bahadur Shah I through Bahadur Shah Zafar (1707–1857)

sources.label: John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire (Cambridge New History of India I.5, 1993)
Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanate to the Mughals — Part Two (1999)

polities.name: Mysore Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Mysore Sultanate — 1761–1799 under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
polities.summary: Hyder Ali's 1761 coup against the Wodeyar maharaja produced the Mysore Sultanate — four wars against the EIC ended at Tipu's death at Srirangapatna in 1799.

date_span.display: 1761 (Hyder Ali deposes the Wodeyars) – 1799 (Tipu falls at Srirangapatna)

sources.label: Kate Brittlebank, Tipu Sultan's Search for Legitimacy (1997)

polities.name: East India Company
polities.tooltip: EIC — 1600 charter to 1858 dissolution; ruled British India after 1772
polities.summary: Trading company that became colonial state — the EIC ran British India from Hastings's 1772 centralisation until the Crown takeover after 1857.
polities.framing: The East India Company was chartered by Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600 as a joint-stock trading monopoly. The 1757 Plassey victory and the 1765 Diwani grant transferred Bengal's revenue to Company hands; by 1772 Hastings had centralised colonial administration at Calcutta. The Regulating Act (1773) made the Company's Governor-General accountable to the British Parliament; the Charter Acts of 1813 and 1833 stripped its trade monopolies and reduced it to a colonial-administration shell. After the 1857 rebellion the Government of India Act (August 1858) transferred all Company territory to the Crown; the EIC was formally dissolved in 1874. The Company's institutional record — the world's most extensively documented commercial entity by archive volume — is held at the British Library's India Office collections.
rulers: Dalhousie (1848–1856; Doctrine of Lapse, last EIC GG)

sources.label: Philip J. Stern, The Company-State (2011)
William Dalrymple, The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company (2019)

polities.name: British Raj
polities.tooltip: British Raj — 1858–1947, Crown direct rule of India after the EIC
polities.summary: The Crown regime that succeeded the EIC after 1857 — eighty-nine years of direct British rule, ending with the 1947 partition.
polities.framing: The Government of India Act (August 1858) transferred all EIC territory and authority to the British Crown, replacing the Governor-General with a Viceroy answering to the Secretary of State for India in London. The Raj's first half-century (1858–1905) consolidated infrastructure, education, and administrative apparatus; from Curzon's 1905 partition of Bengal onwards it was on the political defensive against an organised Indian nationalism. The 1909 Morley-Minto reforms introduced limited Indian representation; the 1919 Government of India Act (Montagu-Chelmsford) added provincial dyarchy; the 1935 Government of India Act produced the constitutional template the Republic would inherit. The Raj ended at midnight on 14–15 August 1947 with the partition that produced India and Pakistan.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983)
Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989)
Judith M. Brown, Modern India: The Origins of an Asian Democracy (2nd ed., 1994)

polities.name: Hyderabad State
polities.tooltip: Hyderabad State — 1724–1948, Asaf Jahi (Nizam) dynasty
polities.summary: The largest princely state under British paramountcy — Asaf Jahi rule from the 1724 Mughal-viceroy breakaway to India's 1948 Operation Polo annexation.
rulers: Nizam Ali Khan Asaf Jah II (1762–1803)
Mir Mahbub Ali Khan Asaf Jah VI (1869–1911)
Mir Osman Ali Khan Asaf Jah VII (1911–1948; reportedly the world's wealthiest individual at his height)

sources.label: Karen Leonard, Locating Home: India's Hyderabadis Abroad (2007)
Lucien D. Benichou, From Autocracy to Integration: Political Developments in Hyderabad State 1938–1948 (2000)

polities.name: Khalsa / Sikh Confederacy
polities.tooltip: Khalsa Panth & Sikh political tradition — 1699 founding through 1849
polities.summary: From Guru Gobind Singh's founding of the Khalsa in 1699 to the misls and Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire — Sikh political tradition through 1849.
polities.framing: The Khalsa was founded by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi 1699 — a religious-military order that fused initiation through the Five Beloved (Panj Pyare) with armed defence of the Sikh community against Mughal persecution. The earlier Mughal executions of Guru Arjan Dev (1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675) had radicalised the Sikh tradition; the Khalsa was the institutional response. After Banda Singh Bahadur's brief 1710–15 conquests in Punjab, the Sikh tradition organised through twelve misls (clan-confederacies) through the 18th century, then consolidated under Maharaja Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire (1801–1849) ruling from Lahore. The Anglo-Sikh wars (1845–46, 1848–49) ended Sikh sovereignty; the East India Company annexed Punjab in 1849.

date_span.display: 1699 (Khalsa founded) – 1849 (annexation of Punjab after the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War)

sources.label: J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge New History of India II.3, 1990)
Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs (2 vols., 1963; rev. 2004)

polities.name: Maratha Confederacy
polities.tooltip: Maratha Confederacy — Shivaji's coronation 1674 to Anglo-Maratha defeat 1818
polities.summary: Shivaji's 1674 coronation founded the Maratha state; the Confederacy's century of expansion ended at the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) defeat by the EIC.
polities.framing: The Maratha state was founded by Shivaji at his coronation at Raigad in 1674 — a deliberate Hindu sovereign-claim against Mughal supremacy in the Deccan. After Shivaji's death (1680) and Sambhaji's execution by Aurangzeb (1689), the Marathas survived twenty-seven years of Mughal pressure, emerging by the 1720s under the Peshwa system as the dominant subcontinental power. At their height (c. 1758) the Maratha Confederacy controlled directly or indirectly most of the subcontinent from Punjab to Karnataka. The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) broke their northern projection; the Anglo-Maratha Wars of 1775–82, 1803–05, and 1817–18 ended Maratha sovereignty. The Peshwa system, the chauth-sardeshmukhi tax structure, and the Mahrashtrian-Konkani administrative tradition the Marathas built persisted into the colonial period.

sources.label: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600–1818 (Cambridge New History of India II.4, 1993)
Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India: Agrarian Society and Politics under the Eighteenth-Century Maratha Svarajya (1986)

polities.name: Bhopal State
polities.tooltip: Bhopal State — princely state 1723–1949, Begum-rule from 1819
polities.summary: Founded 1723 by an Afghan Mughal-army officer; ruled by four successive Begums 1819–1926 — uniquely a matrilineal princely state.
polities.framing: Bhopal State was founded in 1723 by Dost Muhammad Khan, an Afghan officer of Aurangzeb's army who established himself in the central-India fragment after the post-Aurangzeb collapse. The state's distinctive history began in 1819 when Qudsia Begum took power as regent — the start of more than a century of female succession unique among Indian princely states: Qudsia (1819–1837), Sikandar (1844–1868), Shah Jahan (1868–1901), Sultan Jahan (1901–1926). The Begums modernised Bhopal under British paramountcy — administrative reform, female education, the All-India Muslim Ladies' Conference, the Sultania Girls' School. Bhopal acceded to India in 1949, two years after Sultan Jahan's grandson Hamidullah Khan attempted to remain independent.

sources.label: Shaharyar M. Khan, The Begums of Bhopal: A Dynasty of Women Rulers in Raj India (2000)

polities.name: Travancore
polities.tooltip: Travancore — princely state 1729–1947, Marthanda Varma to accession
polities.summary: Marthanda Varma's 1729 consolidation from Venad; the most administratively reformed and high-literacy princely state under British paramountcy.
polities.framing: Travancore was consolidated in 1729 by Marthanda Varma from the older Venad principality of southern Kerala. His 1750 dedication of the kingdom to Sri Padmanabhaswamy made the rulers nominal regents (dasa) of the deity — a sovereignty-claim that survived British paramountcy. Travancore under successive maharajahs and the Setu Lakshmi Bayi regency (1924–1931) ran among the most administratively reformed princely states — universal primary education for boys from 1817, for girls from 1859, the 1936 Temple Entry Proclamation that opened Hindu temples to all castes after the Vaikom Satyagraha pressure. C.P. Ramaswami Iyer's 1947 attempt to remain independent failed; Travancore acceded to the Indian Union on 27 August 1947 and merged with Cochin in 1949 to form Travancore-Cochin (Kerala from 1956).
rulers: Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma (1931–1949, last ruling maharaja)

sources.label: Robin Jeffrey, The Decline of Nayar Dominance: Society and Politics in Travancore 1847–1908 (1976)

polities.name: Vijayanagara Empire
polities.tooltip: Vijayanagara Empire — 1336–1646, four dynasties from Hampi
polities.summary: South Indian Hindu empire founded at Hampi by Harihara and Bukka in 1336; broken at Talikota 1565, survived in reduced form to 1646.
polities.framing: Vijayanagara was conceived in the 1330s as the Hindu political-military counter to the Bahmani sultanate (1347) and the Madurai sultanate (1335). Across 310 years and four dynasties — Sangama (1336–1485), Saluva (1485–1505), Tuluva (1505–1570), Aravidu (1570–1646) — the empire ran the longest sustained Hindu-ruled imperial regime in South India after the Cholas. Its peak under Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529) extended from the Krishna river to Cape Comorin and from the western to the eastern coast. The Talikota defeat of 1565 broke the Hampi-centred empire; the Aravidu dynasty held a reduced state from Penukonda then Chandragiri until 1646. The institutional inheritance — temple-centred land tenure, Telugu-Sanskrit literary patronage, the Nayaka governor system that became the post-Vijayanagara south Indian polities (Madurai, Tanjore, Gingee, Ikkeri) — persisted into the colonial period.
rulers: Sangama: Harihara I (1336–1356), Bukka Raya I (1356–1377)
Tuluva: Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529, the empire's peak)
Aravidu: Aliya Rama Raya (regent, killed at Talikota 1565)
Aravidu later rulers from Penukonda and Chandragiri (1570–1646)

sources.label: Burton Stein, Vijayanagara (Cambridge New History of India I.2, 1989)

polities.name: Madurai Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Madurai Sultanate — 1335–1378, southernmost Indian Muslim sultanate
polities.summary: Tughlaq-derived breakaway under Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan; eight sultans in 43 years; ended by Vijayanagara reconquest under Kumara Kampana.
rulers: Five further sultans through three decades

sources.label: Mehrdad Shokoohy, Muslim Architecture of South India: The Sultanate of Ma'bar (2003)

polities.name: Bijapur Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Bijapur (Adil Shahi) Sultanate — 1490–1686, Bahmani-successor
polities.summary: Adil Shahi dynasty from Bijapur; longest-lived of the five Bahmani-successor sultanates; annexed by Aurangzeb after 196 years in 1686.
rulers: Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580–1627; Kitab-i Nauras)

sources.label: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan (2005)

polities.name: Golconda Sultanate
polities.tooltip: Golconda (Qutb Shahi) Sultanate — 1518–1687, Bahmani-successor
polities.summary: Qutb Shahi dynasty from Golconda then Hyderabad; controlled the Coromandel diamond and textile trade; Aurangzeb annexed in 1687.
rulers: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (1580–1612; founded Hyderabad 1591)
Abul Hasan Tana Shah (1672–1687, last sultan)

sources.label: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan (2005)

polities.name: Mysore Kingdom (Wodeyars)
polities.tooltip: Mysore Kingdom — Wodeyar dynasty 1399–1947, with Hyder/Tipu interregnum
polities.summary: Wodeyar dynasty founded 1399; displaced by Hyder Ali 1761; restored by EIC under Krishnaraja III in 1799 as a princely state to 1947.
polities.framing: The Wodeyar (Wadiyar) dynasty was founded at Mysore in 1399 as a Vijayanagara feudatory. After Talikota (1565) the Wodeyars asserted independence, ruling Mysore as a Hindu kingdom for 162 years until 1761, when Hyder Ali — the Wodeyars' Muslim military commander — deposed the maharaja and took power, founding the Mysore Sultanate that ran 1761–1799. After the EIC's 1799 storming of Srirangapatna and Tipu Sultan's death, the EIC restored the five-year-old Krishnaraja III Wodeyar as nominal sovereign under British paramountcy. The 19th-century reformist maharajas (Krishnaraja III, Chamarajendra X, Krishnaraja IV) made Mysore among the most administratively progressive princely states — universal primary education from 1843, the Mysore University (1916), the Krishna Raja Sagara dam, the Mysore Asiatic Pavilion at the 1924 British Empire Exhibition. Mysore acceded to India 9 August 1947 and was reorganised into Karnataka in 1956.
rulers: Raja Wodeyar I (1578–1617; capital shifted to Srirangapatna)
Hyder Ali (1761–1782; Wodeyar deposed, Mysore Sultanate)
Krishnaraja IV (1902–1940), Jayachamaraja (1940–1949, last ruling maharaja)

sources.label: James Manor, Political Change in an Indian State: Mysore 1917–1955 (1977)

polities.name: Ahom Kingdom
polities.tooltip: Ahom Kingdom — 1228–1826, six centuries in upper Assam
polities.summary: Tai-Shan dynasty founded by Sukapha at Charaideo in 1228; ruled upper Assam for 598 years; ended by Burmese invasions and Treaty of Yandabo.
polities.framing: The Ahom kingdom is among the longest continuous regional dynasties in subcontinental history — 598 years from Sukapha's 1228 founding to the 1826 EIC takeover under the Treaty of Yandabo. The Ahoms originated as a small Tai-Shan migration from Mong Mao (modern Yunnan/Myanmar border), assimilated linguistically into Assamese over the 16th–17th centuries, and developed a distinct administrative system: the paik corvée labour structure, the khel occupational guilds, and the buranji historical chronicle tradition (initially in Tai then Assamese). Crucially, the Ahoms repelled seventeen Mughal invasion attempts across the 17th century — the Battle of Saraighat (1671), in which Lachit Borphukan defeated Mirza Raja Ram Singh's Mughal fleet on the Brahmaputra, ended the Mughal effort permanently. The kingdom was destabilised by the Moamoria rebellion (1769–1805) and broken by the Burmese invasions (1817–1826); the EIC takeover ended the dynasty.
rulers: Chakradhwaj Singha (1663–1670; backed Lachit at Saraighat)

sources.label: Edward Gait, A History of Assam (1906; rev. 1933)
Yasmin Saikia, Fragmented Memories: Struggling to be Tai-Ahom in India (2004)

polities.name: Manipur Kingdom
polities.tooltip: Manipur Kingdom — Meitei (Ningthouja) dynasty c. 33 CE through 1949 accession
polities.summary: Meitei (Ningthouja) dynasty by tradition from 33 CE; survived the 1819–26 Burmese Devastation; princely state under EIC paramountcy; acceded to India 1949.
polities.framing: Manipur's Meitei (Ningthouja) ruling lineage is conventionally traced to Pakhangba (33 CE) — among the longest claimed continuous Indian royal lineages. The Manipuri state ran from the Imphal valley with cultural-political reach into the surrounding hills. Vaishnav Hinduism became the court religion under Pamheiba (Garib Niwaz, r. 1709–1748); the Meitei script (Meitei Mayek) and the Sanamahi religion both have ongoing 20th–21st century revival movements. The kingdom was devastated by the Burmese invasion of 1819–1826 (Chahi Taret Khuntakpa); restored by EIC support under Gambhir Singh; survived as a princely state under British paramountcy after the Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 left a child Maharaja under indirect rule. Acceded to India 21 September 1949 under controversial circumstances; statehood 1972; modern Manipur is among the most ethnically contested states in the Indian Union.

date_span.display: Traditional date 33 CE — accession to India 21 September 1949

sources.label: Lal Dena, History of Modern Manipur 1826–1949 (1991)
Gangmumei Kabui, History of Manipur, vol. I: Pre-Colonial Period (1991)

polities.name: Kingdom of Sikkim
polities.tooltip: Kingdom of Sikkim — Namgyal dynasty 1642–1975
polities.summary: Namgyal dynasty consecrated at Yuksom 1642; survived Tibet/Bhutan/Nepal pressure, EIC protectorate (1861), Indian protectorate (1950); merged into India 1975.
